post_text: WIOA Title I served roughly 5 million participants in PY2022 across Adult, Dislocated Worker, and Youth programs. ↵  ↵ That volume runs on two reporting rails most operators treat as separate systems: the Participant Individual Record Layout that feeds the Section 116 performance measures, and the ETA-9130 financial report series that feeds federal cash management. ↵  ↵ The shops that avoid ETA findings keep the case file, the data entry, and the cost allocation aligned to the same participant record in real time. The shops with findings reconcile PIRL and 9130 once a quarter and discover gaps no one can explain six months later. ↵  ↵ If your case management tool and your accounting system disagree about who was served and how much was spent on them, that's the audit risk. ↵  ↵ GrantPipe ties expenditures to grants and participants in one record so the PIRL and 9130 stories tell the same number. ↵  ↵  ↵ ---

Myth: grant reporting software writes your funder reports for you. ↵  ↵ Reality: most "grant reporting" tools only track deadlines. The actual report has two halves — a financial section (budget-vs-actual, expenditure documentation) and a narrative section (activities, outputs, outcomes). Reminders don't produce either one. ↵  ↵ Software can only generate the financial section if it tracks expenditures against approved budget categories during the grant period. Then the budget-vs-actual table populates from posted transactions linked to the grant. ↵  ↵ Tools without expenditure data give you a template. You still fill it in by hand from the GL, line by line, the night before submission. ↵  ↵ When evaluating a tool, ask one question: can it produce the budget-vs-actual table from real posted transactions, or is it just a calendar with a logo. ↵  ↵  ↵ ---

Step 3 of a subaward budget modification: apply the 10% rule before you escalate. ↵  ↵ Under 2 CFR 200.308(e)(4), a non-federal entity may transfer funds among direct cost categories when the total of transfers does not exceed 10% of the total award budget and the change does not alter project scope. Inside that envelope, the pass-through can approve a subrecipient request without going up to the federal awarding agency. ↵  ↵ Step 4 is where most pass-throughs get the sequence wrong. If the modification crosses 10%, changes scope, adds equipment that wasn't budgeted, or touches a category the prime award restricted, federal prior approval is required before the pass-through can approve the subrecipient. ↵  ↵ Tell the subrecipient up front: federal prior approval typically runs four to twelve weeks depending on the agency. That sets the modification request deadline to roughly three months before the change needs to take effect. ↵  ↵ Document the 10% calculation in the file. Auditors look for the math, not just the email. ↵  ↵  ↵ ---

A donor-advised fund is not a donor. ↵  ↵ The DAF is an account at a sponsoring 501(c)(3) — Fidelity Charitable, Schwab Charitable, Vanguard Charitable, or a community foundation. The donor contributes assets, takes the deduction immediately, and then recommends grants from the account at any future time. Legal control sits with the sponsor; the donor holds advisory rights. ↵  ↵ Operationally this matters because the check arrives in the sponsor's name. Memo line might say "donor advised grant" with no individual attribution. If your CRM records that gift under "Fidelity Charitable," you've just lost the relationship. ↵  ↵ The fix is a stewardship rule: any DAF distribution gets routed for investigation before it posts. The underlying donor is usually identifiable from the cover letter or the sponsor's portal. Code the gift to the human; tag the DAF as the vehicle. ↵  ↵ The acknowledgement letter goes to the donor, not the sponsor. The sponsor already has the deduction on file. ↵  ↵  ↵ ---

AmpliFund typically runs $15,000 to $50,000 per year, with multi-month implementations. ↵  ↵ That price tag exists because AmpliFund (now part of Bonterra) was built for government agencies and large nonprofits managing complex federal portfolios. Budget-versus-actual tied to grant line items, Uniform Guidance awareness, and SF-425-aware workflows are real strengths. Organizations running $10M+ in federal funds get genuine value from the depth. ↵  ↵ The mid-sized question is different. If your federal portfolio is two or three grants and your team is one finance person and one program lead, the implementation tax is the actual cost — not the license fee. You pay for capability you cannot operate. ↵  ↵ The honest evaluation: list the federal grants you actually manage, the staff hours you have for compliance work, and what your audit findings have looked like for the past three cycles. If the answer is "two grants, one person, no findings," AmpliFund is probably oversized. ↵  ↵ If the answer is "fifteen grants across four federal agencies and a single audit every year," it isn't. ↵  ↵  ↵ ---

HUD HOME rental housing compliance lasts 15 to 20 years after the project closes. ↵  ↵ Affordable housing nonprofits running HOME, CDBG, and ESG grants live with a compliance horizon that outlasts most staff tenures. Davis-Bacon wage documentation has to survive the construction phase. Matching fund records have to be reconstructable a decade later. Affordability period rent and income certifications run annually until the obligation expires. ↵  ↵ The standard nonprofit CRM does not handle this. Donor records weren't designed to track a tenant income recertification due in 2039. ↵  ↵ What works in practice: separate the development-phase restricted funds from the operations-phase restricted funds inside the accounting system, store the regulatory file (HUD agreement, Davis-Bacon payrolls, environmental review) against the project as a permanent attachment, and put the affordability period end date on a calendar with annual review triggers — not in someone's head. ↵  ↵ The institutional system has to outlive the people. That's the design constraint. ↵  ↵  ↵ ---

The single audit threshold moved to $1,000,000 in federal expenditures, effective for fiscal years ending September 30, 2025 or later. The old figure is out of date. ↵  ↵ Most organizations crossing the threshold for the first time discover their documentation isn't where the auditors expect it. The OMB Compliance Supplement defines what gets tested and which programs each requirement applies to. The work is mapping that test list to documentation you already have on hand — not assembling it during fieldwork. ↵  ↵ A practical prep approach: build a folder structure organized by compliance requirement (allowable costs, cash management, eligibility, equipment, matching, period of performance, procurement, program income, reporting, subrecipient monitoring, special tests). Keep a running index of where each piece lives. When the auditor asks for the procurement file, you don't go hunting. ↵  ↵ Free download — the 2 CFR 200 Audit Prep Checklist organizes the documentation auditors test, by compliance requirement: grantpipe.com/lead-magnets/2-cfr-200-audit-prep-checklist ↵  ↵  ↵ ---

Salesforce Nonprofit runs $60–$165 per user per month plus $30K–$100K in implementation. Blackbaud runs $5,000–$15,000+ per year with multi-year contracts and exit penalties. ↵  ↵ Both are designed for large nonprofits. Salesforce gives flexibility at high implementation cost — and you need an admin or managed services to keep it running. Blackbaud gives nonprofit specificity with a legacy interface and contract lock-in. ↵  ↵ The mid-sized question is rarely "which one." It's "do we have the administrative capacity to operate either of these without burning a development hire on system maintenance." Under $5M annual revenue, both are usually oversized. Over $20M with dedicated dev ops and IT, the comparison is worth running carefully. ↵  ↵ Between those two thresholds is the awkward middle where the platforms over-serve and the spreadsheets under-serve. That gap is where most $500K–$10M nonprofits actually live. ↵  ↵ What's your administrative capacity look like — are you sizing the tool to the work, or sizing the work to the tool you bought. ↵  ↵  ↵ ---

Finance and operations staff at mid-sized nonprofits usually wear three hats: finance, HR, and ops. No dedicated CFO. Often no dedicated controller. ↵  ↵ The daily list is QuickBooks reconciliation, grant drawdown processing, payroll allocation across restricted funds, audit prep, and vendor management. Sometimes board reporting. Often benefits administration. The tooling has to enforce documentation without the implementation tax of Sage Intacct or Blackbaud Financial Edge. ↵  ↵ Question for the finance/ops people in this network: what's the one task in your week that should be twenty minutes and somehow always becomes two hours. ↵  ↵ For me when I've watched this work, it's almost always payroll allocation across restricted funds — because the time-and-effort documentation lives in one system, the GL allocation lives in another, and reconciling them is manual. What's yours. ↵  ↵  ↵ ---

Custom fields buried in a notes column aren't data. They're archaeology. ↵  ↵ Every nonprofit tracks something the standard donor schema doesn't capture — cultivation score, board relationship, interest area, legacy intent, ask amount, fiscal sponsor, project code. When that lives in a free-text "notes" field, it can't be filtered, exported, reported on, or used to segment a campaign. It exists, but only for the person who wrote it down. ↵  ↵ The fix is typed custom fields: text, number, date, select, or boolean, defined per entity (donor, grant, gift). Once the field has a type, it shows up in filters and reports the same way the standard fields do. The data stays structured from the moment it's entered. ↵  ↵ The discipline is naming and pruning. Every custom field added is a column someone has to maintain. Review the list once a year and delete what no one fills in. ↵  ↵ GrantPipe lets you define custom fields on donors, grants, and gifts that flow into filters, exports, and reports alongside the built-in fields — no notes-column workarounds.

New York's CHAR500 audit threshold sits at $1 million in gross revenue plus support — exactly the same dollar figure as the federal single audit threshold, but governed by NY Executive Law 172-b, not 2 CFR 200.501. ↵  ↵ Same number, different authority. A New York charity that crosses $1M in total revenue and also expends $1M in federal awards in the same year owes both the state-required independent audit under Article 7-A and a single audit under the OMB 2 CFR Part 200 October 2024 revision. Coordinated through one CPA engagement, but two distinct compliance obligations with separate reporting paths. ↵  ↵ Below $1M but above $250K of gross revenue plus support, New York requires a CPA review — not the full audit. Below $250K, neither. ↵  ↵ The CHAR500 itself is due May 15 for calendar-year filers, four months and fifteen days after fiscal year end. Filing fees range from $25 to $750 depending on Article 7-A and EPTL registration. Most rejection notices come from missing the Form 990 attachment, missing the second officer signature, or miscalculating the fee tier. ↵  ↵ GrantPipe tracks CHAR500 deadlines next to federal SF-425 cadence and the audit engagement so the May 15 due date does not collide with single audit fieldwork unsupervised. ↵  ↵  ↵ ---

Myth: a subrecipient with no single audit history is a low-risk subrecipient. ↵  ↵ Reality: 2 CFR 200.332(b) requires the pass-through entity to evaluate risk before issuing the sub-award, and "no audit history" is not the same as "clean audit history." Many smaller subrecipients have never crossed the $1,000,000 single audit threshold in any prior year. The audit silence is informational absence, not risk evidence. ↵  ↵ When a subrecipient lacks audit history, the regulation still requires a documented assessment. The weight shifts to the pre-award questionnaire, financial statement review if available, organizational references, and adequacy of financial management systems. A composite risk score under 1.5 across the six factors in 200.332(b) suggests low risk; between 1.5 and 2.5 suggests medium; above 2.5 suggests high. ↵  ↵ The most common audit finding on subrecipient monitoring is not that the monitoring was inadequate. It is that the pre-award risk assessment was never done. Auditors look for the document specifically because the regulation requires it before the sub-award is issued — and its absence is an automatic finding that cannot be cured after the fact. ↵  ↵ Document the rationale, score each factor, and file the assessment alongside the sub-award agreement. The matrix is the answer when the auditor asks how the risk rating was reached. ↵  ↵  ↵ ---

Step 2 of a nonprofit pledge write-off: determine the treatment under FASB ASC 958-605 before you book the entry. ↵  ↵ The instinct from for-profit accounting is to debit bad debt expense and credit the receivable. Under ASC 958, that is wrong. The write-off of an unconditional pledge receivable reduces the allowance for uncollectible pledges and the pledge receivable — provided the allowance was appropriately estimated when the pledge was originally recorded. It is contra-revenue mechanics, not an operating expense. ↵  ↵ If the original allowance was set to zero, the write-off has nowhere to go but contribution revenue. Organizations that use a blanket zero-allowance policy create exactly that scenario: every write-off becomes a reduction to current-year contribution revenue on the Statement of Activities. ↵  ↵ Step 3 is approval. Typical thresholds under ASC 958-605 documentation discipline: under $1,000 approved by the finance director, $1,000 to $10,000 by the executive director, over $10,000 by the board. Whatever your policy specifies, the written approval must precede the journal entry. ↵  ↵ Multi-year pledges add one more wrinkle. Per ASC 958-605-30-6, multi-year pledges carry a present-value discount that unwinds annually. When the pledge is written off, the unamortized discount on the unpaid portion must be eliminated proportionally. Leaving it in place overstates the discount contra-asset. ↵  ↵  ↵ ---

A grant expenditure report is not a budget-versus-actual report. ↵  ↵ The two documents look similar on paper. Both compare what was spent against the approved budget by category. The difference sits in the legal weight. A budget-versus-actual is an internal management tool. A grant expenditure report is a funder-facing certification — signed, submitted, and binding. Signing it carries compliance responsibility for the truth of the numbers. ↵  ↵ For federal awards, the standard expenditure report is the SF-425 Federal Financial Report. Under 2 CFR 200.328, financial reports are due no less than annually and within 90 days of the end of the award period. The SF-425 captures cumulative obligations, period-specific expenditures, federal cash on hand, program income, and indirect cost rate. ↵  ↵ The reconciliation rule is non-negotiable. Every dollar shown on the SF-425 must trace to the grantee's general ledger by grant fund code for the corresponding period. A discrepancy between the submitted report and the accounting records is an audit finding. Single audits routinely flag this. The funder may refuse to reimburse the questioned costs and require corrective action. ↵  ↵ Practical discipline: pull the GL by grant fund code, reconcile to the planned SF-425 numbers, resolve any variance, then submit. Never the other order. ↵  ↵  ↵ ---

WizeHive Zengine annual contracts run roughly $15,000 to $40,000, with implementations commonly stretching past 90 days. ↵  ↵ Pricing is not published. G2 reviewer estimates and Capterra "Contact Vendor" listings are the public anchors. The product is positioned as a low-code grants platform — every customer configures forms, workflows, and reports themselves or pays WizeHive's services team to do it. Grantmakers running custom application processes, multi-stage review panels, and corporate foundation workflows get genuine value from that flexibility. ↵  ↵ The fit problem starts when grant-receiving nonprofits evaluate it on a peer recommendation. Zengine has no donor CRM. Individual gifts, recurring donations, and donor retention live in a separate subscription. The product's language and sales motion are built around the entity cutting checks, not receiving them. For a $500K to $10M nonprofit managing two or three federal grants and a foundation portfolio, the configuration burden is the real cost — not the license fee. ↵  ↵ The honest evaluation question: does your workflow genuinely require custom application forms and review panels, or are you a grant recipient looking for compliance and reporting? If it is the second one, a packaged product ships in days, not 90. ↵  ↵ GAO-16-573 reports that federal grantees spend a median of 40% of administrative time on compliance documentation. The platform that helps cuts that median, not the platform that takes a quarter to configure. ↵  ↵  ↵ ---

The NEA awarded $174.5 million to arts organizations across all 50 states in FY2023, and most of those grants required 1:1 matching documented contemporaneously. ↵  ↵ That last word — contemporaneously — is where museums get burned. NEA project grants typically require the organization to document non-federal contributions equal to the federal award. Match can come from earned revenue, foundation grants, non-federal government awards, and in-kind contributions. What it cannot do is appear retroactively. An organization that assembles match documentation after the award period ends does not have match documentation; it has a reconstruction project that auditors recognize on sight. ↵  ↵ Museums managing NEA, NEH, and IMLS awards simultaneously face three overlapping compliance frameworks under 2 CFR 200, plus state arts council pass-throughs, plus private foundation grants from places like Mellon and Getty. Each one with its own reporting format. NEA reports through REACH. NEH preservation grants restrict funds narrowly to the approved conservation activity — prior approval required before any reallocation. IMLS Museums for America awards layer program-specific deliverables on top of standard 200 financial requirements. ↵  ↵ Multi-year exhibition grants compound the problem. Spending in Year 2 on activities budgeted for Year 1 may require prior approval and documented reallocation. Cumulative tracking is not a reporting convenience — it is the compliance mechanism. ↵  ↵  ↵ ---

Donor CRM and grant accounting records describe the same funders from two different operational angles, and that is exactly why they drift apart. ↵  ↵ Development enters a gift when the award letter arrives. Finance posts the receipt when cash clears. Two workflows, two timestamps, two restriction classifications, two amounts (pledged versus net of fees). Without an annual reconciliation, the gap compounds until no one can reliably answer "how much restricted funding did we receive from Funder X this year." ↵  ↵ Four discrepancy types account for almost all the variance. Type 1: CRM-only — gift entered but never posted in accounting. Type 2: accounting-only — government grant that bypassed development entirely. Type 3: amount mismatch — full pledged amount in CRM, first installment in accounting. Type 4: classification mismatch — development called it unrestricted general support; finance read the grant agreement and coded it restricted. ↵  ↵ The tie-breaker is always the source document. Grant agreement section reference, award letter, signed pledge card. Not staff recollection. Run the full reconciliation annually before audit fieldwork. Spot-check monthly for funders representing more than 10% of restricted revenue. ↵  ↵ Free download — the Donor-to-Grant Reconciliation Template walks through the matching table, discrepancy classification, resolution documentation, and reconciliation summary: grantpipe.com/lead-magnets/donor-to-grant-reconciliation-template ↵  ↵  ↵ ---

DonorPerfect publishes a 93% retention rate and a 13-year average customer tenure. Those numbers are real. They reflect a mature donor CRM that teams build operations around and stay on. ↵  ↵ The honest comparison with GrantPipe is not "which one is better" — it is which question the Executive Director most often needs answered. If the question is "who gave, when, how much, what campaign did they respond to," DonorPerfect's reporting is fast and the workflow is well-designed for fundraising. If the question is "what is the current balance of the State Housing Grant fund," DonorPerfect holds a fund designation label but not a fund balance. Someone in finance calculates the answer from a separate source. That calculation may or may not be current. ↵  ↵ The Nonprofit Finance Fund 2025 survey found 36% of nonprofits ended FY2024 with an operating deficit, and organizations managing restricted grants without integrated compliance tracking spent an average of 11 additional hours per month assembling manual reports. Eleven hours a month is more than a full work week per quarter spent on data assembly that should be a system output. ↵  ↵ The decision framework is simpler than feature comparisons. Draw a circle around what the ED needs every week. If the circle contains restricted fund balances and grant compliance status, the unified system removes the coordination cost. If it does not, DonorPerfect covers it. ↵  ↵  ↵ ---

Board treasurers carry personal fiduciary exposure for an organization they see for two hours a month. ↵  ↵ The BoardSource Leading with Intent 2021 survey found 75% of board members rate their own financial literacy as basic or below. That is not a character flaw — it is structural. Volunteer boards are composed for governance breadth, not accounting depth. The treasurer is liable for restricted fund misuse they "knew or should have known" about, while reviewing a Statement of Activities that reports net assets with donor restrictions as a single aggregate line. ↵  ↵ FASB ASC 958 does not require grant-level detail on the face of the statements. A nonprofit managing 10 restricted grants can satisfy the standard with one number. The treasurer either trusts that number or asks for a supporting schedule, which usually arrives Friday evening before a Tuesday meeting via spreadsheet. ↵  ↵ GAO-24-106173 reported that 17% of federal award spending from 2017 to 2021 was linked to severe and persistent single audit findings. Median audit costs for $1M to $10M budgets run $10,000 to $45,000, with single audits adding $5,000 to $20,000 on top. ↵  ↵ Question for board treasurers and finance committee chairs: what is the verification step you wish you had between Friday's packet and Tuesday's vote — and how often does that gap actually get closed before you sign Form 990? ↵  ↵  ↵ ---

The split between pre-award tools and post-award tools is the single biggest reason grant data goes stale. ↵  ↵ Most nonprofits run an Instrumentl or GrantHub subscription for the pipeline, then re-key the awarded grant into a spreadsheet or QuickBooks class for compliance tracking. The same grant gets modeled twice, in two systems, with two custodians, and two slightly different sets of facts. By month six of the award, the pipeline tool says "awarded" with a stale amount, the accounting system shows posted expenses, and no one is sure which restriction language is the latest. ↵  ↵ The architectural fix is to make the opportunity and the grant the same record at different lifecycle stages. Pre-award fields stay editable through prospect, LOI, and applied. On award, post-award fields open up — reporting schedule, fund restrictions, allocation rules — and the pre-award history becomes read-only. No re-keying because there is no handoff. ↵  ↵ Default stage probabilities anchor the forecast: prospect 10%, LOI 30%, applied 50%, awarded 100%, declined 0%. Override per opportunity when funder history justifies it. AFP's Fundraising Effectiveness Project shows cold application win rates in the 10-20% range, which is what the prospect default reflects. ↵  ↵ GrantPipe runs the pipeline, the awarded grant, and the restricted fund as one connected record so the forecast a board sees is the same forecast the development director and the finance lead are running on. ↵  ↵  ↵ ---

Audit fees for organizations stuck at the 40 percent major-program coverage threshold typically run $8,000 to $20,000 higher per cycle than for comparable low-risk auditees. ↵  ↵ The five low-risk criteria under 2 CFR 200.520 are mostly inside management's control: a clean Single Audit two years running, no material weaknesses in internal controls over major programs, no GAGAS qualified opinion, no fraud findings affecting major programs, and timely Federal Audit Clearinghouse submission. ↵  ↵ The catch is that you cannot reverse-engineer eligibility at audit time. The two prior fiscal years either qualify or they do not. ↵  ↵ The shops that consistently keep low-risk status track the criteria themselves quarter by quarter, the same way they track cash. The shops that lose it find out from the auditor in March. ↵  ↵ Per the AICPA Government Audit Quality Center benchmarking work, the additional testing required for non-low-risk auditees is the single largest avoidable line item in most Single Audit engagements. ↵  ↵ GrantPipe surfaces low-risk status indicators alongside grant compliance so the criteria do not get rediscovered at fieldwork.

Myth: interest earned on a federal advance drawdown counts as program income. ↵  ↵ Reality: it does not. Program income is governed by 2 CFR 200.307 and means revenue earned by the recipient that is directly generated by activities supported by the federal award. Interest on cash advances is a separate animal handled under 2 CFR 200.305(b)(9), which requires recipients to remit interest above $500 per year to the HHS Program Support Center. ↵  ↵ The two get conflated because both involve money sitting in the recipient's bank account that was not in the original budget. They are not the same thing and they get reported on different schedules. ↵  ↵ The other place this matters: the additive-versus-deductive treatment election under 2 CFR 200.307. Once made at award time, that election is binding for the life of the award. Most program officers never ask about it until the auditor does, and by then changing it requires retroactive correction. ↵  ↵ If your sub-award says nothing about program income treatment, that is itself a finding waiting to happen.

Steps 5 and 6 of the in-kind contribution valuation workflow are where most organizations create their next audit finding. ↵  ↵ Step 5 is the journal entry. Under ASU 2020-07, debit the asset account (food inventory, supplies, property) or the relevant expense account if the goods are consumed in program delivery, and credit contribution revenue with or without donor restrictions depending on intent. Do not net in-kind gifts against expenses. Netting is the most common error and it understates both revenue and program expense on the 990. ↵  ↵ Step 6 is the donor acknowledgment letter. IRS rules require written acknowledgment for any contribution of $250 or more. For in-kind gifts, the letter describes the goods or services in enough detail to support the donor's deduction but does not state a value — that is the donor's responsibility to substantiate. ↵  ↵ The standard took effect for fiscal years beginning after June 15, 2021. Most organizations updated their journal entries and forgot to update their footnote disclosures. Audit firms catch this in year three.

Pass-through entity, defined at 2 CFR 200.1: a non-federal entity that receives a federal award and provides a sub-award to a subrecipient that carries out part of the federal program. ↵  ↵ Pass-through status is functional, not optional. The moment a recipient issues a sub-award, it becomes a pass-through entity for that portion of the award and inherits the responsibilities under 2 CFR 200.332. ↵  ↵ Two examples that show how broad the definition is. A state department of health receives a $5M HHS grant and sub-awards $3M to 12 county health agencies — the state is the pass-through. A nonprofit receives a $1.2M DOL workforce grant and sub-awards $400,000 to a training partner for one program track — the nonprofit is a pass-through for that $400,000. ↵  ↵ The 2 CFR 200.332 obligations include classifying every downstream relationship as subrecipient or contractor, performing risk assessments before issuing sub-awards, and monitoring throughout the period of performance. Pass-through amounts also flow onto the SEFA filed with the Federal Audit Clearinghouse. ↵  ↵ If your organization writes checks to a partner under a federal grant, you are probably a pass-through entity. The right time to find out is before the agreement is signed.

Neon One is not a single product. It is a portfolio assembled through acquisition: Neon CRM at the center, Arts People for arts organizations, Rallybound for peer-to-peer, and a few others stacked around them. ↵  ↵ The pitch is vendor consolidation. The reality for buyers is uneven module quality and a UX that varies depending on which acquired team built the surface you are looking at. Cross-module reporting is the place this shows up first — pulling a clean view across donor activity, event registrations, and grant tracking usually requires either a custom report build or an export-to-Excel step. ↵  ↵ For organizations that mostly need donor management, Neon CRM on its own is a reasonable choice. For organizations that need donor CRM plus active grant management in one system, the bundle approach asks the buyer to integrate modules that were not designed together. ↵  ↵ The tradeoff to know going in: you trade a single login for a sprawl that grows as Neon One acquires more products. Mid-sized nonprofits that already feel stretched thin tend to feel that sprawl most.

Church donor management runs on a weekly cadence — tithes, offerings, designated gifts — not the quarterly cycle most nonprofit CRMs assume. ↵  ↵ A typical secular nonprofit drops appeal letters in Q4, runs an end-of-year campaign, and cultivates major donors across a 12-month plan. A church processes giving every Sunday and every online gift in between, with designated funds for building campaigns, missions, benevolence, and youth programs running in parallel year-round. ↵  ↵ When the same church also receives grants for secular programs — early childhood, food pantry, after-school — the data model gets more complicated. Restricted grant funds cannot be commingled with the General Fund or the Building Fund in the books, even if one bank account holds all of it. ↵  ↵ Most church-specific tools handle the giving side well and ignore grants entirely. Most nonprofit CRMs handle grants and treat weekly tithing as an afterthought. The shops that get this right pick a system that separates donor giving records from restricted grant funds at the data layer, then maps both up to the appropriate fund balance under FASB ASC 958. ↵  ↵ If your accounting system and your donor system disagree about which fund a check belongs to, you have a reconciliation problem waiting to happen.

A sub-award that is missing a required provision is a compliance finding even when the program runs perfectly. ↵  ↵ 2 CFR 200.332(a) lists the data elements that every sub-award document must contain before execution: federal award identification number, federal award date, sub-award amount, federal award project description, name of the federal awarding agency, CFDA/Assistance Listing number and title, indirect cost rate, and a statement of applicable requirements. Missing any one of them is a citable finding regardless of how well the subrecipient performs. ↵  ↵ The most common gap on the audited list is the indirect cost rate — pass-through entities often leave it blank or use language that does not reference the negotiated rate or the de minimis 15 percent rate at 2 CFR 200.414(f). ↵  ↵ The Subrecipient Agreement Checklist walks through every required provision under 2 CFR 200.332(a), the additional provisions that reduce monitoring risk, and program-specific additions that some federal programs require on top of the baseline. Use it before the agreement is signed, not after. ↵  ↵ Free download in the resources section of the GrantPipe site.

Little Green Light at $45 to $200 per month versus GrantPipe at $329 to $1,079. The right answer depends on one variable: do you actively manage federal or foundation grants, or just donors. ↵  ↵ Little Green Light is a strong tool for organizations under $500K in budget that are donor-funded and need clean gift entry, acknowledgments, and basic reporting. Any staff member can learn it without training. The ceiling shows up around $500K to $1M in budget when reporting needs go beyond what an Excel export can handle and when grant management enters the picture. ↵  ↵ GrantPipe assumes grants from day one. Restricted-fund tracking, deadline calendars, budget-versus-actual against grant budgets, and donor CRM all in one system, priced flat per organization rather than per contact. The tradeoff is more surface area than a $250K all-donor nonprofit needs. ↵  ↵ The wrong reason to pick either tool is current pricing. Replatforming in 18 months costs more than the price difference in any direction. ↵  ↵ If your organization is past $500K in budget and your grant load is growing, the cheap tool stops being cheap when you outgrow it.

A grant writer starts the year with 30 to 50 prospects on a spreadsheet. By Q2 the deadlines have shifted, two program officers have changed jobs, the organization has pivoted one program, and the spreadsheet has not kept up. ↵  ↵ The writing itself is maybe 70 percent of the role. The other 30 is pipeline hygiene — tracking deadlines, reusing narrative content across submissions, and handing off won awards to the grants manager with the budget intact. ↵  ↵ The handoff is where most awarded grants quietly start losing money. The proposal said one thing, the grants manager inherits another, and by the second drawdown the budget categories no longer line up with what the funder approved. ↵  ↵ Question for the grant writers and development directors here: when you win a grant, what does your handoff to compliance actually look like? Is it a meeting, a folder, an email thread, or a system that carries the budget and narrative forward without retyping? ↵  ↵ The answer says a lot about how your post-award reporting will go six months from now.

The average mid-sized nonprofit uses three donor segments — everyone, major donors, and lapsed donors. Organizations with strong retention programs use fifteen or more. ↵  ↵ The difference is not the technology. It is whether the segmentation tool stays current as donor records change, or whether it requires a manual Excel export every time someone wants a list. ↵  ↵ Donor segmentation in GrantPipe is a saved-filter system. Build a segment once using any combination of giving history, recency, source, fund, custom fields, and demographics. The segment stays current automatically as gifts post and contact records update. A segment named "Major Gift Prospects — Not Yet Asked" might filter on lifetime giving between $5,000 and $24,999, last gift within 18 months, no open ask in the pipeline, and a custom field flagging board referral. ↵  ↵ The segments drive everything downstream — appeal lists, stewardship workflows, board reports, and renewal campaigns — without re-exporting. When a donor's giving crosses a threshold, they move into the new segment automatically the next time the filter runs. ↵  ↵ If your org is operating on three segments because building more is too much work, the tool is the bottleneck.

Myth: software marketed as "grant tracking" handles post-award compliance. ↵ ↵ Reality: most of it covers the pre-award pipeline only. Pre-award is grant discovery, application stages, deadline reminders, award decisions. Post-award is restricted fund balances by budget category, expenditures linked to grant lines, and SF-425-ready compliance reports pulled from real posted transactions. ↵ ↵ The two are different problems with different data models. A tool that tracks "applied → awarded → reporting" without ever touching the GL is a calendar with a logo. It cannot answer the only question that matters at audit: did the dollars spent against this grant match the approved budget categories. ↵ ↵ Three capabilities separate compliance tools from pipeline trackers — restricted fund balance tracking by budget category, expenditure documentation linked to individual grant budget lines, and compliance report generation from actual expenditure data. If a tool cannot do those three, it tracks grants informally. ↵ ↵ Foundant GrantHub Pro was sunset January 31, 2026, and never covered restricted fund tracking in the first place. Buyers searching for a GrantHub replacement should be very clear about which problem they are actually solving. ↵ ↵ The mistake most buyers make is searching for "grant tracking software" when what they actually need is post-award compliance.

Step 4 of responding to a Single Audit finding: draft the Corrective Action Plan with all five required elements under 2 CFR 200.511(c). ↵ ↵ The five elements are the finding reference number, the auditee's position (agree or disagree), the specific corrective action, the named responsible party with title, and the target completion date. Vague language like "management will strengthen controls" is not acceptable and produces a follow-up letter from the awarding agency. ↵ ↵ Step 5 is committing realistic timelines. Aggressive but achievable — typically 30 to 180 days depending on complexity. A policy update closes in 30. A system implementation may need 180. Missed CAP deadlines become a finding in the next year's audit, which is how organizations end up in repeat-finding territory. ↵ ↵ The package is due the earlier of 30 days after the auditor's report or nine months after fiscal year-end, per 2 CFR 200.512(a)(1). The CAP is part of that package and travels with the report to the Federal Audit Clearinghouse at harvester.census.gov. ↵ ↵ A strong CAP reads like a project plan, not a compliance document. "The CFO will update the procurement policy by May 31, circulate it with attestations, and present completed attestations to the audit committee at the June meeting" is what auditors and program officers want to see.

The Unique Entity Identifier is a 12-character alphanumeric code assigned by SAM.gov. It replaced DUNS effective April 4, 2022. ↵ ↵ Without an active UEI and current SAM.gov registration, a federal grant recipient cannot draw funds — even on an award already in flight. SAM.gov registration is valid for 12 months. There is no grace period. A registration that lapses on Tuesday halts payments on Wednesday. ↵ ↵ The UEI is not the EIN. The EIN is the IRS tax identifier. The UEI is the SAM.gov procurement and grants identifier. Both are required, both go on federal applications, and they are different numbers stored in different systems. ↵ ↵ Domestic activation runs 7 to 14 business days, with IRS verification typically the bottleneck. Renewal reminders go out 60 days before expiration. The recommended practice is to start renewal on the first reminder, not the last one. ↵ ↵ Pass-through entities have a separate obligation under 2 CFR 200.332: collect the subrecipient's UEI before executing any sub-award and check the SAM.gov exclusions list. If the subrecipient is not registered, the pass-through cannot legally execute the agreement. ↵ ↵ Registration lapses are among the top five administrative reasons OMB cites for delayed grant drawdowns. The fix is calendar discipline, not a software purchase.

Bloomerang Standard runs $125 per month for up to 1,000 records and Pro runs $249 per month for up to 5,000. Capterra puts it at 4.66 out of 5 across more than 1,286 reviews — second highest in the nonprofit CRM category. ↵ ↵ The product earns those numbers honestly on the donor side. The retention dashboard, lapse-risk indicators, and donor timeline are the most developed in the under-$300 tier. Development staff coming off spreadsheets find it intuitive on day one. ↵ ↵ The gap is grants. Bloomerang has no grant lifecycle module — not a thin one, a complete absence. No restricted fund tracking, no budget-versus-actual against grant line items, no compliance report generation. An organization that wins a $500,000 federal grant cannot model where the restricted dollars go inside Bloomerang. ↵ ↵ The result for grant-receiving nonprofits is a parallel system: Bloomerang for donors, a spreadsheet or standalone tracker for grants. Duplicate entry, manual reconciliation, and compliance records that drift away from CRM records by month six. ↵ ↵ The honest evaluation question is whether the organization is donor-funded or grant-funded. Donor-funded under $5M with no restricted grant exposure — Bloomerang is a strong choice. Grant-receiving with three or more active awards — the parallel-system tax becomes the actual cost. ↵ ↵ Per-record pricing also keeps climbing as the database grows.

A church that receives a USDA Community Food Projects grant cannot spend a single grant dollar on worship services, religious instruction, or staff time supporting religious activities — even if the food pantry runs out of the same building. ↵ ↵ Federal funding requires documented separation between grant-funded secular programs and religious activity. That means tracking personnel time by grant-funded versus religious duties, allocating facility costs proportionally, and documenting that grant participants were not required to participate in religious activities. Reconstructed records at audit time do not satisfy the standard. ↵ ↵ The data structure most congregations already use makes this harder than it looks. Building Fund, Missions Fund, General Fund, and youth program designations are restricted in the church's internal sense. They are not the same as grant restriction. Commingling a federal award into the General Fund creates Form 990 reporting errors and audit exposure. ↵ ↵ There are roughly 380,000 religious congregations in the U.S. with combined annual revenue of $100-$120 billion (Duke National Congregations Study). Faith-based organizations account for about 32% of all U.S. charitable giving (Giving USA 2023). FEMA Public Assistance, USDA Community Food Projects, and historic preservation grants are the most common federal entry points. ↵ ↵ The compliance fix is fund separation enforced at the transaction level — not a tag retroactively applied to a journal entry someone already posted to the wrong account.

Federal grant closeout is not a single event. It starts 90 days before the period of performance ends and continues for 3 to 7 years after the grant formally closes. ↵ ↵ The 90-day mark is for budget-versus-actual review, no-cost extension decisions, and subrecipient closeout planning. The 30-day mark is for equipment review (capitalization threshold $10,000 under 2 CFR 200.313), unspent funds calculation, and the final obligation lock. The final week is for expenditure lock and reconciliation to the dollar against the accounting system. ↵ ↵ Post-period, the final SF-425 is due within 120 calendar days for most agencies, 90 days for some HUD programs. The cumulative federal expenditures on that report must match the GL exactly. A discrepancy is an audit finding. ↵ ↵ Record retention under 2 CFR 200.334 is 3 years from the date of final expenditure report submission — not from the period end date. USDA and HUD programs commonly require 7 years. Records involved in pending audits, litigation, or claims must be retained until the matter resolves. ↵ ↵ Free download — the Grant Closeout Checklist walks through every phase from 90 days out to post-closeout file archiving and staff debrief: grantpipe.com/lead-magnets/grant-closeout-checklist

Bloomerang at $125-$249 per month versus Keela at $99-$299 per month. Both target the under-$300 mid-market. Both ship modern donor CRMs. Neither handles grant compliance. ↵ ↵ Bloomerang wins on donor retention analytics — the lapse-risk dashboard and donor timeline are the most developed in this tier. Keela wins narrowly on grant tracking because Bloomerang has none and Keela has a basic module covering funder records, grant amounts, status, and deadline reminders. Basic, not compliance-grade. ↵ ↵ For an Executive Director who signs a federal grant agreement, that distinction is the whole game. The ED takes on personal accountability for fund separation and compliance reporting under the agreement. Neither platform tracks restricted fund balances by budget category. Neither produces budget-versus-actual against approved grant line items. Neither generates compliance documentation that survives a Single Audit. ↵ ↵ Three-year cost on 2,500 contacts is roughly $6,120 for Bloomerang and $5,400 for Keela, both scaling with contact volume. Add a separate grant tool for compliance and the gap closes against any unified option. ↵ ↵ The Fifty & Fifty 2025 Nonprofit Peer Report found only 33.3% of nonprofits rate their CRM as effective. The unsatisfied 66.7% are usually managing problems their CRM was not built to solve. ↵ ↵ If donors are the entire universe — Bloomerang. If grants are part of it — neither, by themselves.

Program directors own program outcomes and the budget that funds them — usually with no formal finance training and no purpose-built tool for the budget-to-delivery connection. ↵ ↵ The standard setup at mid-sized nonprofits: program budget in Excel built from the award template, actuals in QuickBooks, reconciliation once a month if someone has time. When a program director approves a subrecipient invoice or authorizes a venue deposit, there is no live check against the remaining budget line. The check happens 30 days later, by which point the overage is booked. ↵ ↵ Cost disallowance was named one of the five most common Single Audit findings in the GAO's April 2024 analysis (GAO-24-106173), contributing to the 17% of federal spending linked to severe findings. The Center for Effective Philanthropy puts reporting alone at 6 to 8 hours per grant per year. Multiply by 10 to 20 active grants and a program director loses one to two weeks annually to report assembly. ↵ ↵ Question for the program directors and grants managers reading this: when you approve a vendor invoice, can you see the remaining balance on that grant's budget line right then, or do you find out at month-end. Does the disconnect between program tracking and the GL ever surface a 70%-consumed warning early enough to actually file a budget modification.

Under 2 CFR 200.430, payroll charges to federal awards must be supported by after-the-fact records reflecting actual time worked — not budget percentages. Personnel costs are 65-75% of expenditures on most human services awards and the largest single category of disallowed costs in federal Single Audits. ↵ ↵ The two-system problem is where this falls apart. Payroll runs in ADP or QuickBooks. The grants manager keeps a salary allocation spreadsheet. Finance posts journal entries to move costs from a general payroll account to grant-specific accounts. The time-and-effort certifications are PDFs in a shared folder. At audit time, the auditor wants three things lined up — the certification, the allocation entry matching the certification, and the payroll register confirming gross pay. Reconciling three sources for every employee, every month, every award, is the manual work that consumes days and still leaves gaps. ↵ ↵ The most common finding is allocation percentages that do not match the certified time — usually because the allocation was entered at budget percentages instead of certified ones. The second most common is late certifications signed more than 30 days after period end. Both create dollar-for-dollar repayment exposure. ↵ ↵ GrantPipe records salary and fringe allocations directly to grant ledgers per pay period, links each entry to the corresponding time-and-effort certification, flags percentage mismatches before audit, and supports CSV imports from ADP, Paychex, and QuickBooks Payroll.

The 2024 Uniform Guidance revision raised the federal single audit threshold to $1,000,000 in federal expenditures.↵ That change pulled smaller cost-reimbursement awardees out of single-audit scope, but it did not change how revenue gets recognized.↵ FASB ASU 2018-08 still governs the two tests for grant revenue under ASC 958-605: contribution vs exchange, then conditional vs unconditional.↵ Cost-reimbursement federal awards are typically conditional contributions. Revenue is recognized only as allowable costs are incurred, not when the award letter arrives.↵ Finance teams that book the full award upfront overstate revenue and end up restating it during audit fieldwork.↵ If your grant ledger does not match your expenditure schedule line for line, the conditional accounting is breaking somewhere.↵ GrantPipe attaches a ledger to each award so revenue recognition tracks expenditures automatically.

Program service revenue is not unrelated business income.↵ This is where mid-sized nonprofits over-file Form 990-T and pay UBIT they do not owe.↵ Program service revenue is income earned from activities substantially related to the exempt purpose. A health center charging sliding-scale fees is program service revenue. A literacy nonprofit selling workbooks tied to its curriculum is program service revenue.↵ Earning it does not jeopardize tax-exempt status. The risk only appears when an activity stops being substantially related and starts looking commercial in scope and substance.↵ Excessive unrelated commercial activity raises private benefit and inurement concerns, which is a separate analysis from whether the revenue itself is taxable.↵ The practical test: review activities annually against the exempt purpose stated in your determination letter. Document the connection. Keep that memo with the 990 workpapers.

For advance federal awards, interest earned above $500 per year across all awards must be remitted annually to HHS PSC under 2 CFR 200.305(b)(9).↵ Most mid-sized nonprofits never compute this until the auditor asks.↵ Steps 5 and 6 of a monthly grant drawdown reconciliation handle it cleanly.↵ Step 5: calculate interest on advance balances. Pull the average daily cash balance for each advance award, apply the operating account interest rate, accumulate the monthly figure. Twelve clean monthly numbers turn the annual remittance into addition.↵ Step 6: document variances and reclassifications. If a draw exceeded expenditures, write down whether it was a timing difference, an accrual, or an overdraw requiring return. If expenditures exceeded draws, plan the next draw to close the gap. Every variance gets a written explanation filed with the reconciliation.↵ Monthly cadence catches errors while they are still fixable. It also makes the quarterly Federal Financial Report a 30-minute task instead of a fire drill.

Questioned costs.↵ Defined at 2 CFR 200.516, a questioned cost is an expenditure flagged during a single audit because it appears unallowable, unsupported, or unreasonable.↵ Three categories. Unallowable: violates statute, regulation, or terms of the award. Unsupported: missing documentation. Unreasonable: exceeds what a prudent person would incur in similar circumstances.↵ The reporting threshold is $25,000 per federal program. When questioned costs attributable to a single program exceed that, they are listed in the Schedule of Findings and Questioned Costs.↵ Two examples that show up frequently. An auditor finds $32,000 in payroll charged to a federal award without time-and-effort documentation — reported as unsupported, exceeds threshold. A nonprofit charges $18,000 in alcohol-related catering to a training grant — unallowable, under threshold, still disclosed.↵ Questioned costs are not automatic disallowances. The pass-through entity or federal agency makes the final determination. The audit just flags them.

Bloomerang is a well-designed donor CRM. The retention analytics, constituent timeline, and lapse-tracking tools were built around a real insight: nonprofits lose nearly half their donors every year, and retention is where development economics get solved.↵ For donor work, the product knows what it is.↵ The breakdown happens when the same development director managing Bloomerang also manages 3 or more active grants with restricted-fund obligations.↵ Bloomerang's grant fields are essentially custom fields on a constituent record. They cannot model the funder reporting calendar, restricted-fund balances, allowable cost categories, or the conditional revenue recognition that ASC 958-605 requires.↵ The choice at that point is binary. Add a separate grant compliance tool and pay for two systems that do not share data. Or move to a platform that handles both donors and grants in one record set.↵ The two-tool path looks cheaper for about six months. After that, the manual reconciliation between systems usually costs more than either subscription.

A mature Federally Qualified Health Center typically manages 15 to 20 simultaneous federal and state awards.↵ The base HRSA Section 330 grant. HRSA supplemental awards. Ryan White HIV/AIDS program grants across multiple Parts. CDC prevention grants. State health department contracts.↵ Each award has distinct allowable cost categories, reporting calendars, and matching requirements. HRSA's Uniform Data System reporting intersects with financial compliance, so program data and expenditure data have to reconcile across systems that were never built to talk to each other.↵ Most donor CRMs cannot support the expenditure coding this requires. Most general accounting systems cannot model funder restrictions in a way that produces a clean spend-down report.↵ The result at most FQHCs: a finance team running parallel spreadsheets for grant tracking, drawdowns, and UDS-aligned program metrics, reconciled by hand at month-end.↵ The compliance environment is not getting simpler. The toolset has to.

A grant that projects $40,000 unspent with two months remaining is not a financial planning problem. It is a compliance problem that requires action now.↵ A spend-down tracker answers one question per active award: given what has been spent and when the period ends, are we on pace to use the full award correctly?↵ The structure is straightforward. One worksheet per grant. Budget vs actual by allowable cost category. Monthly burn rate. Projected end-of-award balance based on current pace. A decision framework for low burn rate situations — accelerate eligible expenditures, request a no-cost extension, or rebudget within funder rules.↵ The point is not the spreadsheet. The point is catching underspend in month 9 instead of month 11 of a 12-month award, when the options are still real.↵ The Grant Spend-Down Tracker is a free download. PDF with the template structure and the decision framework.↵ grantpipe.com/resources/lead-magnets/grant-spend-down-tracker

Givebutter and GrantPipe solve different problems. Putting them head to head only makes sense once you know which problem you actually have.↵ Givebutter is a fundraising-page tool with a free starting tier. Solid peer-to-peer, event ticketing, embeddable donation forms. The CRM piece is essentially gift record keeping. No grant management, no restricted-fund tracking at any tier — including the paid tiers that start at $29/mo.↵ GrantPipe runs $329 to $1,079/mo and bundles donor CRM with grant compliance and restricted-fund tracking in one record set.↵ The decision is not about features. It is about stage.↵ If the organization is early, primarily event- and campaign-funded, and has no active grant portfolio, Givebutter's free tier is the right call. Pay for tools you need.↵ Once there are active grants, restricted-fund obligations, or a board asking for a release-from-restriction report, a fundraising-page tool stops being the right tool. The reconciliation work between Givebutter and a separate grant tracker eats the savings.

A $3M nonprofit typically runs Bloomerang for donors, QuickBooks Online for accounting, a spreadsheet for grants, Google Workspace for documents, and a separate payroll system.↵ That stack is normal. It is also where the operations manager's week disappears.↵ The role's effectiveness correlates almost perfectly with the fragmentation of the toolset the staff uses. Every extra system is another integration, another vendor renewal, another set of permissions, another place audit evidence might live.↵ The question for ops managers reading this: if you wrote down every system the development, finance, and program teams touch in a normal week, how many show up?↵ For most $500K to $10M nonprofits the count lands between 8 and 14.↵ What is the one consolidation that would actually free up the most time — not the most license cost, the most time?

The board asks: how much of the Smith Foundation grant is left.↵ Most nonprofits answer that question by exporting two reports, opening a spreadsheet, and reconciling for 20 minutes. The number is stale before the meeting starts.↵ Restricted fund tracking in GrantPipe attaches a ledger to each grant and donor restriction. Every disbursement posts against the correct restriction at the time it is recorded. The balance owed to the funder is the same number reported to the board.↵ Net asset releases follow FASB ASC 958 categories. Released-from-restriction journal entries are produced from the same data, not built by hand.↵ The spend-down report is a query on live data. Open it during the board meeting and the number is current.↵ This is what makes restricted funds a system of record problem instead of a monthly reconciliation problem.↵ See how it works at grantpipe.com.

The micro-purchase threshold under 2 CFR 200.320(a)(1) is $10,000. The simplified acquisition threshold is $250,000.↵ ↵ Purchases between $10,001 and $250,000 require price or rate quotations from an adequate number of qualified sources — generally two to three, documented and retained.↵ ↵ Purchases above $250,000 require sealed bids or competitive proposals depending on contract type. Construction and commodities use sealed bids; professional services use competitive proposals.↵ ↵ The anti-fragmentation rule in 2 CFR 200.323 prohibits splitting a $500,000 project into five $100,000 purchases to dodge the threshold.↵ ↵ Procurement noncompliance is one of the most cited categories in the OMB 2024 Compliance Supplement. Purchases above $25,000 also require a SAM.gov debarment check before award.↵ ↵ Organizations whose written procurement policies were last updated before the 2024 Uniform Guidance revision are likely citing stale figures. GrantPipe maintains the procurement audit trail at transaction level so testing is a query, not a reconstruction.

Myth: DonorPerfect handles grant compliance because it has a grant tracking module.↵ ↵ DonorPerfect's grant features cover deadline reminders, fund records, and grant status fields. That is calendar tracking, not compliance.↵ ↵ What it does not cover: tracking actual expenditures against approved grant budget lines, flagging over-expenditure on restricted funds, or producing audit-ready reports showing funders how restricted dollars were spent.↵ ↵ Organizations receiving federal grants or multi-year restricted foundation grants typically run compliance documentation in a second system — usually a spreadsheet or the accounting platform — alongside DonorPerfect.↵ ↵ DonorPerfect reports 93% customer retention and a 13-year average tenure. Those numbers reflect mature donor management, not grant compliance depth.↵ ↵ The myth comes from conflating "grant tracking" (knowing when a report is due) with "grant compliance" (proving how every dollar was spent against an approved budget). They are different jobs.↵ ↵ Audit your grant tools by asking: can it produce a funder financial report from system data alone, or does staff rebuild it in Excel each cycle?

Address loan and loan guarantee programs separately on the SEFA.↵ ↵ Federal loans get specialized SEFA treatment under 2 CFR 200.502. The outstanding balance at year-end plus new loans received during the year is typically reportable, not just current-year cash receipts.↵ ↵ This applies to PPP loans, SBA programs, USDA rural development loans, and similar federal lending. Organizations treating these as cash transactions on the SEFA understate program expenditures.↵ ↵ The reportable figure has three components in most cases: prior-year outstanding loan balance carried forward, new principal disbursed during the fiscal year, and any forgiven amounts recognized in the current period.↵ ↵ Consult 2 CFR 200.502 and the auditor before finalizing the schedule. Loan reporting rules vary by program type, and the OMB Compliance Supplement clarifies treatment for the largest federal lending programs each year.↵ ↵ Organizations with any federal loan activity should confirm treatment before SEFA delivery to the auditor — getting it wrong on a loan line can shift major-program determination.

Schedule A is the Form 990 attachment where 501(c)(3) organizations prove they qualify as a public charity under IRC Section 509(a).↵ ↵ The most common path is Section 509(a)(1) combined with Section 170(b)(1)(A)(vi): at least 33.33% of total support over a rolling five-year window must come from public sources.↵ ↵ The 2% cap is where concentrated donor bases get hurt. Contributions from any single source that exceed 2% of total five-year support are capped at the 2% level in the public support numerator. Excess counts in the denominator only.↵ ↵ Program service revenue and investment income count in the denominator (total support) but not in the numerator (public support).↵ ↵ Fail both the one-third test and the 10% facts-and-circumstances test for two consecutive years and the IRS reclassifies the organization as a private foundation by operation of law — triggering the 1.39% excise tax under IRC Section 4940, the 5% minimum distribution requirement, and Form 990-PF filing.↵ ↵ About 100,000 private foundations file Form 990-PF annually compared to 1.5 million public charities. The math behind that ratio runs through Schedule A.

Donorbox at $300,000/year in donations costs $5,250 in platform fees alone. At $400,000/year it costs $7,000.↵ ↵ The free tier is genuinely free — no monthly subscription. The 1.75% platform fee is deducted from each donation. Donorbox Pro at $199/month waives the fee on the first $1,000/month of donations.↵ ↵ What Donorbox does well: embeddable donation forms deploy in hours, recurring gift management with a donor-facing portal for payment updates, and zero setup friction for organizations without a software budget.↵ ↵ What it does not do at any tier: full donor CRM with moves management, major gift officer assignment, restricted fund tracking, or grant lifecycle management. Donorbox Pro adds basic CRM features, but they remain shallow relative to purpose-built CRMs.↵ ↵ Donorbox has processed over $2 billion across 50,000+ nonprofits. The product is good at what it does. The problem is total cost of ownership shifts as donation volume grows past roughly $200,000 annually, where the fee model starts crossing the cost of a dedicated CRM with grant compliance built in.↵ ↵ The break-even calculation is rarely run until the organization is already past it.

The National Endowment for the Arts awarded $147 million in fiscal year 2023. State arts agencies collectively distribute around $500 million annually through state appropriations and NEA grants-to-states.↵ ↵ Arts organizations face a compliance challenge that most nonprofit categories do not: they generate earned revenue. Ticket sales, tuition, facility rentals, and merchandise mix with grant revenue in the operating budget, creating restricted fund separation problems that general-purpose accounting tools handle poorly.↵ ↵ NEA Art Works grants require a final performance report capturing total attendance, demographic data on audiences and artists served, educational programming hours, and geographic reach — separate from the financial report.↵ ↵ State arts agency grants run on each state's fiscal calendar. An organization with a calendar fiscal year, an NEA direct grant on January-December, and a state grant on July-June is managing three different fiscal periods at year-end.↵ ↵ The result: attendance data sits in a program system, financial data sits in accounting software, and connecting them at year-end is a manual exercise that introduces errors and consumes staff time.↵ ↵ 36% of nonprofits ended FY2024 with an operating deficit. Arts organizations cannot afford reporting overhead that does not produce funder-ready output.

A loaded hourly rate calculation: annual salary divided by 2,080 hours, multiplied by 1.30 for benefits and payroll tax. A $60,000 finance coordinator costs the organization roughly $37.50 per hour.↵ ↵ If that coordinator spends 10 hours a week on grant reconciliation, funder report assembly, and audit prep, the annual cost is about $19,500. Add the development director's hours, the finance director's audit-prep weekends, and the program staff time on coordination, and the true compliance cost is rarely under $40,000 annually for a $2M-budget nonprofit.↵ ↵ Most finance directors report only the dedicated compliance hours. They miss the funder calls explaining discrepancies, the weekend before audit fieldwork, and the hours answering the development director's questions about fund balances.↵ ↵ GrantPipe published a free Grant Software ROI Calculator that walks through current compliance cost, risk-adjusted error cost, software investment, and a board-ready three-year net benefit summary.↵ ↵ Numbers, not vibes — that is how this decision should be made.

Bloomerang starts at $125/month. Little Green Light starts at $39/month. Neither manages grants.↵ ↵ Little Green Light is the budget choice for small nonprofits that need a basic donor database — contacts, gifts, pledges, and basic reports. Setup runs 1-3 days. Reporting depth is shallow.↵ ↵ Bloomerang is the mid-tier upgrade. The retention dashboard surfaces at-risk donors, which most nonprofit CRMs ignore entirely. Pricing scales with record count to $249/month. Setup runs 1-2 weeks.↵ ↵ Only 33.3% of nonprofits rate their CRM as effective per the 2025 Fifty & Fifty Nonprofit Peer Report. 46.5% call it neutral. 20.1% call it ineffective.↵ ↵ The shared limitation: neither platform tracks restricted fund expenditures against grant budgets, produces audit-ready compliance reports, or handles the post-award grant lifecycle. Organizations receiving grants run grant management in spreadsheets alongside the CRM and reconcile manually each month.↵ ↵ Choose Little Green Light if budget dominates and the work is donor-only. Choose Bloomerang if retention analytics drive strategy. Choose neither if grants represent more than 20% of revenue — the spreadsheet workaround compounds quickly.

A question for executive directors at $500K-$10M nonprofits: how long does board prep currently take, and how many systems does the staff touch to assemble the packet?↵ ↵ The pattern is consistent. Revenue year-to-date comes from QuickBooks. Pipeline status comes from a CRM or a spreadsheet. Retention metrics come from a different report. Restricted fund balances come from QuickBooks classes if they exist or a spreadsheet if they do not. Compliance deadlines live in Outlook or one staff member's head.↵ ↵ When each number reconciles differently, assembling a packet that holds up under board scrutiny takes a full week. The ED often does it personally because no one else has context across every system.↵ ↵ Mid-sized nonprofits spend an average of 20 to 30 percent of staff time on compliance data entry across at least 12 different reporting systems per the Center for an Urban Future January 2023 research.↵ ↵ Organizations that compress board prep from a week to an afternoon do it the same way: one system holding donor, grant, restricted fund, and compliance data, with reports generated from live data rather than assembled the night before.↵ ↵ What did board prep look like at your organization last quarter — full week or full afternoon?

Approximately 30% of nonprofits with revenues over $1M operate more than one related legal entity per IRS Statistics of Income data.↵ ↵ The single-database problem: running a 501(c)(3), a 501(c)(4), and a related private foundation in one CRM workspace forces all entity data into a shared environment with manual tags as the only separation. A staff member with access to charity data can see advocacy data because they share a workspace. Compliance calendars merge into one list.↵ ↵ The legal separation exists for regulatory reasons. The SF-SAC has two certifications, and missing either one keeps the submission in draft.↵ Step seven of the Single Audit Data Collection Form workflow at fac.gov: the auditee certifies the submission is accurate and complete, then the auditor separately certifies the audit findings.↵ Neither party can submit unilaterally. A form sitting at one signature is not filed, even if every field is complete and the reporting package uploaded cleanly.↵ Deadline pressure compounds this. The SF-SAC is due 30 days after the auditor's report or 9 months after fiscal year-end, whichever is earlier. Late filings affect low-risk auditee status under 2 CFR 200.520 in subsequent years.↵ Confirm both certifications cleared before treating an SF-SAC as submitted. Download the FAC confirmation PDF and retain it in the audit binder.

The de minimis indirect cost rate is 15% of MTDC, raised from 10% by the 2024 Uniform Guidance revision under 2 CFR 200.414(f).↵ Eligible nonprofits — those that have never received a federally negotiated indirect cost rate — can claim it on federal awards without going through NICRA negotiation.↵ Two facts that get organizations into trouble.↵ First, the base is Modified Total Direct Costs, not total direct costs. MTDC excludes equipment, capital expenditures, participant support, and sub-award amounts above $50,000 per subcontract. Applying 15% to the full budget is a recurring audit finding.↵ Second, once a NICRA is executed, there is no return to de minimis — even after the NICRA period closes.↵ Urban Institute analysis of Form 990 data found roughly 25% of eligible nonprofits claim no indirect cost recovery at all. That is real money left unrecovered.

Neon CRM handles donors, members, and event registration in one platform — a fit for organizations running fundraising galas, membership drives, and giving days simultaneously.↵ What it does not include: grant lifecycle management or restricted fund compliance. A mid-sized homeless shelter manages 8-12 simultaneous funding streams: HUD ESG, HUD Continuum of Care, CDBG sub-allocations, state housing authority grants, county homelessness funds, United Way, and three or four foundation awards.↵ Each has distinct allowable expense categories.
