The 2024 OMB revision raised the Single Audit threshold to $1,000,000 — effective for fiscal years ending September 30, 2025 or later.↵ That change matters for how organizations track federal expenditure totals, not just whether they file. The threshold applies across all federal awards combined, not per grant. An organization holding three federal awards totaling $980,000 is below the line. At $1,000,001, a licensed independent auditor must complete and submit the Single Audit package to the Federal Audit Clearinghouse within 9 months of fiscal year end.↵ The same revision raised the de minimis indirect cost rate from 10% to 15% under 2 CFR 200.414 — a meaningful shift for organizations that have never negotiated a rate with a cognizant federal agency.↵ Organizations near the threshold should track cumulative federal expenditures by award, not just by program budget. Crossing the threshold mid-year triggers the Single Audit obligation for the entire fiscal year, not just the portion spent after crossing.↵ GrantPipe surfaces cumulative federal expenditure totals across all active awards so compliance staff see the threshold approach before the obligation lands.

Myth: entering the grant award amount in your system means the award is set up.↵ What most organizations actually enter: a grant name, a dollar total, and a due date. That is not a grant setup — it is a note.↵ A complete grant record has the project period start and end dates from the Notice of Award (not the application), the approved budget broken down by category, the restriction type, every reporting deadline for the full performance period, and the program officer contact. It also needs the accounting system grant code that links expenditures to this award in the GL.↵ The most common error in setup is using the application budget instead of the approved budget. Funders modify budgets at award time. An application that asked for $50,000 in personnel may be awarded with $42,000 in personnel and the remainder cut entirely. If the system holds the application budget, every budget-vs-actual report for the life of the award is wrong.↵ The hour invested in a complete setup at week one eliminates a recurring compliance debt that compounds across every expenditure, every report, and every audit.

Program income Step 3 under 2 CFR 200.307: establish the tracking ledger before any income-generating activity begins.↵ Program income is gross income earned by the grantee that is directly generated by activities supported by the federal award. Patient fees at a federally-funded clinic. Admission to a grant-funded training program. Rental of a federally-funded facility. The revenue is federal money earned under the award's authority — not unrestricted income, not a donation.↵ The ledger tracks the award number, income source description, date earned, amount, and cumulative total by period. Each of those fields is there because the Federal Financial Report SF-425 asks for cumulative program income earned and expended on Lines 10 and 10a — and auditors testing Single Audit compliance cross-reference those lines against the accounting records.↵ Program income deposited into the general operating account without a separate tracking mechanism becomes unrecoverable within 30 days. The accrual basis applies: record when earned, not when collected. A patient visit on September 30 generates program income on September 30 regardless of when the insurance payment arrives.↵ Under 2 CFR 200.307(e)(1), deductive treatment is the default when the award is silent on disposition. Plan the election at award time — changing it mid-award requires written federal agency prior approval.

Net assets without donor restrictions is not the same as cash available.↵ Under FASB ASC 958-210-45, every nonprofit's net assets fall into one of two classes: with-donor-restrictions or without-donor-restrictions. The without-restrictions class includes unrestricted contributions, program service revenue, government contract revenue, investment returns on unrestricted funds, and board-designated amounts. It is the default — funds land here unless a donor has imposed explicit conditions.↵ The term replaced "unrestricted net assets" through FASB ASU 2016-14, effective for fiscal years beginning after December 15, 2017. The substance is identical; only the label changed. Using "unrestricted net assets" in an audited financial statement is now an error.↵ Board designations are the classification that creates the most confusion. A board that votes to designate $250,000 as an operating reserve has created an internal allocation — not a donor restriction. The board can rescind it by resolution at any time. That $250,000 remains within net assets without donor restrictions, disclosed in the footnotes, not moved to a separate net asset class.↵ FASB ASU 2016-14 added a required liquidity and availability footnote precisely because a $2 million without-restrictions balance may consist largely of fixed assets, vehicles, and long-term receivables. The footnote surfaces what is genuinely accessible within 12 months. High unrestricted net assets without the liquidity footnote tells auditors and board members almost nothing.

Network for Good was acquired by Bonterra in 2022, alongside EveryAction, CommunityForce, and Social Solutions.↵ Before the acquisition, pricing was published in tiers. After the acquisition, pricing moved to a custom contract model requiring a demo. Reviews written before 2022 describe a different product structure than what current prospects encounter in a sales conversation.↵ What the platform does: fundraising pages, peer-to-peer campaigns, donor email tools. What it has never done: grant prospect tracking, restricted fund management, grant budget-versus-expenditure tracking, or compliance report generation. These were not features removed at acquisition — they were never part of the product.↵ Transaction fees may apply on processed donations in addition to the subscription cost. The specific fee structure is part of the negotiated contract, not disclosed publicly.↵ For nonprofits whose primary activity is campaign-based fundraising with no grant compliance requirements, the product is coherent. For organizations receiving restricted foundation or government grants, grant compliance still lives elsewhere — usually in a spreadsheet.↵ The evaluation question is not whether the platform works for fundraising. It is whether your organization's workflow requires a system that handles restricted grant compliance alongside donor management, or two separate systems with manual reconciliation between them.

VAWA grantees cannot maintain grant files that link identifiable survivor information to service records accessible to outside reviewers.↵ That requirement is not a suggestion from a program officer. The confidentiality provisions of the Violence Against Women Act are statutory — they prohibit shelters from disclosing personally identifying survivor information without informed, written, reasonably time-limited consent. Critically, confidentiality extends into the grant record itself.↵ This creates a specific data architecture requirement for domestic violence shelters: program tracking systems must report aggregate service data to funders without exposing individual case records. VOCA performance reporting requires aggregate counts of victims served by crime type, services provided by category, and demographic data. OVW semiannual progress reports through GMS require similar aggregate documentation. Neither accepts individual survivor records.↵ Most shelters operate with VAWA, VOCA, and FVPSA grants simultaneously. Each has different period of performance dates, different allowable cost categories, and different reporting timelines. VOCA funds are typically capped at 10% for administrative costs. Time for a shelter director whose salary is split across VAWA, VOCA, and operating funds must be documented separately for each funding source.↵ Using a single case management database for both service delivery and grant compliance tracking creates the linkage that the VAWA confidentiality provisions prohibit. The compliance architecture and the service delivery architecture must be designed separately from the start.

Grant compliance failures happen after the award, not during the application.↵ The obligations begin the moment the grant agreement is signed. Spending restrictions, reporting cadences, documentation standards, and time tracking requirements are all active before the first dollar is spent. Most mid-sized nonprofits discover the scope of those obligations when the first report is due, not when the award letter arrives.↵ The Nonprofit Grant Compliance Checklist covers the post-award sequence: reading the award letter before any spending begins, setting up restricted fund tracking in the accounting system, calendaring every reporting deadline immediately, implementing time documentation for grant-funded staff, and running budget-vs-actual comparisons monthly. It also covers the warning signs that the current system is approaching its limits — spreadsheets typically break at three to five active grants with different fiscal years and staff splitting time across programs.↵ The threshold at which a dedicated system replaces the spreadsheet is around $500,000 in grant revenue or three active grants managed simultaneously.↵ The checklist is free at grantpipe.com/free/grant-compliance-checklist.

"We manage grants in spreadsheets and it works fine."↵↵It works fine for 1–2 simple foundation grants with annual reporting. The failure is usually invisible until it is not.↵↵The most common breakdown: a compliance review or audit reveals that expenditure documentation is incomplete because the spreadsheet was not maintained consistently by whoever owned it last.↵↵The second most common: restricted funds that got commingled with general revenue because spreadsheets cannot prevent it — they can only record it after the fact.↵↵Under 2 CFR 200, federal grants require audit trails that spreadsheets cannot reliably provide. No record of who changed what. No automated check that restricted funds are being spent within approved budget categories. No deadline alert for the funder report that is due in 11 days.↵↵The practical threshold: if you manage 3 or more grants, or any grant with restricted fund requirements, the time spent on manual tracking and reconciliation likely exceeds the cost of dedicated software.↵↵Only 33.3% of nonprofits rate their CRM systems as effective, per the Fifty & Fifty 2025 Nonprofit Peer Report. A Single Audit finding is not a disaster. A weak Corrective Action Plan response is.↵↵Under 2 CFR 200.511(c), every finding requires a written CAP with five required elements: the finding reference number, the auditee's position (agree or disagree), the specific corrective action, the name and title of the responsible party, and the target completion date.↵↵"Management will strengthen its procurement controls" does not meet that standard. It will invite awarding-agency follow-up and likely result in additional reporting requirements.↵↵A strong CAP reads like a project plan: "The CFO will update the procurement policy by May 31, circulate it to all staff with a signed attestation, and provide completed attestations to the audit committee at the June meeting."↵↵Completion dates should be aggressive but achievable — typically 30 to 180 days. Missed CAP deadlines are themselves a finding risk in the following audit.↵↵Repeat findings in two or more consecutive audits trigger specific conditions under 2 CFR 200.208: prior approval for draws, enhanced monitoring, or high-risk designation. Breaking that pattern often requires more structural change than the first response suggested.↵↵Disagreeing with a finding is legitimate. Unsupported disagreement damages credibility with both the auditor and the awarding agency.↵↵#singleaudit #grantcompliance #federalgrants #nonprofitfinance

Matching funds: the term nonprofits misunderstand most often.↵↵Under 2 CFR 200.306, match contributions must be non-federal, verifiable from your records, necessary and reasonable for the project, allowable under applicable cost principles, and included in the approved budget. All five requirements apply simultaneously.↵↵The most common audit finding: using another federal grant as match. A HUD CDBG grant cannot match a HOME grant. An AmeriCorps award cannot match an HHS program. The prohibition is strict, with narrow statutory exceptions that most nonprofits do not qualify for.↵↵The second most common problem: in-kind match that was not documented contemporaneously. Volunteer hours estimated at year-end based on memory do not satisfy the requirement. Volunteer hours logged weekly, with position descriptions and market rate comparisons, do.↵↵A 1:1 match on a $500,000 federal award means the grantee must contribute $500,000 in non-federal resources — cash, in-kind, or a combination. Falling short is a compliance violation reportable in a Single Audit and can result in a proportional reduction of the federal award.↵↵One more trap: voluntary committed match. If you pledged match beyond the minimum in your application to improve competitiveness, that commitment is legally binding once it appears in the award agreement. An auditor will test it.↵↵#matchingfunds #grantcompliance #federalgrants #uniformguidance

Genuinely strong for organizations where events and community fundraising are the primary revenue channel.↵↵What Classy does not include: donor relationship management beyond campaign records, grant tracking, restricted fund allocation, or compliance reporting. Organizations using Classy for their full donor program typically run a separate CRM alongside it.↵↵Classy's pricing is not transparent. Mid-sized nonprofits consistently report paying $3,000–$12,000 per year based on G2 and Capterra reviews, plus platform fees on donations that commonly run 2–5% on lower tiers. Both a platform fee and a payment processing fee apply on each transaction.↵↵For nonprofits whose revenue comes primarily from individual major gifts, recurring donors, and grants — rather than event campaigns — the cost calculus changes significantly.↵↵The peer-to-peer tooling is mature. If that is the primary need, Classy is worth a genuine evaluation. If it is not, the gap between what Classy costs and what it covers becomes the real problem.↵↵#nonprofitfundraising #donormanagement #peertopeerfundraising #nonprofittools

WIOA requires tracking employment outcomes at the 2nd and 4th quarter after program exit.↵↵For an organization serving 200 participants per year, that means 400 active follow-up contacts at any given point, each at a different stage of the outcome measurement window.↵↵A participant who exits in January must be tracked in April (2nd quarter) and again in October (4th quarter). These are the metrics that determine whether the organization meets state-negotiated performance targets under WIOA Section 116 — and whether it faces sanctions.↵↵The six primary performance indicators for adult and dislocated worker programs include employment rate at 2nd quarter after exit, employment rate at 4th quarter after exit, and median earnings at 2nd quarter after exit. All measured from the date of program exit.↵↵Organizations that track participants in spreadsheets lose participants to follow-up at higher rates. When auditors and state monitors see low employment rates, they examine whether the rates reflect actual outcomes or tracking failures.↵↵The cost allocation layer adds complexity. A career counselor serving Adult, Dislocated Worker, and Youth programs under WIOA must have time records that support the allocation across all three. Estimated proportions without documentation create findings.↵↵WIOA funds approximately $2.7 billion annually for adult, dislocated worker, and youth employment programs. The data infrastructure requirements are proportional to that accountability.↵↵#WIOA #workforcedevelopment #grantcompliance #federalgrants

Five signs your nonprofit's restricted fund tracking is creating audit risk:↵↵QuickBooks class tracking is the system of record for restricted funds. Class tracking is a reporting filter, not fund accounting. It cannot prevent a transaction from being miscoded to a fund that has been fully expended, and it cannot generate a statement of financial position for a single fund.↵↵Finance staff spend 8–15 hours per month on shadow spreadsheet maintenance. That is the median for teams managing 5–10 active grants. At a loaded staff cost of $30–$50 per hour, that is $240–$750 per month in hidden labor costs — before any audit findings.↵↵Restricted fund balances in the spreadsheet do not reconcile to the general ledger at month-end. This is the failure mode auditors see most often: two sources of truth that diverge over time and cannot be traced.↵↵Funder reports require pulling data from three systems and reformatting in a template that may have changed since the last report cycle. GAO consistently cites late and missing grantee financial reports as a recurring compliance deficiency; the cause is almost always assembly time, not missing information.↵↵No one can explain who changed what in the restricted fund records. The spreadsheet has no audit trail. Anyone with file access can modify restricted fund balances without a log entry.↵↵Each of these is a management letter comment waiting to happen. Several together are a qualified opinion risk.↵↵#nonprofitaccounting #restrictedFunds #fundaccounting #grantcompliance

Funder reports are late almost never because the deadline was missed. They are late because assembly takes longer than the reporting window.↵↵The financial figures live in the accounting system. Booking a pledge write-off as bad debt expense is one of the most common accounting errors in nonprofit finance — and under FASB ASC 958, it is wrong.↵↵The correct entry debits the allowance for uncollectible pledges and credits the pledge receivable. The write-off reduces the contra-asset and eliminates the receivable. It does not create a new expense on the Statement of Activities.↵↵This matters because most accounting staff coming from for-profit environments do exactly the opposite. The for-profit instinct is a debit to bad debt expense — which is not the correct account under ASC 958-605.↵↵The complication is the allowance itself. If the organization set the allowance to zero when the pledge was recorded, the write-off has nowhere to absorb: it becomes a direct charge to contribution revenue, reducing the current period's reported contributions.↵↵Multi-year pledges add a second entry that gets missed: the unamortized present-value discount attributable to the written-off portion must also be eliminated per ASC 958-605-30-6. Leaving the discount in place after the receivable is gone overstates the discount contra-asset.↵↵Auditors testing pledge receivables will sample write-offs and look for: the original pledge documentation, payment history, collection effort evidence, the collectibility assessment memo, and approval at the threshold specified in your policy.↵↵What dollar threshold triggers board approval at your organization for a write-off decision?

The SF-425 Federal Financial Report is not a routine form. It is a compliance obligation submitted under the False Claims Act, and one specific error accounts for most of the findings it generates.↵↵Line 10f — Federal Share of Expenditures — must show cumulative expenditures for the entire period of performance, from day one of the award through the last day of the reporting period. Not just the current quarter. Cumulative.↵↵If your grant started October 1 and you are submitting the March 31 quarterly report, line 10f must show total expenditures from October through March. An agency receiving reports that appear to show expenditures declining or fluctuating rather than steadily accumulating will flag the discrepancy.↵↵The final SF-425 is due no later than 120 calendar days after the period-of-performance end date. Some agencies specify shorter deadlines in the notice of award. The final report must reconcile exactly to your general ledger — a discrepancy is a compliance finding in the financial reporting area of a single audit and prevents award closeout.↵↵Line 10g (unliquidated obligations) should be zero on the final report: all obligations should be liquidated before submission.↵↵Line 10j (program income) requires reporting and accounting for any gross income earned directly as a result of federally funded activities, per the method specified in the award.↵↵A wrong number on the SF-425 is not a clerical error in a program monitor's view. It is a finding.

USDA Rural Development administers over $20 billion in loans, loan guarantees, and grants annually across three mission areas — and each program has its own authorizing statute, compliance requirements, and eligible activity definitions.↵↵A nonprofit managing Community Facilities grants, Rural Business Development Grants, and REAP energy grants simultaneously is not managing one compliance framework. The documentation requirements were written for program densities that do not reflect rural operational reality.↵↵What compliance infrastructure does your rural development organization have in place for geographic eligibility documentation across multi-county programs?

CRM migrations fail at the field mapping step or the data quality step — not the software step.↵↵The field mapping problem is structural: every data element in the source system needs a documented destination in the target, a defined transformation if formats differ, and a validation rule that confirms the migration succeeded. Most source systems contain years of accumulated quality problems — duplicate contacts, blank required fields, inconsistent fund designation naming, phone numbers in five formats — that transfer directly into the new system if not addressed first.↵↵The pre-migration data audit should take two to three weeks. Target zero duplicate contacts by primary identifier. Run a report of records where required fields are blank in the target system. Establish a merge rule for duplicates before you start. Decide which records to migrate (active donor records, five to seven years of giving history, active grants) versus exclude (closed grants older than five years, test records, deprecated fields with no current use).↵↵Post-migration validation requires record count reconciliation, a random sample of 20 donor giving histories, and financial validation confirming total giving history in the target matches the source for the same period.↵↵A free CRM migration data map template — with field-level mapping tables, transformation documentation, and validation checklists — is available at grantpipe.com. No form required.

Myth: a nonprofit on cash-basis books can report to federal agencies the same way it reports internally.↵↵Reality: federal grant reporting is accrual-only, under 2 CFR 200.302(b)(3).↵↵The SF-425 Federal Financial Report is the clearest proof. Block 10e captures accrued expenditures — costs incurred but not yet paid. Block 10g captures unliquidated obligations. A cash-basis organization that enters only cash disbursements on Block 10e is underreporting federal expenditures, even if the books look correct internally.↵↵Under FASB ASC 958, audited nonprofit financial statements must also be on accrual. Form 990 preparation follows the same standard.↵↵The practical fix for a cash-basis organization: at each reporting date, identify unpaid vendor invoices, calculate any pay-period proration for accrued wages, isolate grant receivables not yet submitted for reimbursement, and document the cash-to-accrual reconciliation in a worksheet retained with the FFR.↵↵Missing reconciliation worksheets are one of the more reliable indicators of accounting control weaknesses in single audits.↵↵Cash books and federal reporting can coexist. The bridge is documented, repeatable, and auditable.

A post-closeout cost transfer on a federal grant requires written authorization from the awarding agency before any journal entry is booked.↵↵That is the step most organizations get wrong: they discover the misposting, assess it, and move the cost — then ask permission. That sequence creates a second compliance problem on top of the original one.↵↵Under 2 CFR 200.344, grantees have 120 calendar days after the period of performance ends to liquidate obligations and submit final reports. A transfer discovered after that window closes is in different territory.↵↵The correct sequence: document the specific cost and why it needs to transfer, confirm whether the 120-day window is still open, notify the federal program officer and grants management specialist in writing, submit a formal prior approval request package with original expenditure documentation, wait for written authorization (typically 30 to 90 days depending on the agency), then book the entry.↵↵If the transfer changes figures on the final SF-425, an amended FFR must be submitted.↵↵Program officers are helpful. Verbal concurrence from a program officer is not written authorization from a grants management specialist. The distinction matters.↵↵Strong monthly reconciliation is the real answer: it catches mispostings while awards are still open.

Post-award grant management is not the glamorous half of the grants function. Pre-award — prospecting, writing, submitting — has a clear narrative arc. Post-award is the operational discipline that runs quietly in the background for months or years.↵↵It is also where most compliance failures happen.↵↵Proposals are reviewed before any money moves. The funder evaluates the budget and work plan before making the award. Post-award management happens without that external review layer. Expenditures are approved internally. Documentation is maintained — or not — by staff with many other priorities.↵↵The four phases are setup (entering the award, establishing restricted fund tracking, calendaring all obligations), active management (expenditure approvals, time records, drawdown reconciliation, interim reports), reporting (producing funder-required reports from accumulated data), and closeout (stopping expenditures, reconciling all transactions, submitting final reports, archiving the file).↵↵Setup quality in the first two weeks of an award predicts compliance quality for the entire grant period.↵↵Organizations with strong post-award systems have documented workflows that connect development, program, and finance staff. The typical audit finding is not a fraudulent application. It is a documentation gap that accumulated gradually — time records not collected, budget modifications without required prior approval.↵↵What does your organization's post-award setup process actually look like in week one?

After-school nonprofits managing 21st Century Community Learning Centers grants face a quarterly reporting requirement that no standard donor CRM or general-purpose accounting system was built to handle.↵↵The 21st CCLC program distributed approximately $1.3 billion in federal grants in fiscal year 2023, serving more than 1.7 million students at 6,600 centers operated primarily by nonprofits.↵↵Quarterly attendance reporting requires documentation by school, grade level, and program type — data that lives in a student enrollment database, not a financial system. Calendaring SF-425 submissions and programmatic reports at award setup should be the system's job, not yours.↵↵Three: does report generation pull from live transaction data or require manual formatting? Development directors managing both donors and grants who maintain parallel systems rebuild the same organizational story in two places every month.↵↵Five: does it give finance the same visibility it gives development? Grant compliance is a shared function. A tool only the development team can use leaves finance reconciling from exports.↵↵Only 33.3% of nonprofits rate their CRM systems as effective, per the Fifty & Fifty 2025 Nonprofit Peer Report. Myth: if a cost is in the grant budget, it is allowable on a federal award.↵↵Under 2 CFR Part 200, every cost charged to a federal grant must pass three separate tests simultaneously. A cost can appear in the approved budget and still be disallowed.↵↵Test 1 — Allowability: the cost must not be explicitly prohibited under 2 CFR 200.420–200.475. Alcoholic beverages (200.423), entertainment (200.438), lobbying (200.450), and fundraising costs (200.442) are never allowable — regardless of what appears in the budget.↵↵Test 2 — Allocability: the grant must have actually benefited from the cost. Charging 100% of a shared cost to one grant when multiple programs benefited is a common allocability error, even when the total amount is small.↵↵Test 3 — Reasonableness: would a prudent person pay this amount for this good or service in the ordinary course of business? Above-market contracted services, procurements without competitive quotes above the micro-purchase threshold, and equipment that exceeds program requirements can produce partial disallowances based on reasonableness alone.↵↵Budget approval does not substitute for any of these three tests. Document each cost on its own merits at the time of the transaction.

The most common subaward budget modification error is not forgetting to file paperwork. It is approving a change before checking who actually has the authority to approve it.↵↵Under 2 CFR 200.308(e)(4), pass-through entities can approve direct cost transfers across budget categories without federal prior approval — but only when the transfer does not exceed 10% of the total award budget and does not alter the project scope. That threshold is calculated against the total federal award, not the category being modified.↵↵An organization with a $500,000 award can transfer up to $50,000 across categories on its own authority. Beyond that, a written request must go to the federal program officer before the subrecipient incurs costs under the new budget.↵↵Approving first and seeking federal sign-off after is itself a compliance violation. Expenditures incurred under an unauthorized modification may be questioned or disallowed.↵↵The second-most common error: treating a reallocation that funds an activity not in the original scope as a routine budget transfer. If the modified budget funds something new, federal prior approval is required regardless of the dollar amount.↵↵Federal prior approval timelines vary by agency — HHS Grants Management often responds within 30 days; DOJ and HUD can take 60 to 90 days. Build those timelines into every subaward monitoring calendar from award day.

The OMB Compliance Supplement is the document auditors use to decide what to test in your federal programs. Most nonprofit staff have never read it.↵↵It is published annually by the Office of Management and Budget, organized by federal agency and CFDA/Assistance Listing number. For each significant federal program, it identifies which of 12 standard compliance requirements apply — Activities Allowed, Allowable Costs, Cash Management, Eligibility, Equipment, Matching, Period of Performance, Procurement, Program Income, Reporting, Subrecipient Monitoring, Special Tests and Provisions — and describes exactly what the auditor will examine.↵↵Not all 12 requirements apply to every program. The Supplement designates each requirement as applicable ("A") or not applicable ("N/A") for each specific program. Auditors test the applicable ones.↵↵For a nonprofit managing a HRSA health workforce grant under CFDA 93.884, reading the Supplement section for that program tells the organization precisely what documentation it needs to survive fieldwork — before the auditor arrives.↵↵The Supplement is written for auditors, but its most practical use is audit preparation by the organizations being audited. Reading the sections covering your major programs is the most efficient pre-audit activity available.↵↵It is updated annually. Check which version applies to your audit period.

Individual nonprofit grants ranged from $100,000 to $20 million.↵↵Each of those awards comes with compliance requirements that go beyond standard nonprofit financial reporting.↵↵EPA grants require environmental outcome metrics alongside financial data — community engagement counts, environmental improvements measured, program reach figures. Tracking outcomes separately from financial records creates reconciliation work at every reporting period.↵↵A significant portion of EPA funding reaches nonprofits through state environmental agencies as pass-through sub-awards. Procurement rules, conflict-of-interest policies, and Title VI civil rights compliance requirements flow through from EPA to the sub-recipient.↵↵USDA NRCS conservation grants — particularly through the Regional Conservation Partnership Program, which obligated over $4 billion in FY2023 — add project-phase complexity. Annual financial reports must document expenditures by phase, tied to approved budget line items and conservation plan milestones.↵↵Most environmental nonprofits manage this compliance load with general-purpose tools that were not designed for it.

Before issuing a sub-award, the first question to answer in writing is: is this organization a subrecipient or a contractor?↵↵The 2 CFR 200.331 five-factor test determines the classification. Subrecipient indicators include: the entity determines who is eligible for the federal assistance, its performance is measured against federal program objectives, it has programmatic decision-making responsibility, it is accountable for federal compliance requirements, and it uses the funds to carry out its own program.↵↵Contractor indicators are the opposite: the entity provides goods or services in normal business operations, serves many purchasers, operates in a competitive market, and is not subject to federal program compliance requirements.↵↵The classification matters because the monitoring obligations in 2 CFR 200.332 — pre-award risk assessment, ongoing financial report review, documentation desk review for medium/high-risk organizations, site visits for high-risk subrecipients, and fac.gov single audit verification for organizations expending $1,000,000 or more in federal awards — apply to subrecipients, not contractors.↵↵A free subrecipient monitoring checklist covering every step under 2 CFR 200.332 — pre-award risk assessment through file documentation requirements — is available at grantpipe.com/free/subrecipient-monitoring-checklist.

Myth: Foundant GLM and GrantHub are the same product for different users.↵↵They are three separate products — GLM for grantmakers, SLM for scholarship administrators, and GrantHub for grantseekers — each with separate pricing and separate implementations.↵↵If your organization is both a grantseeker and does some grantmaking, you are buying two subscriptions.↵↵G2 and Capterra reviews place Foundant GLM implementations at 60 to 120 days, with a dedicated project manager required on both sides. A donor refund in January for a December gift does not just affect the payment processor. It affects the donor's prior-year charitable deduction.↵↵The organization's obligation is specific: issue a correction letter stating the original gift date and amount, the refund date and amount, and the net contribution of zero for a full refund. The letter must note that the refund crossed a tax year so the donor knows to consult their tax advisor about any previously claimed deduction.↵↵Under FASB ASC 958, refunding a restricted gift also requires eliminating the associated donor restriction from net assets. The restricted net asset cannot remain on the books once the cash is returned.↵↵IRS Publication 1771 requires written acknowledgment for contributions of $250 or more. A revised acknowledgment for a refunded gift is not optional — it is what allows the donor to represent their giving accurately on their return.↵↵The CRM update is equally non-negotiable. A refund that is processed in the payment system but not reflected in the donor database inflates LYBUNT and SYBUNT retention metrics, giving totals, and year-end summaries.↵↵What refund procedures does your organization currently have in writing?

"Management decision" has a specific legal meaning in federal grant compliance that differs from ordinary usage.↵↵Under 2 CFR 200.521, a management decision is the written determination issued by a federal awarding agency or pass-through entity in response to a finding from a single audit.↵↵The federal agency has six months from the date the audit is accepted by the Federal Audit Clearinghouse to issue it.↵↵The management decision either accepts the finding as written, modifies its scope, or in rare cases disputes it. For questioned costs, it determines whether those costs are allowable or must be repaid. For internal control or compliance findings, it establishes the required corrective actions and the timeline for completion.↵↵Once issued, the corrective actions become tracked obligations. Status is reported in the Summary Schedule of Prior Audit Findings in every subsequent single audit until the finding is resolved. If the deadline passes and corrections are not complete, the finding may be characterized as a repeat finding in the next audit — treated as more serious than a new finding.↵↵Organizations that disagree have appeal rights, but appeals must generally be filed within 60 to 90 days of receiving the management decision.↵↵Most finance teams know what a finding is. Fewer know exactly what triggers the six-month clock.

A mid-sized veterans service organization may simultaneously manage VA SSVF grants, DOL Homeless Veterans Reintegration Program funding, and HUD-VASH service contracts — each with different compliance frameworks, performance metrics, and audit standards.↵↵VA SSVF grants require veteran status verification before funds are expended on behalf of any participant. That means a DD-214 or equivalent documentation, income eligibility documentation, and housing status documentation in the case file before the first dollar is charged.↵↵DOL veterans employment grants require something different: tracking job placements, wages at placement, and employment retention at the 2nd quarter and 4th quarter after placement. That is an ongoing data collection obligation that extends months beyond the service period.↵↵When a case manager's time is split across VA-funded and DOL-funded activities, that cost must be allocated to the correct program — documented and defensible under two different compliance frameworks simultaneously.↵↵The VA awarded approximately $490 million in SSVF grants to community organizations in FY2023. The documentation requirements that come with those awards are not incidental to the compliance process. They are the compliance process.↵↵Organizations that cannot produce complete veteran eligibility files during a site visit face findings. The documentation must exist before the auditor asks.

The five document categories auditors request most often from grant files, in order of frequency:↵↵Time-and-effort records for a sample of payroll periods for grant-funded employees. For employees splitting time across programs, monthly personnel activity reports accounting for 100% of compensated time are required — semi-annual certifications apply only to single-program employees.↵↵Source documents for a sample of direct cost expenditures. Every non-personnel direct expenditure needs a receipt or invoice filed in the grant file, not just in accounts payable.↵↵Competitive bidding or sole-source justification documentation for above-threshold procurement. For federal grants, the solicitation documents, bids received, evaluation records, and award rationale must be in the file.↵↵Subrecipient risk assessments and sub-award agreements. Under 2 CFR 200.332(b), a pre-award risk assessment is required before the sub-award is made — not retroactively.↵↵The general ledger reconciliation underlying the final SF-425. The reconciliation confirming that SF-425 figures match accounting records exactly.↵↵The 3-year retention clock under 2 CFR 200.334 starts from the final expenditure report submission date — not the grant end date.↵↵The full Grant File Audit Checklist (pre-award through closeout and record retention) is available free at grantpipe.com.

Under 2 CFR 200.430, employees on multiple federal awards cannot use semi-annual time certification — but most organizations apply it to them anyway.↵↵Semi-annual certification is permitted only for employees working solely on a single federal award or cost objective. An employee working 80% on one federal award and 20% on administrative duties does not qualify. Monthly certification is required for that employee.↵↵Auditors know this rule and test for it by looking at how employees are classified and whether the certification frequency matches the classification. It is one of the most reliable single-audit findings in the personnel cost category.↵↵The correct process: pull a list of every employee with federal grant charges for the period, determine certification frequency based on whether they are single-award or multi-award, distribute certification forms within two weeks of month-end, collect and review for completeness, then reconcile certification percentages to posted payroll allocations.↵↵That reconciliation step — comparing what employees certified against what payroll actually posted — is the control that makes the entire system credible. Filing certifications without reconciling provides no assurance.↵↵Certifications requested 90 days after the period they cover are reconstructions from memory. Auditors can tell the difference.

Form 990 is a public document. That sentence changes how you should think about filing it.↵↵Every officer, director, trustee, and key employee's compensation is disclosed by name in Part VII. The five highest-compensated employees earning over $100,000 are also listed. A mid-sized nonprofit with $350,000 in gross receipts and $600,000 in assets files the full Form 990 — gross receipts over $200,000 or assets over $500,000 triggers the full return.↵↵The due date is the 15th day of the 5th month after fiscal year end — May 15 for calendar-year organizations. An automatic 6-month extension is available by filing Form 8868 before that date, extending to November 15. That extension is not a grace period; it is a formal mechanism that requires affirmative action before the due date.↵↵The IRS revokes tax-exempt status of approximately 30,000 organizations per year for failure to file for three consecutive years under IRC Section 6033(j). Reinstatement requires a new application and may attract additional IRS scrutiny.↵↵Grant funders, major donors, and watchdog organizations review 990s on ProPublica's Nonprofit Explorer — which has indexed more than 3 million filings — before engaging with an organization. Inaccurate restricted fund accounting flows directly into 990 inaccuracies on Parts VIII, IX, and Schedule D.↵↵The 990 is both a compliance filing and a credibility document. Treat it like both.

A youth program managing 21st Century Community Learning Centers funds, an AmeriCorps grant, and two foundation grants is operating four separate compliance frameworks simultaneously.↵↵21st CCLC compliance is not only financial — it requires participant attendance tracking, outcome reporting (teacher surveys, grade progression data), and demographic records submitted to both the federal Department of Education and the state education agency. The format and data requirements differ by state.↵↵AmeriCorps compliance runs through Corporation for National and Community Service systems — a separate portal, separate member hour tracking, and prohibited activities compliance that has nothing to do with 21st CCLC documentation.↵↵Foundation grants add a third reporting format and a third deadline calendar.↵↵For a lean program team — often one director managing 15 part-time program staff — this is not a coordination problem that more effort solves. Administrative overhead in multi-grant environments is part of that pressure.↵↵Youth programs carrying federal grants need compliance infrastructure, not just a spreadsheet with color-coded deadlines.

A grant reporting deadline tracked only by due date is a deadline that will eventually be missed.↵↵The fields that distinguish a reporting system that works from one that produces scrambles: named primary owner (a person, not a role), named backup owner, prep start date calculated from the report type, submission method and portal URL, and current status.↵↵For a combined interim report — narrative plus financial in a single submission — the prep lead time is 12–15 business days before the due date. Five federal grant compliance tasks that most grant tracking software does not handle — and where the audit findings originate.↵↵First: SEFA preparation. The Schedule of Expenditures of Federal Awards requires every federal program expended during the year to be listed by Assistance Listing Number (formerly CFDA number), with pass-through entity information for any sub-awards received. Most grant trackers record grant amounts and deadlines. They do not store ALN numbers or pass-through entity data in the structure the SEFA requires.↵↵Second: time-and-effort certification. Under 2 CFR 200.430, salaries charged to federal awards must be supported by signed certifications from employees or supervisors confirming actual time distribution. Most general-purpose grant trackers have no certification workflow.↵↵Third: NICRA indirect cost rate application. A Negotiated Indirect Cost Rate Agreement specifies the rate at which overhead can be charged to each federal award against a Modified Total Direct Costs base. Manual rate lookup across multiple concurrent awards produces both under-recovery and disallowances.↵↵Fourth: SF-425 federal financial report data organization. SF-425s are due 30 days after each calendar quarter for most awards. The data must reconcile to the general ledger. Assembling this manually from accounting exports each quarter is where errors compound.↵↵Fifth: budget-to-actual monitoring by object class. Federal awards are awarded against approved budget categories. Expenditures that cross category lines above defined thresholds require prior agency approval. Software that tracks total award balance but not category-level spend misses this control entirely.↵↵The gap between a pipeline tracker and a federal compliance system shows up at audit time, not at setup.

How to request a no-cost extension on a federal grant. Eight steps.↵↵Step 1: Confirm your award allows an NCE. Review the Notice of Award. Some awards prohibit extensions or cap them at one extension of up to 12 months. Confirm before drafting the request.↵↵Step 2: Confirm an NCE is the right tool. An NCE is for time, not money. If the real problem is insufficient funding, that is a budget supplement request — a different process with much lower approval odds. Be honest about which problem you have.↵↵Step 3: Request at least 30 days before the period end date. Most agencies require 30–60 days minimum. If your grant ends September 30 and you request on September 15, a 30-day processing timeline means the approval arrives October 15 — after expiration. Costs incurred after the end date but before the extension is approved are unallowable.↵↵Step 4: Contact your program officer before submitting. An informal conversation gives you early indication of approval likelihood and guidance on what justification the agency wants to see. Program officers often have preferences not documented in written guidance.↵↵Step 5: Write a specific justification. Name external factors that caused the delay — personnel vacancy, regulatory approval delay, disrupted program delivery — and describe exactly what work remains. Vague justifications ("we need more time") are routinely denied.↵↵Step 6: Prepare a spend-down projection by budget category. Show what funds remain in each line and the expected expenditures during the extension. Unexplained balances in categories with no spending plan raise flags.↵↵Step 7: Submit through the correct channel. HHS uses different portals than NIH eRA Commons, NSF Research.gov, or HUD's IDIS. Confirm the channel with your program officer.↵↵Step 8: After approval, update your grant record immediately. The new period end date shifts the final SF-425 due date (120 days after period end under 2 CFR 200.344), the final programmatic report, and any compliance calendar items tied to the original end date. File the approval letter in the grant file as an amendment to the Notice of Award.↵↵GrantPipe tracks NCE status and automatically updates compliance deadlines when extension dates change. grantpipe.com/signup

Feature gaps — not cost — are the primary driver.↵↵Before evaluating any CRM on grant capability, run three scenarios in the trial: enter a grant award, record a restricted expenditure, generate a funder compliance report. Scenario testing with your actual data tells you what it will do every month.

Under 2 CFR 200.430, posting payroll at the budgeted percentage and reconciling annually creates a full year of questioned costs if actual time differed from the budget.↵↵This is the single most common payroll compliance error in federal grant audits. The rule is the after-the-fact confirmation principle: payroll charges to federal awards must reflect actual hours worked, not what the grant budget assumed.↵↵Here is the step most organizations skip: reconciling allocation percentages to time-and-effort documentation at month-end, not at audit time.↵↵An employee whose time sheet shows 55% on Grant A but whose payroll was posted at 60% requires a correcting journal entry — dated in the period the time occurred, supported by the certified time record.↵↵Monthly reconciliation is not optional. Quarterly reconciliation is common but insufficient — it allows misallocations to compound over three months before correction. By the time an auditor samples your pay periods, you want those corrections already in the record.↵↵Two regulation references to keep on file: 2 CFR 200.430 governs the after-the-fact requirement. 2 CFR 200.430(i) permits semi-annual certification only for employees working 100% on a single federal award — not employees split across multiple grants.↵↵The 2024 Uniform Guidance revision also raised the de minimis indirect cost rate from 10% to 15% of Modified Total Direct Costs under 2 CFR 200.414(f), for organizations that have never negotiated a rate.

A subaward is not a contract. That distinction determines whether your organization has subrecipient monitoring obligations that go far beyond vendor management.↵↵The definition comes from 2 CFR 200.1: a subaward is an award provided by a pass-through entity to a subrecipient for the subrecipient to carry out part of a federal award. The key phrase is "carry out part of a federal program" — not provide goods or services for the pass-through entity's own use.↵↵The 2 CFR 200.331 five-factor test is what auditors apply to determine whether a payment is a subaward or a procurement contract. A subaward exists when the receiving entity determines who is eligible for federal assistance, has performance measured against federal program objectives, makes programmatic decisions, and is responsible for federal compliance.↵↵When those factors are present, the pass-through entity's obligations under 2 CFR 200.332 are triggered: pre-award risk assessment, a written subaward document with required provisions including the FAIN and CFDA number, ongoing monitoring, single-audit verification, and finding resolution.↵↵Characterizing a subaward as a procurement contract to avoid monitoring obligations is a common audit finding — and it generates two findings, not one: a missing written agreement and inadequate monitoring.↵↵The subaward document must exist in writing. A verbal arrangement does not satisfy 2 CFR 200.332(a). The documentation failure is itself a finding, independent of whether the program operated well.

Bloomerang starts at $125/month for up to 1,000 records. At 1,001 records, the bill becomes $166. At 5,001 records, it becomes $249.↵↵The per-record pricing model penalizes nonprofits for doing what a donor CRM is supposed to encourage: building a large donor database. A single fundraising event that adds 101 contacts can push an organization into the next tier regardless of whether those contacts ever donate.↵↵The less-discussed issue is what Bloomerang does not include at any tier: grant management. No restricted fund tracking, no grant lifecycle management, no compliance reporting automation, no expenditure tracking against specific grants.↵↵For organizations managing active grants, adding a purpose-built grant tool — Submittable, Foundant, or similar — typically adds $100 to $500 per month to the total operating cost. That changes the affordability calculation significantly compared to the headline $125 to $249 range.↵↵Bloomerang's donor retention dashboard is genuinely well-designed — one of the better-built features in the mid-market CRM space. The platform earns its reputation for individual giving programs. The limitation is structural: donor CRM and grant compliance require different data models, and Bloomerang was built for one of them.↵↵The right budgeting question is not the monthly subscription. It is what the total software cost looks like for the full workflow.

Grant-funded nonprofits answer to multiple audiences at the same time: funders want budget and outcome reports, boards want restricted vs. available resource visibility, and auditors need transaction-level support.↵↵The hard part is not generating one report. It is keeping every version of the funding story consistent when each audience works from a different system.↵↵Federal awards raise the stakes further. The Single Audit threshold increased to $1 million in federal expenditures effective October 1, 2024. Under the 2024 Uniform Guidance revision, nonprofits above that threshold face routine audit scrutiny — not occasional. And the GAO found that $1.17 trillion (16.7%) of federal awards were linked to severe audit findings over the 2017-2021 period.↵↵The operational pressure in this segment is not about finding more features. It is about reducing coordination failure. Development tracks the funder relationship in one system. Finance tracks revenue and expenses in another. Program leads keep narrative deliverables in email and shared drives. By the time a board packet is due, staff are rebuilding the same story from scratch.↵↵The software requirement is one system that keeps donors, grants, restricted funds, and reporting deadlines aligned before the month-end or audit pressure arrives — not one that creates more exports to manage.↵↵Restricted fund tracking is the baseline. Every active grant behaves like its own operating constraint. Teams need to see what was awarded, what has been spent, what remains, and what reporting work is next.

SEFA errors that appear at the start of a single audit — missing awards, misclassified cluster programs, period-of-performance mismatches — are almost always preventable.↵↵They happen because organizations reconstruct the Schedule of Expenditures of Federal Awards during fieldwork instead of maintaining the data throughout the year.↵↵The SEFA must list, per 2 CFR 200.510(b): the federal agency name, the Assistance Listing (CFDA) number, the FAIN, total federal expenditures for the fiscal year, and the aggregate amount passed through to subrecipients. One row per award — not per program.↵↵Five errors account for most SEFA deficiencies: a missing award not tracked in the grants register, a wrong CFDA number copied from the application rather than the notice of award, a period mismatch where fiscal year totals include prior-year costs, a cluster misidentification using last year's OMB Compliance Supplement, and a pass-through amount omitted because subrecipient payments were not tagged to the federal award at origination.↵↵The SEFA Prep Worksheet on GrantPipe's site walks through award-level data collection, cluster program identification, period-of-performance matching, subrecipient pass-through disclosure, and a pre-audit reconciliation checklist — structured to build the SEFA before auditors ask for it.↵↵Download it free at grantpipe.com.

Choosing between GrantPipe and Salesforce Nonprofit is a buy-versus-build decision disguised as a software comparison.↵↵Salesforce's core strength is optionality. A well-resourced organization can shape Salesforce around its own processes: custom data models, workflow automations, report structures, integrations. For organizations with strong internal admin capacity and complex process requirements, that flexibility is real.↵↵The cost is operating overhead. Before go-live, someone must define data structure, page layouts, permissions, automations, and governance. After go-live, someone must maintain it. Permissions change. Reports break. Teams turn over. New programs require new structure. The recurring pattern from organizations that have gone through implementation: the license is rarely the regret. The ownership model is.↵↵Salesforce Nonprofit licenses at $60 per user per month as a baseline, but implementation for a mid-sized nonprofit typically runs separately and substantially. The total operating budget — subscription, implementation, admin, and ecosystem add-ons — is where the comparison becomes visible.↵↵GrantPipe is built for the opposite preference: a purpose-built donor-plus-grant workflow without the shape-and-maintain burden. Flat tiers at $329, $539, and $1,079 per month, grant compliance built into the operating path, and no implementation consultant required before the system reflects your actual process.↵↵The question to ask before choosing either product: how much design work is required before it reflects our process, and who owns the system after go-live?

California nonprofits registered with the Attorney General's Registry of Charities and Fundraisers file Form RRF-1 every year. For calendar-year filers, the deadline is May 15 — four months and fifteen days after fiscal year end.↵↵Here is how to complete the filing without getting a deficiency notice.↵↵Step 1: Confirm Registry status. Use the Registry Search tool to verify current standing and your CT file number before doing anything else. A lapsed or suspended registration changes the filing path.↵↵Step 2: Calculate gross annual revenue accurately. This figure determines your fee tier and whether the $2 million audit threshold applies. Fees range from $0 for organizations under $25,000 to $1,200 for those above $500 million. The most common fee mistake is using the wrong revenue tier.↵↵Step 3: Engage an auditor now if at or above $2 million. The Nonprofit Integrity Act of 2004 (Government Code Section 12586(e)) requires an audited financial statement prepared by an independent CPA. The audit must be complete before you file. For calendar-year filers already at this point in April, the window is short.↵↵Step 4: Prepare RRF-1 and attach Form 990. The Registry requires the complete federal Form 990, 990-EZ, or 990-PF. Organizations filing the 990-N postcard must still provide California-level detail on the RRF-1 itself.↵↵Step 5: Submit with the correct fee. File online through the Registry portal — online filing reduces deficiency notices caused by attachment errors and missing signatures. Mail submissions with a check payable to "Department of Justice."↵↵Note: California's $2 million audit threshold is separate from the federal Single Audit threshold of $1 million in federal expenditures under 2 CFR 200.501. If your organization sits above both, you may face parallel audit obligations — often handled in a single engagement by the same CPA firm.↵↵GrantPipe tracks state charitable registration renewals alongside federal grant reporting deadlines in one compliance calendar — so RRF-1, federal SF-425 cadence, and restricted fund workflow share the same operating record.

post_text: 79% of nonprofits now run five or more third-party systems on top of their main CRM.↵↵That number, from the Omatic 2025 Nonprofit Integration Report, is not surprising to anyone who has been in the operations seat at a mid-sized nonprofit for more than a year.↵The donor database, the grant tracking spreadsheet, the accounting software, the email platform, and the file-sharing drive for compliance documents — each one is a siloed record of the same organization.↵The cost shows up every month-end close when the same numbers need to be reconciled across systems that do not talk to each other.↵For grant-active organizations, the risk is compounded: restricted fund balances live in the accounting system, grant deadlines live in a shared calendar, and donor context for a foundation funder lives in the CRM.↵None of those systems confirm whether the picture they each hold is current or complete.↵The integration tax is real — and most organizations accept it because the individual system choices seemed reasonable at the time they were made.↵↵GrantPipe was built to reduce that stack for nonprofits carrying both donor and grant work. If you are currently reconciling three or more systems every reporting cycle, it is worth a look.

Winning a grant is not the end of a process. It is the start of a multi-year compliance obligation.↵↵A 24-month federal grant will typically require: grant agreement execution, an initial budget submission, quarterly financial reports, semi-annual programmatic reports, budget modification approvals, and a final report with full supporting documentation.↵Each step has deadlines. Missing a single reporting deadline can trigger compliance findings that affect future funding eligibility.↵The most common compliance failure is not fraud — it is fund commingling. Grant dollars tracked only in a spreadsheet, deposited into the general operating account, with no separate accounting code to prove the restricted funds were spent on approved programmatic activities.↵When an auditor asks how $50,000 was spent, 'we think it went to these things' is not an acceptable answer.↵The second most common failure is personnel cost documentation. A time sheet that says '40 hours, program work' does not meet federal documentation standards. Time records must identify the grant or cost objective for each hour logged.↵Audit readiness does not begin six months before the audit. It begins on the day of award.↵↵Nonprofits that maintain organized grant files and current reconciliations throughout the grant period pass audits. Nonprofits that reconstruct documentation retroactively find the process much harder.

Every Single Audit finding requires a written Corrective Action Plan under 2 CFR 200.511(c).↵↵The CAP is not optional, and 'we will strengthen controls' is not a CAP. The regulation requires five specific elements for each finding: auditee position (agree or disagree), the specific corrective action being taken, the name and title of the responsible party, the completion date, and the finding reference number.↵Vague responses invite the awarding agency to escalate — imposing specific conditions, requiring prior approval for draws, or designating the organization as high-risk in future years.↵The deadline is strict: the CAP is included in the Single Audit reporting package due to the Federal Audit Clearinghouse at the earlier of 30 days after the auditor's report or nine months after fiscal year-end, per 2 CFR 200.512(a)(1).↵One specific point that organizations frequently miss: corrective action is not finished when the CAP is filed. It is finished when the action is implemented and documented with dated evidence — signed policy, training attendance, reconciled records. Auditors test CAP completion in the following year's audit as prior-year follow-up.↵Repeat findings in two consecutive audits trigger specific conditions under 2 CFR 200.208 — prior approval requirements, enhanced monitoring, or high-risk designation that persists until the pattern is broken.↵↵A strong CAP reads like a project plan: specific actions, named owners, firm dates. That same document works for internal accountability.

Voluntary committed cost share is the cost share trap most nonprofits do not see until they are in an audit.↵↵Under 2 CFR 200.306, cost share is the non-federal portion of total allowable project cost. It can be mandatory — required by the NOFO — or voluntary and committed, meaning the organization offered additional match in the application to improve its competitive score.↵Here is the part that catches organizations off guard: the moment that voluntary cost share is written into a federal award agreement, it becomes legally binding. A nonprofit that pledges $50,000 in volunteer hours to strengthen a proposal must document and achieve that $50,000 in contributions during implementation. A shortfall is an audit finding with the same consequences as a mandatory match failure.↵The documentation requirements for voluntary match are identical to mandatory match: verifiable from grantee records, necessary and reasonable for the project, allowable under applicable cost principles, and not sourced from another federal award.↵In-kind match — volunteer labor, donated goods, facility use — is not a softer requirement than cash match. Auditors test in-kind the same way they test direct costs: they look for contemporaneous documentation, fair market valuations, and consistency with the approved budget.↵The risk is concentrated in organizations that over-propose match to be competitive and then run short of documentation during implementation.↵↵Federal pass-through funds cannot serve as match — even when the federal origin of the state dollars is not obvious in the funding flow.

Qgiv was acquired by Bloomerang in 2024. If you are evaluating Qgiv today, you are evaluating Bloomerang's product direction, not an independent platform.↵↵Qgiv built a real position in nonprofit fundraising: peer-to-peer campaign pages, event ticketing, auction management, and embedded donation forms at accessible price points. It served organizations that needed fundraising form infrastructure without a full CRM.↵What Qgiv was not, and was never designed to be, is a donor CRM or a grant management system. Contact records in Qgiv were functional enough to track donors across transactions, but the platform had no relationship depth — no grant tracking, no restricted fund allocation, no compliance reporting.↵The acquisition does not change Qgiv's scope. It changes who sets the roadmap. Features requested by existing Qgiv customers now compete with Bloomerang's own development priorities.↵The practical question for a nonprofit evaluating its software stack is: what problem are you actually trying to solve? If the problem is fundraising form infrastructure and peer-to-peer events, Qgiv still covers that. If the problem is managing donor relationships and grant compliance in one place, the tool category is different.↵Organizations using a fundraising-form-only platform alongside a separate CRM manage two sets of donor records in over 60% of cases.↵↵Treating platform selection as a category question — not a feature comparison — usually produces a better outcome.

Mental health nonprofits managing SAMHSA grants and CCBHC program funding face a compliance problem that most grant software does not model: the same service cost cannot be claimed to both federal grant funding and Medicaid billing simultaneously.↵↵SAMHSA's FY2023 budget was approximately $7.5 billion, with the majority flowing through block grants to states and then to local mental health and substance use disorder service providers. The organizations receiving those funds are typically running MHBG, SABG, and CCBHC funding streams alongside Medicaid reimbursement for the same clinical services.↵When the same staff member serves both Medicaid-eligible clients and clients covered under grant funding, time records must allocate labor costs to the correct funding source for every hour worked. A time sheet that says 'program work' is not sufficient. Neither is a general allocation percentage applied at month-end without contemporaneous records.↵Cost duplication between Medicaid billing and federal grants is a primary OIG audit focus in behavioral health organizations. The finding is often unintentional — it results from accounting systems that cannot track costs by payer at the service delivery level.↵CCBHC programs add another layer: the prospective payment system rate is recalibrated based on actual cost reports by service type, so the documentation requirement is more detailed than standard grant financial reporting.↵Organizations providing substance use disorder services also carry 42 CFR Part 2 confidentiality obligations that restrict what patient-level data can be shared in grant reports — requiring aggregate metrics that satisfy funder requirements without violating patient consent rules.↵↵Multi-funder behavioral health compliance is not a spreadsheet problem. The required granularity of cost tracking by payer, service type, and funding source exceeds what manual processes can reliably sustain.

Release-from-restriction is one of the most frequently mishandled events in nonprofit accounting — and the error is almost always about timing, not intent.↵↵Under FASB ASC 958, a purpose restriction is released when the organization incurs qualifying expenditures for the specified use — not at year-end, not when the grant closes, not when the auditor asks. The release amount equals the qualifying expenses actually incurred in the period.↵A common error: organizations hold the full restricted fund balance until year-end and release it in a single journal entry. If expenses were incurred throughout the year, the releases should have happened throughout the year. Recording them all in December creates a presentation that does not match when conditions were actually satisfied.↵For auditors reviewing restricted fund management, the question is not whether the total release amount is correct. It is whether each release was recorded in the correct period, supported by qualifying expenditures, and documented with a journal entry that references the supporting GL detail.↵The three release types under ASC 958 require different triggers: purpose restrictions release when qualifying expenses are incurred; time restrictions release when the required date or event occurs; perpetual restrictions on principal never release, only investment income may be released according to the organization's spending policy.↵Endowment income release is a separate calculation from operating grant releases — they should not share the same journal entry or documentation file.↵↵A free restricted funds release calculator — covering fund-by-fund release calculations, documentation requirements, and journal entry references — is available at grantpipe.com/free.

Procurement deficiencies are among the top 10 compliance findings in HHS, DOE, and DOJ-funded single audits every year — and the most common specific finding is inadequate competition documentation.↵↵The 2024 Uniform Guidance revision (89 FR 30046, effective October 1, 2024) did not raise the simplified acquisition threshold. It clarified it at $250,000. Organizations whose written procurement policies still reference older figures are technically out of compliance before a single purchase is made.↵↵There are five procurement methods under 2 CFR 200 Subpart D, each with different competition requirements. Micro-purchases up to $10,000 need no competition. Small purchases between $10,001 and $250,000 require price quotations from adequate sources. Sealed bids and competitive proposals apply above $250,000. Sole source requires one of four specific written justifications.↵↵The written policy itself is the first finding. 2 CFR 200.318 requires it in writing. An undocumented process — even a competitive one — fails the standard.↵↵SAM.gov debarment checks are required before any federally funded award over $25,000. The check must be documented and dated before award, not at the start of solicitation.↵↵GrantPipe's grant management module captures procurement method, competition documentation status, and debarment check dates at the transaction level — the format auditors need without pulling files from multiple staff members.

Bloomerang has grant fields. That does not mean it handles grant compliance.↵↵The difference matters operationally. Bloomerang can record a funder name, an award amount, and a report due date. What it cannot do is model the restriction on those funds, track expenditures against approved budget categories, flag when a budget line is approaching its ceiling, or generate a financial report to send to the funder.↵↵A $75,000 grant restricted to youth programming is not the same as $75,000 in unrestricted revenue. Every expenditure charged to that grant must fall within the approved scope. Bloomerang records the grant. It does not monitor compliance with it.↵↵The three-grant threshold is real. Organizations managing one or two active grants with light restrictions can hold the compliance workflow in a spreadsheet alongside Bloomerang. At three to five active grants — different funders, different fiscal years, different restriction types — that spreadsheet becomes a liability.↵↵Federal grants accelerate the timeline. SF-425 quarterly reports require expenditure-level data that Bloomerang's grant fields cannot supply. The compliance overhead increases substantially the first time a federal award enters the portfolio.↵↵The clearest signal: your grants manager maintains more compliance spreadsheets than Bloomerang grant records. That gap is the workflow Bloomerang was not built to cover.

The most common pledge accounting error is not the math. It is the classification.↵↵Under FASB ASC 958-605, a pledge is conditional when a donor-imposed barrier must be overcome before the organization is entitled to the funds — a matching requirement, a milestone, a future event. Without a barrier, the pledge is unconditional and must be recorded as contribution revenue and receivable when the promise is made, not when cash arrives.↵↵ASU 2018-08 sharpened the definition of a barrier: it must be specific, measurable, and related to the purpose of the agreement. A donor who says 'I will give $50,000 if you hire a program director' has imposed a barrier. A donor who says 'I hope you will hire a program director with this $50,000' has not.↵↵Misclassifying unconditional as conditional understates current-year revenue. The financial statements are misstated, not just conservative.↵↵Multi-year pledges add another layer. A $100,000 pledge payable $20,000 per year over five years is worth less than $100,000 today. ASC 958-605 requires discounting to present value using a risk-adjusted rate, typically 3-5%. Skipping the discount overstates both pledge receivables and contribution revenue.↵↵Every pledge portfolio also needs an allowance for uncollectible pledges. An allowance of zero is almost never defensible — even strong portfolios see 1-5% attrition.

The difference between a grant pipeline and a grant portfolio matters operationally.↵↵A grant pipeline is the pre-award stage: opportunities in research, applications in progress, submissions awaiting decision. The development director uses it to forecast revenue and prioritize staff time. A well-maintained pipeline shows every opportunity by funder, amount, probability of award, and expected decision date — enabling a 6-18 month revenue projection.↵↵A grant portfolio is the post-award stage: active awards with restrictions, spending trajectories, compliance deadlines, and reporting obligations. Finance and program staff operate here. This is where compliance failures actually occur.↵↵These phases connect but are managed differently. When a pipeline opportunity becomes an award, it enters the portfolio — and the work shifts from relationship management and writing to expenditure tracking, restricted fund monitoring, and funder reporting.↵↵Most compliance problems happen in the portfolio phase, not the pipeline phase. Organizations that treat the grant lifecycle as ending at the award decision lose visibility into the post-award work at exactly the point where the real risk sits.↵↵Revenue risk concentrates in the pipeline. Compliance risk concentrates in the portfolio. A development director who only manages pre-award data is managing half the picture.↵↵Probability weighting works better than raw totals for forecasting. A $100,000 application with a 60% probability of award has an expected value of $60,000. Assigning 90% to every open application is not forecasting — it is wishful thinking with extra steps.

A restricted fund tracking spreadsheet works until it does not. Knowing which point that is matters.↵↵The template structure is straightforward: one row per active restricted grant, with fund name, funder, restriction type (purpose, time, or perpetual), award amount, received to date, monthly actuals by period, cumulative expenses, remaining balance, award end date, release conditions, and documentation reference.↵↵The monthly update process has six steps: pull current period expenses from the general ledger after month-end close, enter the period actuals exactly (no rounding, no estimating), verify the cumulative total against the GL, recalculate remaining balances, update statuses for funds that closed, and date and initial the spreadsheet to establish the documentation trail.↵↵The reconciliation is not optional. Every month, total receipts, total expenses by fund, and remaining balance by fund in the spreadsheet should match the general ledger exactly. When they do not, investigate immediately. Small discrepancies caught early are traceable. Accumulated discrepancies require forensic-level investigation at audit time.↵↵The signals that the spreadsheet has reached its limit: more than six to eight active restricted grants, a federal grant with 2 CFR 200 compliance requirements, staff turnover creating knowledge gaps, the monthly reconciliation taking more than two hours, or an auditor noting the manual methodology as a finding.↵↵At any of those points, the tracking system has been outgrown — not the people managing it.↵↵Download the free Restricted Fund Tracking Spreadsheet at grantpipe.com/free/restricted-fund-tracking-spreadsheet.
