Five questions that cut through grant compliance software evaluations faster than any feature list:↵↵1. Where are restricted fund balances visible right now, without opening a spreadsheet? If the answer requires a phone call or a manual pull, the tracking system is not working.↵↵2. How is documentation attached to the underlying spend? Receipts and supporting documentation need to live alongside the transaction, not in a separate folder that has to be assembled at audit time.↵↵3. Who sees the reporting calendar before deadlines become urgent? The compliance calendar should be visible to finance, development, and leadership — not just the grants manager with the spreadsheet.↵↵4. Can finance and development describe the status of the same grant without translating between two systems? Dual-system workflows produce two versions of the same data and one recurring reconciliation problem.↵↵5. What still depends on a named individual after implementation? Any system that works only because one specific person knows how to maintain it is not a system — it is institutional knowledge with a tool on top.↵↵The answers expose where the real operational burden sits: before award in the pipeline, or after award in the portfolio. Purpose-built compliance workflow focuses on post-award because that is where the compliance risk actually lives.↵↵Spreadsheets stay common for too long because they are cheap and already present. The cost shows up later as coordination time, delayed reporting confidence, and the recurring risk that the next answer leadership needs will take too long to assemble.

How to set up restricted fund tracking that survives an audit:↵↵Step 1: Separate each restricted grant into its own fund code in the accounting system before any expenses are posted. Coding transactions retrospectively creates gaps that compound. Set up the fund code at award, not at first expenditure.↵↵Step 2: Build the restriction profile from the grant agreement — not from memory. Record the purpose restriction exactly as the funder wrote it, the approved budget by category, the award period start and end dates, and the conditions under which the restriction is released.↵↵Step 3: Pull monthly actuals from the general ledger after month-end close, by fund code. Enter exact figures — no rounding, no estimates. The cumulative total in the tracking system must match the GL for the same period exactly.↵↵Step 4: Monitor budget-to-actual by category, not just by total award. A grant budget with $10,000 approved for program supplies that has been charged $12,000 in supplies is a compliance issue, even if the total award balance is still positive.↵↵Step 5: Flag restrictions for release when the condition is met — either the purpose has been fulfilled or the time period has lapsed. Delayed reclassification overstates restricted net assets on the statement of financial position.↵↵Step 6: Reconcile the tracking register to the GL before every funder report, not after. A discrepancy discovered during report preparation creates pressure to submit incorrect numbers.↵↵GrantPipe automates steps 3 through 5 as standing reports, so the compliance picture is current without a monthly manual rebuild. Bloomerang is not a grant compliance tool. That distinction matters more than most organizations realize until a federal audit arrives.↵↵Bloomerang tracks grants as fundraising relationship records. There is no mechanism for seeing "Grant X: $100,000 awarded, $67,340 spent, $32,660 remaining."↵↵There is no SF-425 generation capability because Bloomerang does not hold the financial data an SF-425 requires.↵↵There is no time and effort tracking for personnel charged to federal awards — a requirement under 2 CFR 200 that cannot be satisfied with a CRM relationship record.↵↵There is no non-editable audit trail for grant expenditure changes.↵↵Organizations managing federal grants or five or more simultaneous restricted awards from Bloomerang are relying on a system that was genuinely not designed for those functions. A December gift refunded in January is not a simple reversal. The donor's prior-year charitable deduction has been affected.↵↵IRS Publication 1771 requires written acknowledgment for contributions of $250 or more. When a gift is refunded — especially across a tax year — that original acknowledgment letter is no longer accurate. A correction letter must be issued stating the original gift date and amount, the refund date and amount, and the net contribution of zero for a full refund.↵↵The letter should explicitly note that the refund occurred in a different tax year and recommend the donor consult their tax advisor about any prior deduction they claimed.↵↵Three other things that go wrong when this process is handled manually: the CRM record is not updated, leaving giving totals inflated and LYBUNT/SYBUNT metrics overstated; the restricted fund balance is not reversed, which distorts net asset reporting under FASB ASC 958; and the Form 990 Part VIII contribution total is wrong because the refund happened in a prior fiscal year and was not tracked at the transaction level.↵↵Same-year refunds are straightforward. Cross-year refunds require communication, documentation, and careful accounting treatment. Organizations that process one refund per quarter rarely have a consistent workflow for this — until an audit asks for the file.

MTDC is not total direct costs. That distinction costs organizations money on federal awards every year.↵↵Modified Total Direct Costs, defined at 2 CFR 200.1, is the cost base you multiply by your indirect cost rate — whether that is the 15% de minimis rate or a negotiated NICRA. It begins with total direct costs and removes eight mandatory categories before the rate is applied.↵↵The exclusions: equipment at or above your capitalization threshold (generally $5,000), capital expenditures, patient care charges, tuition remission, rental costs for off-site facilities, scholarships and fellowships, participant support costs, and sub-award amounts above the first $25,000 per subcontract.↵↵That last one is where organizations consistently leave recovery on the table or overclaim. If a grant includes a $75,000 sub-award, only $25,000 of it counts toward MTDC. The remaining $50,000 is excluded. Applying the indirect rate to the full $75,000 overclaims indirect costs and produces an audit finding.↵↵The GAO reports that approximately 30% of single audits identify at least one cost-claim finding. Indirect cost base errors are among the most frequently cited categories.↵↵2 CFR 200.414(f) specifies MTDC as the base for the 15% de minimis rate. Applying 15% to total direct costs is wrong and it is a routine finding.

Processing a nonprofit donor refund involves eight distinct steps. Here is how to do it without creating tax problems for the donor or compliance problems for the organization.↵↵Step 1: Confirm the request in writing and verify the original gift details — amount, date, fund designation, payment method.↵↵Step 2: Determine whether the refund crosses a tax year. A December gift refunded in January affects the donor's prior-year return. Document this before anything else.↵↵Step 3: Refund through the original payment method. Credit card to the same card. ACH to the originating account. Retain the transaction confirmation as primary documentation.↵↵Step 4: Void or revise the tax acknowledgment. Under IRS Publication 1771, the original letter must be corrected. Issue a revised letter stating the original amount, refund amount and date, and net contribution. For cross-year refunds, explicitly note that the donor should consult their tax advisor.↵↵Step 5: Book the general ledger reversal — credit cash, debit contribution revenue — dated as of the actual refund date, not the original gift date.↵↵Step 6: Update the CRM record. An unaddressed refund inflates giving totals and corrupts LYBUNT/SYBUNT metrics.↵↵Step 7: Address restricted fund implications. If the gift was restricted and program costs were already incurred, the fund may have a deficit. Management decides how to cover it. Do not leave a restricted fund with a negative balance.↵↵Step 8: Assess Form 990 impact. Same-year refunds reduce Part VIII gross contributions. Cross-year refunds reduce net assets in the year processed.↵↵GrantPipe connects the donor CRM record to the gift accounting record so a refund updates both simultaneously and the tax acknowledgment status auto-flags. Try it at grantpipe.com.

A donor's verbal commitment is not a pledge. It is a prospect record until someone papers it.↵↵Under FASB ASC 958-605, a pledge is an unconditional promise to give — legally enforceable, with documentary evidence. Signed pledge card, countersigned letter, or grant agreement. Without that, many auditors require the item be treated as intent rather than pledge.↵↵The distinction has real accounting consequences. An unconditional pledge is recognized as contribution revenue and receivable when the promise is made, not when the cash arrives.↵↵A conditional pledge — one with a donor-imposed barrier like a matching requirement or milestone — stays off the balance sheet entirely until the barrier is substantially met. ASU 2018-08 sharpened exactly how specific that barrier must be.↵↵Multi-year pledges add another layer: ASC 958-605 requires discounting to present value for pledges collectible beyond one year. A $100,000 pledge payable over five years at a 4% discount rate is recorded at roughly $89,000 today.↵↵Skipping the present-value step overstates receivables and distorts financial statements. Missing the conditional classification delays revenue and creates disclosure burden.↵↵What pledge-tracking errors are most common in your audit experience?

The 15% de minimis indirect cost rate under 2 CFR 200.414(f) requires no proposal, no cognizant agency, and no annual renewal.↵↵For organizations whose actual indirect rate falls in the 8-12% range and whose federal funding is under $1-2M annually, the administrative savings usually outweigh any marginal recovery gain from negotiating a full NICRA.↵↵The math changes above roughly 13-15%. On $2M of Modified Total Direct Costs, a 15% NICRA recovers $300K vs. $200K under de minimis — a $100K annual difference. That gap usually pays for the 40-80 hour first-time proposal effort within two years.↵↵To negotiate a NICRA: identify your cognizant agency (typically HHS Division of Cost Allocation for most nonprofits), define the cost pool and allocation base, reconcile every number to your audited financials, and submit a proposal package that includes audited financials, IRS Form 990, personnel time allocation evidence, and a Certificate of Indirect Costs.↵↵The cognizant agency will not negotiate off numbers that do not tie to the audit. Unreconciled proposals are returned immediately.↵↵Rate type choice matters too. Fixed-with-carryforward is the sweet spot for most mid-sized organizations: variances roll into the next period instead of requiring retroactive adjustment.↵↵The 2024 revision to 2 CFR 200.414(f) extended de minimis eligibility significantly. Run the math before committing to the proposal path.

Time and effort certification is the documentation that connects salary charges to actual work performed on federal grants — and it is the most frequently missing documentation in federal grant audits.↵↵Under 2 CFR 200.430, charges to federal awards for salaries must be based on records that accurately reflect the work performed. The key word is 'contemporaneous' — records prepared at or near the time the work is done, not reconstructed months later.↵↵Two tracks exist. Employees working solely on a single federal program may use semi-annual certifications. Employees whose time is split across multiple activities — a mix of grants, federal and non-federal work — must complete Personnel Activity Reports at least monthly.↵↵Auditors examine the dates on T&E records carefully. A batch of monthly certifications for an entire year, all signed on the same day in June, is retroactive. It does not matter how accurately the person believes they are reflecting actual effort — the standard is not met.↵↵Missing T&E records for federally charged salaries produce questioned costs. Questioned costs that cannot be supported become disallowed costs requiring repayment.↵↵Salary is typically the largest budget line on any grant. Without T&E documentation, the whole line is at risk.

Neon CRM does not publish pricing. Every quote requires a demo cycle before you can put a number in a board-approved budget.↵↵The base platform covers donor management, fundraising pages, and email marketing. Events management, membership tracking, and advanced analytics are separate add-ons — each an additional line item on the contract.↵↵For nonprofits with active grant portfolios: comprehensive grant lifecycle management, restricted fund tracking, and compliance documentation are not standard features. Organizations managing foundation or government grants with expenditure reporting requirements typically need custom configuration or a separate grant tool on top of what the base CRM provides.↵↵The module-by-module billing structure means a mid-sized nonprofit managing donors, running events, and handling membership renewals assembles a meaningfully different contract than the base platform suggests. Request an itemized quote for your specific module list.↵↵What does your current toolchain actually cost when you add up every piece?

Disability services organizations receiving HHS ACL grants, IDEA flow-through funding, and Medicaid waiver reimbursements are running three different compliance systems on the same staff and the same participants.↵↵The Administration for Community Living administers over $2.5 billion in grants annually. ACL grant compliance follows 2 CFR 200 Uniform Guidance plus ACL program-specific requirements. Each participant must be documented as meeting program eligibility criteria before grant funds are spent on their behalf.↵↵IDEA flow-through adds a nested layer: federal IDEA requirements, state implementation requirements, and local education agency program requirements. Part C and Part B have different documentation standards.↵↵The Medicaid coexistence creates a specific compliance risk: the same costs cannot be claimed to both Medicaid billing and a federal grant. Cost allocation documentation — time records, allocation methodology, reconciliation between Medicaid billing and grant expenditure records — is not optional.↵↵DOL disability employment grants add outcome tracking that extends months past the service period: employment status at placement, wage rate, and retention at the 2nd and 4th quarters post-placement.↵↵Multi-funder federal compliance is a daily operational requirement for disability services organizations, not an annual audit exercise.

ASU 2016-14 eliminated temporarily restricted and permanently restricted net asset categories in 2018. Many nonprofit accounting systems, funder reports, and staff still use the old terminology.↵↵The current GAAP framework under FASB ASC 958 uses two classifications: net assets with donor restrictions and net assets without donor restrictions. Board-designated funds belong in the second category regardless of how internal they feel — an internal designation is not a donor restriction.↵↵The most expensive misapplication: treating reimbursement-basis government grants as restricted revenue and recognizing the full award amount when it is received. Reimbursement-basis grants typically contain conditions under ASU 2018-08 — revenue is recognized as expenses are incurred, not at award.↵↵Five audit findings related to ASC 958 appear repeatedly: restricted net assets not supported by a fund-level sub-ledger, premature revenue recognition on conditional grants, board-designated funds misclassified as donor-restricted, functional expense allocation undocumented, and underwater endowments not disclosed.↵↵The FASB ASC 958 Quick Reference covers net asset classification, contribution recognition rules, the conditions vs. restrictions test, and an annual close checklist. Free download at grantpipe.com/free/fasb-asc-958-quick-reference.

Blackbaud Raiser's Edge NXT and Financial Edge NXT are two products with two licenses that must integrate. When the development director needs the current restricted fund balance and the finance director needs the cultivation history, each is asking for data in the other person's system.↵↵RE NXT typically runs $30,000-$100,000 per year in the mid-market range. Financial Edge NXT is a separate license. Combined cost for both products commonly exceeds $60,000-$200,000 per year before implementation — which typically requires a Blackbaud-certified partner at $20,000-$60,000.↵↵For a $2M nonprofit, that combined cost is 3-10% of total revenue before the system is operational.↵↵Large institutions where Blackbaud is the organizational standard have valid reasons to maintain it. The question for mid-sized organizations is whether the capability that comes with that cost is actually used.

Six donor management platforms, evaluated against the question most comparisons ignore: does this tool handle grant compliance, or does your team still need a separate system for that?↵↵Bloomerang ($125/mo): strong donor retention analytics, no grant lifecycle management, no restricted fund tracking.↵↵DonorPerfect ($99/mo): large user community, basic grant tracking fields, no compliance automation or audit trail on grant records.↵↵Little Green Light ($39/mo): entry-level, accessible for small organizations, no grant management features.↵↵Salesforce Nonprofit ($60/user/month before implementation): the most flexible platform, the highest total cost of ownership. Implementation typically runs $30,000-$100,000 for mid-sized organizations.↵↵Keela ($99/mo): modern interface, built-in email marketing, limited grant management, no restricted fund compliance automation.↵↵GrantPipe ($329/mo): donor CRM, restricted fund tracking, grant compliance, and compliance reporting in one system.↵↵The platforms with serious grant compliance capability in this group: two. The rest store grant records as data you can look up, not as a system that produces audit-ready reports.↵↵What is your team's current setup for grant compliance?

The sector average nonprofit retains fewer than half its donors each year. New donor retention is worse: 19-26% in the first year. Here is the step-by-step that actually moves the number.↵↵Step 1: Calculate your current retention rate. Retained donors divided by total prior-period donors, times 100. If you do not know this number, start here.↵↵Step 2: Acknowledge within 48 hours. Donors who receive a personal thank-you referencing the specific program their gift supports retain at materially higher rates than those receiving a generic receipt.↵↵Step 3: Segment by LYBUNT and SYBUNT. LYBUNT (Last Year But Unfortunately Not This Year) is your primary re-engagement list. SYBUNT requires a different message — what has changed, what they may have missed.↵↵Step 4: Report impact at least once per year. 'Your support helped fund the 87 families who received emergency rental assistance through our HUD grant' is a retention message. A generic year-in-review is not.↵↵Step 5: Convert one-time donors to recurring gifts. Monthly programs typically retain 80-90% of participants vs. the 43-46% sector average. The ask should come soon after the first gift.↵↵Step 6: Cultivate major gift prospects deliberately. The top 20% of donors by gift size typically generate 80% of revenue. Mass communications without segmentation accelerate lapse at the mid-level.↵↵GrantPipe connects donor records to grant-funded program outcomes so development staff can generate impact reports without manually reconciling two systems. The Growth tier at $539/month includes LYBUNT/SYBUNT segmentation and acknowledgment tracking built in.

The IRS processed approximately 42,000 Forms 990-T from 501(c)(3) organizations in fiscal year 2023 — and most of those filings became harder the moment the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act took effect.↵↵The TCJA silo rule under IRC Section 512(a)(6) ended loss netting across unrelated activities. A nonprofit with a $50,000 parking lot profit and a $40,000 bookstore loss now pays 21% tax on the full $50,000 — the bookstore loss stays in its own silo.↵↵Before 2018, those activities could offset each other. That option is gone.↵↵The $1,000 gross income threshold for filing applies per silo, not in aggregate. An organization with two unrelated activities can hit the filing threshold twice — even if the net across both is zero.↵↵Pre-TCJA net operating loss carryforwards remain available as aggregate offsets. Post-TCJA NOLs are silo-specific. Tracking which bucket a carryforward lives in is essential to getting the 990-T right.↵↵State filing obligations typically follow the federal trigger — California at 8.84%, New York at 7.25%, each with their own modification rules.↵↵GrantPipe tracks revenue by activity type, which is the same categorization your CPA needs to run the silo analysis. If your organization generates parking, advertising, or affinity program income, that conversation should happen before year-end.

A common misconception: the restricted funds dashboard is a finance tool.↵↵It is not. It is a management tool — and the people who need it most are Executive Directors, not accountants.↵↵Finance already knows the balances. The problem is that information stays inside the accounting system, translated into reports that require context to interpret.↵↵An ED needs four things in one view: total restricted fund balances by grant, active risk flags (low burn rate, over-budget lines), upcoming reporting deadlines, and funds approaching expiration with remaining balances.↵↵A grant with $40,000 remaining and 45 days left in the award period needs roughly $27,000 per month in spend. If the current burn rate is $8,000 per month, that gap is visible — and actionable — if the dashboard shows it.↵↵Board-designated funds belong in the unrestricted net asset class under FASB ASC 958, not in the restricted fund summary. A common dashboard error is including board designations alongside donor-restricted funds, which overstates the restricted balance and misleads the ED.↵↵The weekly update takes fifteen minutes for a finance staff member who is already maintaining the fund records. The cost of an inaccurate dashboard — an expiring grant found too late — is considerably higher.↵↵What does your current system show an ED about restricted fund health at a glance?

Pledge write-offs are one of the most commonly misbooked entries in nonprofit accounting.↵↵Under FASB ASC 958, an uncollectible pledge is not a bad debt expense. The correct entry debits the allowance for uncollectible pledges and credits the pledge receivable — no income statement expense.↵↵The instinct coming from for-profit accounting is to book bad debt expense. That instinct is wrong here, and auditors test for it.↵↵Where things go further wrong: organizations that recorded pledges with a zero allowance have nowhere to put the write-off except contribution revenue — a direct reduction to the top line that should have been anticipated at pledge recognition.↵↵Multi-year pledges carry an additional step. When a pledge discounted to present value is written off, the unamortized discount on that portion must also be eliminated. Leaving the discount in place after the receivable is removed overstates the contra-asset.↵↵Approval documentation must exist before the journal entry is posted — not added after the fact. Auditors look for the collectibility assessment, the signed approval, and the journal entry in a single file.↵↵Under FASB ASC 958-605, unconditional pledges must be recorded when the promise is made. The allowance estimated at that moment is the organization's first defense against a write-off hitting revenue.↵↵When did your organization last review the adequacy of its pledge allowance relative to the current aging?

A restricted fund holds money the organization legally cannot spend in any way it chooses.↵↵The distinction between holding assets and controlling them is the foundation of fund accounting. A $100,000 restricted grant increases the bank balance. It does not increase freely available resources — the money is obligated before it arrives.↵↵Under FASB ASC 958, restricted funds fall into three categories. Purpose restrictions limit spending to a specific program or activity. Time restrictions make funds unavailable until a future date — the unpaid installments of a multi-year pledge are a time-restricted asset. Perpetual restrictions require the principal to be held indefinitely; only investment income may be spent.↵↵FASB ASU 2016-14, effective for fiscal years beginning after December 15, 2017, consolidated the prior three-class system into two: net assets with donor restrictions and net assets without donor restrictions. All three restriction types now appear in a single balance sheet class, with footnote disclosure about the composition.↵↵Board-designated funds are a frequent source of misclassification. A board designation sits within net assets without donor restrictions — the board can rescind it at the next meeting. Confusing a board designation with a donor restriction overstates restricted net assets. Auditors test for this directly.↵↵The restriction releases when the donor's conditions are satisfied and documented. For purpose restrictions, that happens as qualifying expenditures are incurred. Without documentation, the release is an assertion.

Keela starts at $99/month and has a clean interface. For nonprofits focused on individual giving, it is a capable platform.↵↵The gap shows up when you manage grants alongside donors.↵↵Keela's grant tracking records award amounts and deadlines. It does not model the post-award lifecycle: restricted fund allocation to specific programs, expenditure tracking against those pools, or compliance documentation tied to funder requirements.↵↵For a nonprofit where grants represent 30–40% of revenue, that gap forces fragmentation: donor CRM in Keela, grant compliance in spreadsheets, manual reconciliation every month.↵↵The Omatic 2025 Nonprofit Integration Report found that nearly half of nonprofits are considering switching CRMs in the next 12 months — driven primarily by feature gaps, not cost. The most common trigger is operational fragmentation, where staff can still enter data but cannot get from transaction to funder report without rebuilding context in another tool.↵↵The question before switching is whether the replacement actually closes the gap. A lower price or cleaner interface at the same level of compliance depth is not an upgrade for grant-funded organizations — it is a lateral move.↵↵Three reports to identify before any demo: what does your team produce every month, what restricted-fund detail does leadership actually review, and what workflows break when one staff member is out?

Legal aid organizations receiving LSC funding operate under two simultaneous compliance frameworks — and they do not map cleanly onto each other.↵↵The financial layer: 2 CFR 200 Uniform Guidance applies because LSC is a federal funder. Single audit requirements, allowable cost documentation, time-and-effort certifications, and procurement standards apply in full.↵↵The programmatic layer: 45 CFR Part 1600-1644 adds LSC-specific requirements on top. Restrictions on case types, client eligibility verification, outcome definitions, and use of funds rules that go beyond standard federal grant compliance.↵↵LSC's 2017 Performance Criteria require grantees to maintain systems capable of producing case outcome data, client demographic information in aggregate, financial expenditure data by cost category, and case type allocations — all reconciled to the grant budget semi-annually.↵↵IOLTA funds add a third requirement: trust accounting rules under state bar regulations require separate account maintenance and reporting demonstrating allowable use — a legal authority distinct from both federal grant compliance and donor restriction law.↵↵The compliance failures that show up in LSC audits are consistent: client eligibility documentation gaps, financial reporting reconciliation errors, and case-type allocation discrepancies. Each is a documentation problem, not a practice problem.↵↵Organizations managing LSC, IOLTA, OVW, and foundation grants simultaneously are running four different reporting frameworks with four different regulatory bodies.

The math on donor retention is straightforward and frequently ignored.↵↵A nonprofit with 2,000 donors and a 40% retention rate loses 1,200 donors every year. Moving from 40% to 50% retention keeps 200 more donors — at a modest $150 average gift, that is $30,000 in revenue that did not require a new acquisition.↵↵For organizations in the $500K–$10M budget range, retention is where growth actually comes from.↵↵First-time donor retention runs 20–25% at most organizations. That single segment has more improvement leverage than almost anything else in a development program — and the highest-leverage intervention is acknowledgment timing.↵↵The 48-hour window after a first gift is when the donor's connection to the cause is strongest. An automated email receipt is table stakes. A personal acknowledgment within 48 hours for gifts of $100 or more sets the tone for the entire relationship.↵↵Recurring donors deserve a different treatment. A donor giving $25 per month is worth $300 per year and typically retains for three to five years with good stewardship — a $900–$1,500 lifetime value donor. Failed payment monitoring, separate from the monthly acknowledgment rhythm, is the most commonly missed step.↵↵The full Donor Retention Playbook covers acknowledgment timing, recurring donor stewardship, lapsed donor reactivation, segmentation by giving level, and how to calculate and report retention rates to the board. Free download at grantpipe.com.

How to document personnel costs on a federal grant every pay period — without creating an audit problem.↵↵2 CFR 200.430 requires salary charges to federal awards to be based on records reflecting actual work performed. Not budgeted percentages. Not end-of-year certifications. Contemporaneous records tied to each pay period.↵↵Step 1. Identify every employee whose compensation flows to a federal award — including employees funded 100% by one grant and employees split across multiple funding sources.↵↵Step 2. Determine the documentation standard. Employees funded solely on one federal program qualify for semi-annual certification. Split-funded employees require full effort reporting showing 100% of compensated time distributed across all activities, federal and non-federal.↵↵Step 3. Complete the effort record at the end of each pay period. Hours or percentage by grant and program activity for each day in the period. Employee signs. Supervisor reviews and signs.↵↵Step 4. Finance processes payroll charges based on the approved effort record — not the budget, not last period's allocation.↵↵Step 5. File the signed effort records in the grant file. Auditors check that record dates are near payroll dates, not completed weeks or months later.↵↵Step 6. When corrections are needed: document the original allocation, the corrected allocation, the reason, and the supervisor approval. 2 CFR 200.430(i)(8) permits after-the-fact adjustments when properly supported — undocumented retroactive reallocations are not permitted.↵↵The cycle takes five to ten minutes per employee per pay period. Missing T&E documentation typically results in questioned costs and potential repayment.↵↵GrantPipe connects staff cost allocation to effort records and grant budgets, so the documentation that satisfies a 2 CFR 200.430 audit is a byproduct of normal payroll processing rather than an end-of-year reconstruction.

42% of non-government funders cap indirect cost allowances at 10% or less — while actual nonprofit overhead runs 25–35%.↵↵That gap is not hypothetical. It shows up every grant cycle as unreimbursed costs your organization absorbs.↵The MacArthur Foundation has publicly stated that 29% is the minimum for a financially healthy nonprofit.↵The OMB de minimis rate is 15% — a floor, not a target.↵When only 20% of grants include enough overhead coverage, the math compounds quietly across a grant portfolio.↵Budget-vs-actual tracking that surfaces this line item per award is the first step to quantifying the real net grant value.↵A $50,000 award with $10,000 in compliance costs is effectively a $40,000 grant — every grant manager should know that number before acceptance.↵↵GrantPipe tracks expenditures against approved budget lines in real time, so indirect cost shortfalls appear in the dashboard before they compound. See how it works at grantpipe.com.

The myth: if a cost is necessary for the grant, it is allowable under 2 CFR 200 Subpart E.↵↵The reality: a cost must pass four separate tests simultaneously.↵Necessary and reasonable — the prudent-person standard, evaluated at the time of purchase, not in hindsight.↵Conforms to limitations — the award terms can prohibit a cost even if it passes the reasonableness test.↵Consistently applied — a cost type treated as indirect for non-federal work cannot be claimed as direct on a federal award.↵Adequately documented — no documentation means no deduction, regardless of whether the cost was legitimate.↵↵Cost allowability and allocability findings represent over 40% of all questioned cost findings in federal single audits, per GAO's annual high-risk program analysis.↵The most commonly disallowed items: entertainment, alcohol (never allowable under 200.423), lobbying, and compensation above established organizational pay scales.↵Passing the necessity test while failing documentation is a compliance finding. Both matter.↵↵Which of the four tests does your team check most consistently?

A release from restriction is not a revenue event. It is a reclassification — and the date it is posted matters.↵↵Under FASB ASC 958-205, a restricted net asset releases when the donor-imposed stipulation expires or is fulfilled — not when the accountant gets to the journal entry.↵For purpose restrictions, the release date is the date the last qualifying expenditure was incurred.↵For time restrictions, the release date is the date the restriction expired.↵Releasing the full grant balance at year-end without verifying that expenditures equal or exceed the release amount is the most common error in this workflow.↵If $80,000 was received and $65,000 was spent, only $65,000 releases — the remaining $15,000 carries forward as restricted.↵The audit file needs the GL expenditure detail, the donor agreement, the dated journal entry, and the roll-forward schedule that ties to the GL.↵↵Do your restricted fund release entries carry a supporting expenditure schedule, or is the journal entry standing alone?

Program income is the grant compliance category that most organizations undercount — not because they ignore it, but because the definition is broader than it sounds.↵↵"Program income" under 2 CFR 200.307 means gross income earned from activities supported by the federal award during the period of performance.↵Not net of expenses. Gross. If participants pay a $50 registration fee for a grant-funded training program, $50 is the program income figure — not $50 minus delivery costs.↵Insurance reimbursements (Medicaid, Medicare, private) for services delivered under a federally-funded health grant are typically program income.↵Proceeds from selling items fabricated with grant funds are program income.↵There are three treatment methods: deduction (default), addition, and cost-sharing. If the grant agreement is silent, the deduction method applies automatically.↵Unreported program income is a compliance finding under 2 CFR 200.307 even if the money was used appropriately.↵The finding is not misuse — it is failure to report and formally apply the required treatment method.↵↵The communication gap between program staff who know income was earned and finance staff who prepare the SF-425 is the most common failure point.

Blackbaud does not publish pricing. Every organization negotiates blind.↵↵Mid-sized nonprofits ($500K–$10M) report paying $5,000–$15,000/year in base licensing for Raiser's Edge NXT.↵Implementation with a certified partner runs $10,000–$50,000+ — required, not optional.↵Year-one total cost typically lands between $20,000 and $65,000 for a mid-market organization.↵Multi-year contracts are standard, early termination carries penalties, and annual price increases of 5–10% are built in.↵Online giving forms, email marketing, and advanced analytics are frequently separate paid add-ons not included in base pricing.↵Raiser's Edge NXT does not include grant compliance at any tier — restricted fund tracking and compliance reporting require manual workarounds.↵↵The headline monthly equivalent looks manageable until you model year-one cost in three buckets: subscription, implementation effort, and ongoing process overhead.↵↵What was the actual year-one cost when your organization last adopted a platform like this?

A mid-sized food bank can be running five separate federal compliance frameworks simultaneously — each with different deadlines, different documentation requirements, and different contacts.↵↵USDA TEFAP requires pounds-by-category commodity distribution logs, eligibility verification records, and storage documentation.↵FEMA EFSP requires expenditure tracking by allowed categories on a quarterly basis — and reports go to the local board, not the state agency.↵CDBG, Feeding America network allocations, and foundation grants each add another set of reporting requirements.↵TEFAP reports typically go to the state TEFAP agency; EFSP reports go to the local EFSP board and National Board.↵These are separate systems with separate contacts, separate formats, and separate consequences for missed deadlines.↵Seasonal demand spikes in December and summer create pressure to reallocate restricted funds quickly — but grant restrictions do not flex for demand patterns.↵↵The cumulative administrative load is what breaks spreadsheet-based compliance management for food banks, not any single grant's complexity.↵↵How many separate compliance frameworks is your team tracking today?

Under 2 CFR 200.308, a grant budget modification requires prior approval when it involves a change in scope, a key personnel change, or a transfer that exceeds the award's rebudgeting threshold — commonly 10% of the total award.↵↵The threshold applies cumulatively, not per transaction.↵A series of small transfers that each fall below 10% can collectively exceed it if you are not tracking the running total.↵Every modification below the threshold still needs to be documented internally in a cumulative log — the absence of that log is a compliance finding when the award is reviewed.↵The formal request must describe the specific change (exact categories, dollar amounts, direction of transfer), justify the operational need, and demonstrate the modification does not alter project scope or objectives.↵Do not spend from modified budget categories until the approval is received and filed.↵↵A free grant budget amendment request template covering all six required sections — including the cumulative modification log — is available at grantpipe.com/free.

Givebutter vs Bloomerang is often framed as "free vs $125/month." The more accurate frame is: a fundraising platform vs a donor CRM.↵↵Givebutter earns revenue through optional donor tips at checkout — no subscription, but standard payment processing fees (2.9% + $0.30) apply.↵It runs campaigns, events, peer-to-peer fundraising, and livestreams well. Donor CRM depth is basic — no segmentation, no at-risk dashboards, no lapsed donor workflows.↵Bloomerang starts at $125/month and scales by constituent records. The at-risk donor dashboard and multi-year giving analytics are the main arguments for the subscription cost.↵Only 33.3% of nonprofits rate their CRM systems as effective, per the Fifty & Fifty 2025 Nonprofit Peer Report.↵Neither platform includes grant lifecycle management or restricted fund compliance.↵Organizations receiving restricted grants manage compliance separately from both — either in a third system or in spreadsheets.↵↵If grant compliance is a material part of your development operation, that gap is worth weighing in any platform comparison.

GrantHub Pro was sunset January 31, 2026. Before picking the replacement, answer one question: were you primarily using GrantHub for pipeline tracking, or for post-award compliance?↵↵Most GrantHub users fell into two groups.↵Group one tracked applications, deadline calendars, and funder contacts — and managed post-award compliance separately in spreadsheets.↵Group two wanted both in one place and lived with the gap.↵For group one, almost any modern grant tracking tool replicates the visible function. For group two, a replacement that only covers pipeline management re-creates the original problem.↵Five tools worth evaluating: GrantPipe (post-award compliance + donor CRM), Instrumentl (pre-award discovery), Salesforce Nonprofit (configurable, heavy implementation), Neon CRM (donor-first, minimal compliance depth), Submittable (grantmaker-side only — not a recipient tool).↵Salesforce Nonprofit typically requires $20,000–$50,000+ in implementation consulting before it is usable for mid-sized compliance workflows.↵Submittable is the funder's portal. You submit to it as an applicant — you would not own a subscription.↵↵The migration window is the opportunity to close the compliance gap, not just replicate a sunset product's features.

How to build a grant reporting calendar that actually prevents missed deadlines — step by step.↵↵Step 1: Pull every active grant agreement and extract every required report. Do not rely on memory. Federal notices of award, foundation grant letters, and state passthrough subgrant agreements each specify their own schedules.↵↵Step 2: For each report, record five things: due date, report type (financial or programmatic), submission method (portal URL, email, mail), responsible person, and current status. Financial and programmatic reports for the same grant often have different due dates and different owners.↵↵Step 3: Set internal lead-time reminders at 30 days and 10 days before each external deadline. The 30-day trigger is for data collection; the 10-day trigger is for drafting and review.↵↵Step 4: Identify deadline stacking periods 60–90 days in advance. Federal fiscal year end (September 30) and calendar year end (December 31) routinely stack multiple reports in the same two-week window.↵↵Step 5: Update the calendar immediately when an amendment arrives, a no-cost extension changes the period-of-performance end date, or a program officer confirms a deadline change in writing. A calendar built at award inception and never updated gives false confidence.↵↵Step 6: Connect each calendar entry to the underlying grant file — prior reports, performance measures, budget-vs-actual data, and portal login credentials. The deadline alert is useless if the responsible person cannot find the grant file.↵↵Final reports for federal awards are typically due within 120 days of the period-of-performance end date. Missing a federal deadline generates a delinquency flag that can suspend draw-down access and affect future award eligibility.↵↵GrantPipe centralizes the reporting calendar alongside the grant file, budget tracking, and compliance documentation — so the alert and the supporting data are in the same place. Try it free at grantpipe.com.

FFATA requires prime federal recipients to report subawards of $25,000 or more — and most organizations miss the deadline without realizing it.↵↵The report is due by the end of the month following the month the subaward was obligated.↵A subaward obligated March 15 must be filed by April 30 — not 30 days after the obligation date, but the end of the following calendar month.↵The report goes through the SAM.gov FFATA Subaward Reporting System (formerly FSRS.gov), linked to the prime award by the Federal Award Identification Number.↵If the FAIN is wrong, the subaward does not appear under the correct prime on USAspending.gov — and that gap shows up in reviews.↵Executive compensation reporting applies only when the subrecipient met the $25M / 80% federal revenue test in the prior fiscal year and the data is not already public via a Form 990.↵↵Most prime recipients also carry a separate obligation under 2 CFR 200.332 for subrecipient monitoring — both apply to the same subaward but serve different purposes.↵↵GrantPipe tracks FFATA reporting deadlines and 200.332 monitoring tasks on the same grant record so neither obligation falls through.

Data migration is cited as the top barrier to CRM adoption by 44% of nonprofits that have delayed a software switch.↵↵The most common reason a CSV donor import fails is not a technical problem — it is name formatting in the source file.↵A spreadsheet that has 'John and Jane Smith' in one row and 'Smith, John' in another cannot be automatically de-duplicated.↵Standardizing name columns — last name and first name as separate fields — eliminates the majority of import failures before the file is uploaded.↵The other failure mode: giving history rows that reference donor records not yet in the system.↵Import donors first, then gifts in a second pass linked by email or external ID.↵↵The full import failure rate drops dramatically when the source file is clean.↵Spending 20 minutes cleaning the export before uploading is faster than correcting records one at a time after the fact.↵↵What is the messiest data situation you have inherited from a previous system?

A donor pledge is not a donation until it is unconditional.↵↵Under FASB ASC 958-605, an unconditional pledge is recorded as contribution revenue and receivable on the date the promise is made — not when cash arrives.↵A conditional pledge, where the donor has imposed a barrier such as a matching requirement or milestone, stays off the balance sheet entirely until that barrier is met.↵Multi-year pledges collectible beyond one year must be discounted to present value; a five-year $100,000 pledge at 4% is recorded at roughly $89,000 today.↵Every pledge portfolio needs an allowance for uncollectibles — zero is almost never defensible, even for strong donor relationships.↵↵The most common pledge accounting error: misclassifying a conditional pledge as unconditional, which overstates current-year revenue.↵↵The second most common: skipping present-value discounting because the math looks complicated.↵Both are adjusting items at audit.↵↵When a pledge is written off, it reduces contribution revenue — not bad debt expense.↵That distinction catches organizations coming from for-profit accounting backgrounds every time.

The CFDA number was renamed the Assistance Listing Number (ALN) in 2019 — but most grant agreements, audit reports, and accounting systems still say CFDA.↵↵The format is XX.XXX: first two digits identify the federal agency, last three identify the program.↵CFDA 93.044 is the Aging Services program. CFDA 14.231 is HUD's Emergency Solutions Grants.↵The ALN does three things simultaneously: links the award to the program catalog, drives the SEFA structure under 2 CFR 200.510, and points the auditor to the right chapter in the OMB Compliance Supplement.↵Getting the ALN wrong on the SEFA is a compliance finding in its own right — approximately 15% of single audit financial-reporting findings involve SEFA ALN reporting errors, per Federal Audit Clearinghouse data.↵↵Pass-through entities have an additional obligation: when sub-awarding, 2 CFR 200.332 requires the ALN to be included in the sub-award agreement.↵Omitting it is a finding even when everything else is correct.↵↵One more common misconception: the ALN does not change when a new award is issued under the same program.↵Your award number changes; the program identifier does not.

Little Green Light starts at $45/month for up to 2,500 records — one of the most transparent pricing structures in the nonprofit CRM market.↵↵All features are included at every tier, there are no user limits, and no long-term contracts are required.↵The tier scales by roughly $15/month increments as the record count grows: $60 for 5,000 records, $75 for 10,000, $90 for 20,000.↵Every contact counts toward the tier — active donors, lapsed donors, event attendees, volunteers.↵A 10-year-old organization with a large lapsed file can find itself in a higher tier than expected.↵↵What the pricing page does not say: there is no grant management at any tier.↵No restricted fund tracking, no expenditure reporting tied to specific grants, no compliance documentation for audits.↵For organizations managing three or more active grants with different funders and reporting requirements, adding a separate grant tool typically exceeds the cost of a platform that handles both.↵↵The headline price question is not whether the monthly fee fits today.↵It is whether the tool keeps the process simple enough to avoid added software spend later.

There are approximately 1,400 HRSA-funded health center organizations operating more than 14,000 service delivery sites — and HRSA Health Center Program grants totaled $6.6 billion in FY2023.↵↵Community health centers occupy a compliance position unlike most nonprofits: they are simultaneously a healthcare provider under 42 CFR Part 51c and a federal grant recipient under 2 CFR 200.↵Section 330 grantees must maintain documented cost allocation methodologies for all shared costs — staff, facilities, medical supplies — across programs.↵An arbitrary allocation percentage applied without documentation is a finding waiting to happen during a HRSA site visit or OIG audit.↵The annual Uniform Data System report compounds the complexity: it integrates financial data with patient visit counts by payer type, clinical quality measures, and service data in a single submission.↵↵When a center receives both a base Section 330 grant and a SAMHSA behavioral health co-location award, each program's expenditures must be tracked independently — commingling is the most common finding in HRSA compliance reviews.↵↵This dual obligation is where standard donor management tools stop and purpose-built grant compliance software earns its cost.

Boards do not approve software purchases because of features.↵They approve them because the current approach is creating a documented risk.↵↵The framing that moves a board: 'We have a compliance gap that creates audit exposure' is more compelling than 'this system has better reporting.'↵The three dimensions boards are actually evaluating: Is the current approach creating compliance risk? Is the proposed investment proportionate? Is there a credible implementation plan with a named owner?↵For total cost of ownership framing, boards respond to specific dollar amounts — 'Finance staff spend 12 hours per month on manual reconciliation at a loaded cost of $450 per month' lands harder than 'this takes too much time.'↵↵The 3-year TCO comparison is the format finance committee members expect.↵Model year-one cost in three buckets: subscription, implementation labor, and process overhead — the ongoing cost of exports, manual reconciliation, and report reformatting that continues after launch.↵↵Free board approval memo template for software purchase: covers the current-state risk framing, TCO comparison table, implementation plan, and resolution language.↵Download at grantpipe.com/free/board-approval-memo-software-template.

Blackbaud vs a focused mid-market platform is not a question of which vendor is more capable.↵It is a question of how much operating complexity the organization can absorb.↵↵Blackbaud's strength is ecosystem breadth: advancement tooling, finance modules, institutional credibility.↵That breadth is a genuine advantage for large organizations that have the staff depth, process maturity, and budget to operate it well.↵For a mid-sized nonprofit with lean finance and development capacity, the same breadth can become a tax — more setup decisions, longer time to steady state, and more surface area than the team actually uses.↵↵The four questions worth asking before the evaluation: How long before staff can rely on the system weekly? How much grant and restricted-fund context still has to be translated manually after implementation? What does leadership need to see every month? How much of the platform will the team actually use?↵↵If the answer to the fourth question is 'not much,' ecosystem depth stops being a strength.↵↵The hidden cost in enterprise-leaning systems is rarely on the invoice.↵It is in the organizational drag that comes before the team reaches confident, weekly use.

Grant tracking software divides into two distinct categories — and most buyers searching for the term need the second one.↵↵Pre-award grant tracking: discovering opportunities, managing application pipelines, tracking submission deadlines.↵Post-award grant tracking: expenditure management against approved budget categories, restricted fund balance monitoring, compliance report generation, audit documentation.↵↵The top-ranked tools in most search results are optimized for pre-award pipeline management.↵Post-award compliance is less marketable, but it is where compliance failures actually happen.↵↵Three capabilities determine whether a tool can support compliance work:↵First, restricted fund balance tracking by budget category — not just award-level totals.↵Second, expenditure documentation linked to individual grant budget lines.↵Third, compliance report generation from actual expenditure data.↵↵A tool that cannot do all three tracks grants informally.↵It does not manage compliance.↵↵GrantHub Pro was sunset by Foundant/CommunityForce on January 31, 2026 — it is no longer available.↵If it appears on a shortlist, it should not be there.↵↵Spreadsheets work for one or two simple grants.↵At three or more active grants with different funders, restrictions, and reporting cycles, the fragility typically outpaces the flexibility.

Time and effort certification under 2 CFR 200.430 has one central compliance point: the after-the-fact rule.↵↵Personnel costs charged to federal awards must be supported by records that reflect actual work performed — not budgeted, planned, or estimated time.↵A payroll system that automatically allocates 60% to one grant and 40% to another each pay period, without employee confirmation, is a budget-based allocation. It does not satisfy the requirement.↵The clearest audit red flag: timesheets that mirror budget percentages exactly, month after month, with no variation.↵Auditors treat that pattern as presumptive evidence the certifications are prospective, not after-the-fact.↵↵Acceptable formats under the 2024 Uniform Guidance revision include paper timesheets, spreadsheet logs, electronic time-tracking systems, and payroll systems with project coding confirmed by the employee at period end.↵The format does not matter. What matters is that a qualified person confirms what actually happened, after the period ends.↵↵Personnel costs represent 65-75% of federal grant expenditures in human services awards.↵Missing or inadequate time records generate dollar-for-dollar disallowed costs — partial documentation does not reduce the exposure proportionally.↵↵GrantPipe tracks certification status by period and flags late or missing records in the compliance dashboard before the audit, not during it.↵Start a free trial at app.grantpipe.com/signup.

The median nonprofit spends 6–8 hours per grant per year on reporting — 30+ cumulative hours over a grant's lifetime.↵↵That is not time spent on program work. That is time spent assembling budget-vs-actual tables, hunting for expenditure documentation, and formatting numbers a funder already has in their system.↵↵Most of the labor comes from two sources: the financial reconciliation by line item, and the narrative that ties outcomes to the targets written into the original application.↵↵A federal grant report needs both. So does a foundation progress report. The format differs — SF-425 for federal awards, PDF or web form for most foundations — but the core content is identical.↵↵Budget vs. actual by category. Actual participant counts versus committed targets. Explanation of any variance above 10%.↵↵If those three elements are current and organized throughout the grant period, the 6–8 hours compresses significantly. If they are not, the report becomes the reconciliation.↵↵GrantPipe tracks restricted fund balances and budget-vs-actual by line item throughout the grant period — so the data is ready when the report deadline arrives, not assembled at deadline pressure.

The myth: three donor segments is enough — everyone, major donors, lapsed.↵↵The problem: three segments cannot drive differentiated action.↵↵AFP Fundraising Effectiveness Project data shows first-year donor retention averaging 19–22%. Donors retained for three or more years retain at 60–65%. Those two populations need entirely different outreach. One list treats them the same.↵↵Organizations with retention programs that actually work use fifteen or more saved segments, each connected to a specific workflow: LYBUNT re-activation, first-year second-gift cultivation, mid-level upgrade asks, lapsed sustainer re-engagement.↵↵The cost difference matters here. Acquiring a new donor runs $50–$100. Re-activating a lapsed donor costs $15–$30. Segmentation that surfaces the right LYBUNT population before each appeal is among the highest-ROI activities in the development calendar.↵↵A saved segment is not a static list. It is a live query that updates as records change. When a lapsed donor gives again, they leave the re-activation segment automatically. No manual refresh, no spreadsheet reconciliation.↵↵The difference between three segments and fifteen is not complexity. It is whether the development team has actionable lists or a single undifferentiated pile.

A release from restriction is not a revenue event. Under FASB ASC 958-205, it is a reclassification.↵↵Debit net assets with donor restrictions. Credit net assets without donor restrictions. The total net asset number does not change. The columns shift.↵↵That distinction matters because it determines when the entry is dated — and dating it incorrectly is one of the most common year-end close errors in nonprofit accounting.↵↵The release should be dated at the moment the restriction was satisfied. For purpose restrictions, that is the date the last qualifying expenditure was incurred. For time restrictions, it is the date the time condition expired. Not the date the accountant posted the entry. Not December 31 by default.↵↵A year-end procedure that batches all releases at fiscal close — regardless of when expenditures occurred — misrepresents when restricted funds became available. Auditors testing restricted net assets will trace back to expenditure evidence. If the entry date does not align with the documented fulfillment date, it is a finding.↵↵The practical fix: run purpose-restriction releases monthly as program expenses post. By year-end, the calculation is already done. The close becomes a verification exercise, not a three-day reconciliation.↵↵FASB ASU 2016-14 requires footnote disclosure of the nature, amounts, and expected timing of remaining restrictions.

Your board sees total gifts received. That number is not actionable.↵↵It tells them what came in. It does not tell them whether the donor base is healthy or declining. Two organizations can show the same revenue total — one retained 70% of donors, the other retained 35% and replaced churn with expensive new acquisition. The revenue line hides that difference.↵↵The four metrics that produce a useful board conversation:↵↵Overall retention rate with year-over-year trend. Retention rate by giving segment — major ($1,000+), mid-level ($250–$999), general. LYBUNT count with estimated recapture revenue in dollars. Average gift size trend over four or more quarters.↵↵Major donor retention should sit at 80% or higher. If it falls below that, the board needs to see it — major donors typically represent a disproportionate share of total revenue and falling retention is not a quarterly metric problem, it is a relationship problem.↵↵Translate the retention rate into dollars before the board meeting: 260 lapsed donors at an average prior gift of $185 equals $48,100 in revenue that must be replaced through acquisition or recapture. That is a board-level decision, not a staff-level observation.↵↵Report this quarterly. Annual retention reporting arrives too late to adjust strategy in the same fiscal year.

GrantHub Pro was sunset January 31, 2026. If your organization ran on it, the migration is not just a data transfer — it is a compliance infrastructure rebuild.↵↵GrantHub's export files contain grant names, funder contacts, deadline records, and application history. What they do not contain: expenditure data, restricted fund balances, approved budget by category, or compliance documentation. GrantHub never tracked those things.↵↵The post-award compliance layer has to be built from scratch in the replacement system, sourced from award letters, your accounting system, and institutional memory. Budget 30–60 minutes per active grant for that reconstruction.↵↵The replacement evaluation checklist has two sections. The first covers what GrantHub did — pipeline management, deadline calendar, funder contact history. The second covers what GrantHub did not do — restricted fund balance tracking, expenditure mapping to budget lines, SF-425 generation, audit documentation trail.↵↵Both sections matter. A replacement that only replicates GrantHub's pre-award capabilities leaves the compliance gap open.↵↵Under 2 CFR 200.334, grant records must be retained for a minimum of three years from the final expenditure report submission date. Archive GrantHub export files accordingly before the cleanup.↵↵The full GrantHub Migration Checklist — covering all seven phases from export validation through decommission — is available free at grantpipe.com.

Bloomerang starts at $125/month and deploys in one to two weeks. Salesforce Nonprofit Cloud often carries $30,000–$100,000 in implementation costs before any staff log in.↵↵That gap is the most important number in the comparison, and it rarely appears in the demos.↵↵Bloomerang is a donor-first CRM. It does donor retention and fundraising workflows well. It does not do restricted fund accounting or post-award compliance in the way a grant-heavy organization needs those functions to work.↵↵Salesforce can be configured to track grants and related compliance, but that means scoping, building, and maintaining custom objects, fields, workflows, and reporting — by consultants, at $150–$250 per hour, with ongoing admin costs of $10,000–$25,000 per year.↵↵The practical filter for the comparison: which product gives your team a trustworthy report faster with less manual reconstruction after the demo ends?↵↵For organizations whose primary question is donor engagement, Bloomerang is usually the more practical choice. For organizations that also manage restricted grants and need finance-grade compliance, neither product gives you the answer without additional work.↵↵The buying mistake that repeats: comparing both tools only at the CRM layer and finding out after implementation what the grant compliance workflow actually costs.

Only 33.3% of nonprofits rate their CRM as effective. The other 66% are paying for a system they cannot trust to answer the basic questions.↵↵Five things executive directors need from a CRM that feature comparison tables miss:↵↵Board-ready reports without a weekend of prep. If pulling the quarterly donor retention summary requires exporting to Excel and rebuilding formulas, the platform is adding work rather than removing it.↵↵Predictable total cost. Salesforce NPSP lists free licenses through TechSoup. The implementation runs $30,000–$100,000. Ongoing admin costs $10,000–$25,000 per year. The license is not the cost.↵↵Grant compliance in the same record as donor context. Development staff and finance staff should look at the same grant record — not a development record in the CRM and a compliance record in a spreadsheet that require manual reconciliation.↵↵Staff adoption without sustained training investment. A platform that requires certification to produce a standard report will be adopted by one person and avoided by everyone else.↵↵Answers to the questions board members actually ask: What is our donor retention rate. How many grants are active and are we compliant. What does the development pipeline look like for next fiscal year. Those questions should take minutes, not hours.↵↵The evaluation question worth asking before any demo: can this platform reduce the time between a board question and a verified answer?

Every cost charged to a federal grant must pass three tests simultaneously under 2 CFR Part 200.↵↵Allowability — the cost is not prohibited by the terms of the award, by 2 CFR 200.420–200.475, or by any other applicable regulation. Explicit unallowable categories include alcoholic beverages (200.423), entertainment (200.438), fundraising costs (200.442), and lobbying (200.450). No exceptions on these.↵↵Allocability — the grant actually benefited from the cost. A staff member who works 40% of their time on a federal grant can allocate 40% of their salary to that grant. A supply purchase used entirely on a different program cannot be allocated to the grant regardless of how it is coded.↵↵Reasonableness — a prudent person would pay this amount for this good or service in the ordinary course of business. Costs established through competitive procurement are easier to defend. Costs from related parties without arm's-length pricing, or costs that significantly exceed market rates, may fail this test even if they are otherwise allowable.↵↵A cost that passes two tests but fails one is disallowable and must be removed from the grant ledger — typically absorbed from unrestricted funds or repaid to the federal agency.↵↵The documentation principle: if you had to explain the cost to a skeptical auditor who has never heard of your organization, write that explanation at the time of the transaction. Documentation assembled retroactively carries far less weight.↵↵GrantPipe tracks budget-vs-actual by line item against 2 CFR 200 cost categories, so compliance gaps surface during the grant period — not at audit.

The median nonprofit spends 6–8 hours per grant per year on funder reporting — and 30+ hours over a grant's full lifetime.↵↵That number comes from the Center for Effective Philanthropy's Grantee Perception Reports and it understates the problem for organizations managing five or more active grants simultaneously.↵↵The time is not wasted on complex analysis. It goes to reformatting the same budget-vs-actual table for four different funder templates, hunting down expenditure records scattered across spreadsheets and email folders, and reconciling financial figures that do not quite match what is in the accounting system.↵↵A reporting calendar mapped twelve months out — with data collection tasks assigned in advance of each deadline — cuts that time significantly. The report itself is not the work. The scramble to assemble the inputs is.↵↵Federal, state, and foundation funders each expect different formats and levels of detail. No universal template exists. But a baseline structure covering the eight common elements (grant ID, executive summary, activities, outcome data, budget-vs-actual, variances, next-period plans, certification signature) handles 80% of the packaging work before funder-specific formatting begins.↵↵GrantPipe generates funder-specific financial report drafts directly from the grant ledger — no spreadsheet rebuild before each deadline. See how at grantpipe.com.

Payroll allocation errors are rare. They are the opposite: they appear in roughly 25% of single-audit engagements every year.↵↵The HHS Office of Inspector General cross-cutting findings report identifies payroll allocation as a persistent top-five single audit finding. The reason is structural, not negligent.↵↵Most nonprofits run payroll in ADP or QuickBooks. The grants manager maintains a separate spreadsheet showing how each employee's time should split across awards. Finance makes journal entries to move costs to grant-specific accounts. Time-and-effort certifications live in a shared folder somewhere.↵↵At audit time, the auditor needs three things: the certification, the allocation entry matching the certification, and the payroll register confirming the gross pay amount. Reconciling those three sources — for every employee, every month, every award — is where the gaps appear.↵↵The 2024 revision to 2 CFR 200.430 clarified explicitly that budget-based allocations without after-the-fact verification remain non-compliant. Organizations that entered allocations at planned percentages rather than certified actual percentages have a finding waiting for them.↵↵The fix is not more spreadsheet columns. It is linking the allocation entry, the certification, and the payroll register so the comparison happens before the auditor does it.

Before you submit an Indirect Cost Rate proposal, run this check: does every number in your cost pool and allocation base trace directly to a line in your audited financial statements?↵↵If the answer is anything other than yes, the cognizant agency will return the proposal without negotiating.↵↵The ICR proposal process under 2 CFR 200.414 starts earlier than most organizations realize. There is a threshold decision before any paperwork: if your actual indirect rate is below 10%, the de minimis rate under 2 CFR 200.414(f) likely beats the NICRA. No proposal, no negotiation, no annual renewal. For organizations under $1–2M in federal funding with modest indirect costs, the administrative savings outweigh the marginal recovery difference.↵↵When a NICRA does win — typically when actual indirect rates run 15% or higher — the math is concrete. On $2M of Modified Total Direct Costs, a 15% rate recovers $300K versus $200K at de minimis. A $100K annual difference justifies the 40–80 hours of first-time proposal effort.↵↵The rate type choice is separate from the rate level. Fixed-with-carryforward is the most common structure for mid-sized nonprofits: the rate is set in advance, variances roll into the next period rather than triggering retroactive adjustments, and the administrative burden is manageable.↵↵The cognizant agency for most nonprofits without a dominant single federal funder is HHS Division of Cost Allocation. First-time negotiations take 90–180 days from submission. Plan accordingly.

A federal grant drawdown is not automatic. The awarding agency loads the grant funds into a payment system — usually ASAP, the Automated Standard Application for Payments — and the grantee must actively request disbursement.↵↵ASAP processed more than $700 billion in federal disbursements in fiscal year 2023. Every one of those transactions started with a grantee initiating a request.↵↵Under 2 CFR 200.305, two payment methods govern when the request can happen.↵↵Advance payment releases funds before expenses are incurred — the grantee requests an amount projected to cover the next 30 days. The advance must reconcile against actual expenses, and any excess must be returned promptly. Most mid-sized nonprofits use advance payment because they cannot float payroll while waiting for reimbursement.↵↵Reimbursement releases funds after expenses are posted in the accounting system. The grantee documents the costs, runs an expenditure report, and requests the documented amount. Impossible to over-draw when the request is based on posted actuals.↵↵Three things create drawdown problems: over-drawing (requesting more than posted allowable expenses support), under-drawing (leaving documented costs without requesting reimbursement — which can trigger automatic deobligation near award end dates), and drawing against unallowable costs.↵↵None of these are exotic compliance failures. They are the predictable result of drawdown schedules that fall out of sync with actual expenditure records.

Blackbaud quotes $8,000–$15,000 per year. The actual year-one cost for a mid-size nonprofit is typically $18,000–$45,000 once implementation is included.↵↵Data migration, configuration, and initial training with a Blackbaud-certified implementation partner runs $10,000–$30,000 on top of the software contract. That cost does not appear in the headline price.↵↵The compounding problem is the escalation clause. Standard Blackbaud contracts include annual renewal increases of 8–15%. An organization signing at $8,000/yr faces: Year 1 $8,000 / Year 2 $9,200 / Year 3 $10,580 / Year 4 $12,167. That is a 52% cost increase over four years without any change in usage.↵↵Custom reports, workflow changes, and integration work go through professional services at $150–$250/hr. Organizations that need funder-specific compliance report formats often end up on a recurring services retainer.↵↵Exit terms complete the picture: early termination fees equal to 50–100% of remaining contract value, plus migration assistance billed at professional services rates. Exiting a year-two $10,000/yr contract can cost $5,000–$10,000 in penalties before migration.↵↵The practical budget question is not whether the monthly fee fits. It is whether the platform keeps your process simple enough to avoid added software or consulting spend for the next three to five years.

When evaluating a nonprofit CRM, separate two distinct categories before looking at any vendor feature list.↵↵The first category: donor management features. Constituent records with complete giving history, household and relationship tracking, recurring gift management, LYBUNT/SYBUNT segmentation, automated acknowledgment letters, and retention reporting. Most platforms in this space cover these adequately.↵↵The second category: grant compliance features. Restricted fund tracking with expenditure association, spending tracked against approved budget line items by category, funder-specific financial report generation, and documentation tied to individual transactions. Most donor CRMs do not cover this category at the depth grant-active organizations require.↵↵The operational cost of parallel systems is underestimated at purchase time. The TCJA silo rule turned Form 990-T compliance into a fundamentally different problem for nonprofits with multiple revenue streams.↵↵Before 2018, a nonprofit with a money-losing bookstore and a profitable parking lot could net those activities. Under IRC Section 512(a)(6) — effective for tax years beginning after December 31, 2017 — each unrelated trade or business is calculated separately. The bookstore loss stays in the bookstore silo. The parking lot income is taxed at 21%.↵↵Six steps govern 990-T preparation under the current rules.↵↵Identify unrelated activities: all three elements must be present — trade or business, regularly carried on, and not substantially related to exempt purpose. Gross income of $1,000 from any single silo triggers the filing obligation, even if aggregate UBI nets to zero.↵↵Assign each activity to a silo using its 6-digit NAICS code. Activities within the same code may combine.↵↵Calculate UBTI per silo: subtract directly connected expenses, apply Section 512(b) modifications (dividends, interest, and passive rents are excluded — not deducted, excluded entirely).↵↵Apply pre-TCJA NOL carryforwards: these remain aggregate offsets against total UBTI. Post-TCJA NOLs are silo-specific and can only offset future income in the same silo.↵↵File a separate Schedule A for each silo with $1,000 or more of gross income. The main 990-T aggregates them.↵↵File by the 15th day of the 4th month after fiscal year-end. Pay estimated taxes quarterly when expected liability exceeds $500. Late-filing penalties start at 5% per month, up to 25%.↵↵If your organization tracks revenue by activity type, the silo identification is straightforward. GrantPipe's restricted fund and activity tracking surfaces the categorization your CPA needs to complete the analysis.
