Little Green Light has no compliance reporting.↵↵A free CRM solves the contact database problem. It does not solve the grant compliance problem — which is often the more expensive gap to leave open.↵↵What is your organization using for grant tracking alongside your CRM?

The SEFA (Schedule of Expenditures of Federal Awards) determines how much of your Single Audit is testing versus procedural.↵↵A clean SEFA narrows audit scope and reduces findings. A messy one expands scope, raises cost, and produces findings that could have been avoided.↵↵The most common SEFA error: pass-through awards listed under the state or local agency instead of the prime federal agency. A state-administered CDBG award through HUD belongs under HUD on the SEFA, not under the state housing authority — regardless of who actually sent you the check.↵The second most common error: CFDA/ALN numbers that do not match the current grant agreement or SAM.gov. ALN replaced the CFDA term; both appear in practice but should resolve to the same number.↵The third: expenditure totals that do not reconcile to the Statement of Activities.↵↵GAO's April 2024 analysis (GAO-24-106173) identifies incomplete SEFA among the five most common Single Audit findings. $1.17 trillion in federal spending from 2017–2021 was linked to severe and persistent findings.↵↵Grant coding in the general ledger throughout the year is the single largest predictor of clean SEFA. Organizations with class-level coding in QuickBooks or fund tracking in a purpose-built system can assemble the SEFA from a single export. Organizations without it rebuild it annually from bank records.↵↵Deliver the SEFA draft to your auditor at least 30 days before fieldwork begins.

Grant compliance is not about avoiding doing anything wrong — it is about being able to prove you did everything right.↵↵The compliance obligation starts at award acceptance, not at report time. For federal awards, 2 CFR Part 200 (Uniform Guidance) is the primary framework. It governs three categories: cost principles (what is allowable, allocable, and reasonable under 2 CFR 200 Subpart E), administrative requirements (financial management systems, procurement, property), and audit requirements (the Single Audit threshold of $1,000,000 in federal expenditures per 2 CFR 200.501).↵↵For private foundation grants, the framework is simpler: the grant agreement governs. Most foundations require narrative and financial reports, restrictions on approved spending, and record retention. Foundations do not conduct single audits, but they share information among themselves.↵↵The most frequently cited federal compliance failures: inadequate time-and-effort documentation for personnel costs, missing expenditure documentation, failure to obtain prior approval for budget changes, and inadequate subrecipient monitoring.↵↵Compliance is a coordination problem across development, finance, and program staff — no single department owns the full obligation.↵↵What does your organization use to track the documentation layer across departments?

Givebutter is a fundraising platform. That is an honest description, not a criticism.↵↵It is well-designed for peer-to-peer campaigns, events, and individual donor fundraising — the free core tier is real, and the interface is straightforward for small teams.↵↵The constraint is visible when grants become a meaningful revenue source. A foundation that requires a quarterly budget-vs-actual report will receive something assembled manually in Excel, because Givebutter does not organize data for grant-level reporting. A first federal grant brings 2 CFR 200 compliance requirements that Givebutter has no tools to address.↵↵The operational pattern: a quarterly compliance report for one restricted grant takes two to four hours the first time — and does not get meaningfully faster with repetition, because the source data is not structured for grant reporting.↵↵Organizations that receive restricted grants need fund balance tracking, expense traceability, and funder-facing financial reports. These are not Givebutter features, and they will not become Givebutter features because they are not in the platform's design focus.↵↵The organizations that stay on Givebutter past this inflection point are not making a tool decision. They are paying a labor cost that compounds with every additional grant.

Restricted contribution tracking is a continuous practice, not an end-of-year cleanup exercise.↵↵The organizations that manage restricted funds cleanly do three things throughout the year that others do once at year-end.↵↵First, they capture the restriction at the moment of receipt. The accounting entry (debit cash, credit restricted contribution revenue) must be coded to a specific sub-account representing the particular restriction — not a generic 'with restrictions' bucket. Under ASC 958, unconditional contributions should be recognized when received, even for multi-year grants.↵↵Second, they code every related expenditure to the correct fund at the time the transaction is entered. For personnel costs, time sheets document hours by grant each pay period, and payroll is allocated based on actual time — not on budget percentages. An employee who was 50% on Grant A for nine months and 100% on Grant B for three months should have payroll coded accordingly, not averaged.↵↵Third, they monitor fund balances monthly. A restricted fund balance should never go negative. A negative balance means the organization has spent more from the restricted fund than it contains — either a data entry error or actual misuse of funds.↵↵At year-end, the sum of all restricted fund closing balances must equal the with-donor-restrictions net asset balance on the Statement of Financial Position. Any variance requires a documented explanation before the audit.

A no-cost extension request gets denied for predictable reasons.↵↵The most common: vague justification. 'We need more time to complete project activities' is not a justification — it is a restatement of the request. Program officers look for specific external circumstances that caused the delay and evidence that the remaining work can be completed within the proposed extension.↵↵Most agencies require the NCE request at least 30 days before the period of performance end date. Many prefer 60 days. A request submitted fewer than 10 days before period end will almost always be denied on timing alone.↵↵Strong justifications cite named circumstances: a key position that was vacant from Month X to Month Y, an external disruption that suspended program delivery, a required regulatory approval that arrived later than expected. Weak ones cite internal factors like staff busyness or underestimating project complexity.↵↵The request also needs a spend-down projection showing that sufficient funds remain and a work plan mapping remaining deliverables to the extension timeline. A significant remaining balance in a budget category with no corresponding activity in the extension plan will generate questions.↵↵GrantPipe's free No-Cost Extension Request Template includes all five sections — justification, remaining work plan, spend-down projection, impact statement, and a submission checklist broken down by federal agency (NIH, NSF, HHS, DOL, DOEd, HUD, and private foundations).

The compliance obligation for a federal grant begins at award acceptance and does not end at the final report.↵↵Four things every grant compliance system must demonstrate at any point during the grant period:↵↵That restricted funds are being spent on approved activities. This is not something to reconstruct at report time — it must be visible continuously through real-time fund balance tracking.↵↵That costs are allowable and adequately documented. Under 2 CFR Part 200.403, a cost must be necessary and reasonable, allocable to the grant activity, and adequately documented. For personnel costs, that means contemporaneous time records for each pay period showing the grant allocation — not reconstructed estimates.↵↵That required reports were submitted on time. Missing a reporting deadline is a compliance finding independent of whether the underlying spending was compliant. Late federal reports can also delay drawdown from the Payment Management System.↵↵That records are retained for the required period. Federal grants require a minimum of three years from submission of the final expenditure report under 2 CFR 200.334. Some programs specify longer. Records must be organized for reconstruction by someone unfamiliar with the grant, years after closeout.↵↵Generic accounting software handles the general ledger. Grant compliance software handles the grant-level obligations that the ledger cannot produce — budget vs. actual by individual grant, funder-formatted reports, and documentation organized at the transaction level.↵↵What is your organization's current approach to the documentation layer?

Evaluating a nonprofit CRM: five tradeoffs worth writing down before the demo.↵↵Grant management coverage. Most CRMs — HubSpot, Bloomerang, Little Green Light — record a grant as a contribution entry. None of them manage post-award compliance: restricted fund tracking, funder-formatted reports, or budget-vs-actual by grant. Bloomerang starts at $125/month with no grant features at any tier. If grant income is operationally significant, this gap defines the evaluation.↵↵Pricing structure under growth. Bloomerang's pricing scales with constituent records — the cost increases as the database grows, which penalizes an organization for successful development. Little Green Light uses the same per-record model. Flat-rate pricing (HubSpot's paid tiers, GrantPipe at $329–$1,079/month) is more predictable.↵↵Implementation cost on nominally free options. Salesforce's TechSoup program provides 10 free licenses but not a functional CRM. Implementation, configuration, and training run $30,000–$100,000 before the system is usable. The license cost is zero; the total cost of deployment is not.↵↵What the free tier actually includes. HubSpot's free tier provides unlimited contacts with no time limit — the only genuinely free nonprofit CRM option. The free tier excludes advanced reporting, sequences, and most automation. Evaluate whether the free-tier capabilities match your actual daily workflow, not the capabilities you anticipate needing later.↵↵Reporting workflow fit. The right filter is not feature count. It is whether the system supports the handoff between development, finance, and executive reporting without requiring an additional spreadsheet layer. A platform that looks inexpensive in a comparison table can generate weekly cleanup work if staff need exports or manual reconciliations to produce a funder report.

Food banks receiving USDA TEFAP funds report up through the state distributing agency (SDA), which files Form FNS-667 with USDA Food and Nutrition Service.↵↵The local food bank's job is not to file FNS-667 — it is to maintain the source records the SDA needs to file accurately, and to survive the monitoring visit that the SDA and single auditors conduct.↵↵Four records drive every TEFAP compliance determination: the commodity receipt log, the household distribution log, the subrecipient transfer log, and the loss and adjustment report. Every TEFAP finding in a single audit traces back to a gap in those four documents.↵↵The month-end reconciliation equation: beginning inventory + SDA receipts + other USDA receipts − distributions to households − transfers to subrecipient agencies − documented losses = ending inventory. State tolerance for unexplained variances is typically 1%, though state plans vary. A 12% variance with no documented cause is a finding and typically a repayment demand at the USDA-published per-pound valuation.↵↵TEFAP commodity value counts as federal award expenditure at the USDA-published per-pound valuation and counts toward the $1,000,000 single audit threshold under 2 CFR 200.501. A mid-sized food bank receiving commodity allocations may push over the threshold without receiving a single dollar of cash administrative funds.↵↵Regional food banks distributing to partner pantries are pass-through entities under 2 CFR 200.332. Inadequate records at a partner pantry generate a finding against the regional food bank.↵↵GrantPipe tracks restricted fund balances, grant reporting calendars, and audit-ready activity logs — built for food banks managing TEFAP alongside foundation and government grants. Start a free trial at grantpipe.com.

The other half comes from unrestricted dollars that could have funded program delivery.↵36% of nonprofits ended FY2024 with operating deficits — the highest rate in a decade. The indirect cost gap is not the only cause, but it contributes to that number directly.↵What your finance team can control is the compliance labor cost on top of the indirect gap. CharityEngine does not publish its pricing — any budget comparison requires completing a full sales cycle before you see a number.↵That two-to-four week delay is not a minor inconvenience. For nonprofits planning a fiscal year budget, it means committing staff time to a demo process before getting the one figure you need to decide whether to continue.↵All-in-one platforms carry a second cost that the headline price (once revealed) still doesn't show: you pay for feature depth across donor management, events, advocacy, and payment processing regardless of which functions your organization actually uses.↵For nonprofits whose primary complexity is grant compliance rather than event and advocacy operations, the math rarely works in their favor.↵CharityEngine's Enterprise tier includes compliance tools, but restricted fund tracking, expenditure reporting tied to individual grants, and compliance documentation for program officers are not primary platform capabilities.↵Organizations managing three or more active grants should ask one specific question during any demo: can the platform generate a report showing expenditures by restriction against each grant budget? The answer tells you immediately whether the compliance gap is real for your use case.↵Pricing transparency matters as much as feature lists. Under 2 CFR 200.430(i), employees working solely on a single federal award may certify time semi-annually. Employees split across multiple awards — or across an award and non-award duties — must certify more frequently.↵Most organizations over-apply semi-annual certification. An employee working 80% on one federal grant and 20% on administrative duties is not a single-award employee. Monthly certification is required for that person.↵Single Audit fieldwork tests this directly. Auditors look at employee classification, then at certification frequency. A mismatch is a finding.↵The most defensible system: certify monthly for everyone on federal awards, distribute within two weeks of period end, require return within one week of distribution.↵The certification itself must reflect an after-the-fact distribution of actual time — not a projection. A form that shows only the employee name and grant number without actual time percentages is not compliant.↵The reconciliation step that most organizations skip: compare certification percentages to what was posted to payroll for the same period. If an employee certified 50% on Grant A and payroll shows 55%, the posting is wrong and needs a correcting entry.↵Personnel cost findings are among the most frequent in federal single audits. Inadequate time documentation and misallocated charges appear in GAO reports every cycle.↵The system itself is not complicated. Running it every month, without exception, is where most teams struggle.

UBTI — Unrelated Business Taxable Income — applies when a tax-exempt organization earns money from a commercial activity that fails all three of these tests: it is a trade or business, it is regularly carried on, and it is not substantially related to the exempt purpose.↵All three must apply. Failing any one of them means the income is not UBTI.↵The word "substantially" in the third test is where most analysis concentrates. The question is not whether the profits fund the mission. The question is whether the activity itself contributes importantly to accomplishing the exempt purpose.↵A nonprofit hospital's parking garage open to the general public: UBTI. A university bookstore selling required textbooks to enrolled students: program service revenue. The same bookstore selling branded merchandise to the general public: potentially UBTI on that portion.↵Since the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017, each unrelated business activity is treated as a separate silo under IRC Section 512(a)(6). Losses from one activity cannot offset income from another. The strategy of using a rental property loss to shelter a profitable parking lot is no longer available.↵The Form 990-T filing threshold is $1,000 in gross UBTI income. The tax rate is 21%, regardless of the organization's exempt status.↵More than 30,000 tax-exempt organizations file Form 990-T annually. The distinction between program service revenue and UBTI is one of the most consequential — and most frequently miscategorized — lines in nonprofit tax compliance.

EveryAction (now Bonterra) was built for political campaigns and issue advocacy organizations. Its core capabilities — petition management, email to elected officials, volunteer mobilization at scale — are genuine and well-designed for that use case.↵That design is precisely the problem for most nonprofits evaluating it.↵G2 and Capterra reviewers report annual EveryAction costs for nonprofits ranging from $5,000 to $30,000+ depending on organization size and features. Implementation fees are standard and often significant.↵A workforce development nonprofit or a community health center does not need petition management. It needs donor records, restricted fund tracking, and grant expenditure reporting that a program officer can verify.↵EveryAction includes basic grant tracking — award records and deadline reminders. It does not include grant lifecycle management: no restricted fund allocation, no expenditure tracking against grant-specific budgets, no compliance report generation tied to funder requirements.↵The FASB ASC 958 model for tracking restricted versus unrestricted net assets is not a feature that advocacy platforms prioritize.↵When a platform is designed for advocacy and priced for that complexity, organizations that buy it for donor management and grant compliance pay for capabilities they will never use while still lacking the ones they need.↵The better question before entering any vendor process: does the platform's origin match your operational model?

Under 2 CFR 200.303, federal grantees must maintain effective internal controls over federal awards. "Effective" means written, operational, and demonstrable — not a reference to a general purchasing policy.↵Most nonprofits have a purchasing policy. Grant spending controls are a specific layer on top of it.↵The distinction: a purchasing policy governs how the organization buys things generally. Grant spending controls govern expenditures against specific restricted funds, within specific approved budgets, subject to specific funder requirements.↵Organizations that point to their purchasing policy when asked about grant spending controls are describing a gap, not a system.↵The authorization framework needs three defined levels: routine expenditures within approved categories, non-routine expenditures requiring finance or executive review, and items that require written funder prior approval before the expenditure is made.↵Segregation of duties under 2 CFR 200.303 requires distributing the initiation, authorization, recording, and reconciliation functions across different individuals. For small teams where full segregation is not achievable, compensating controls substitute — typically a second-level review documented in writing and actually performed.↵The test that matters most: before your auditor arrives, pull 10 recent grant expenditures and verify each one had a documented prior approval from the correct person under your authorization matrix. If any fail, that is a finding preview.

A grant kickoff meeting done in 20 minutes without an agenda is not a kickoff. It is a formality that leaves the program lead, finance staff, and grants manager with different understandings of the same award.↵A useful kickoff covers seven specific items before any spending begins: award overview, approved budget walkthrough line by line, fund restrictions and prior approval requirements, the complete reporting schedule with named owners, roles and responsibilities for each compliance function, grant management system setup confirmation, and an open items log.↵The approved budget walkthrough is where most kickoffs fail. The finance director needs to know what each line covers and what documentation is required. The program lead needs to know what cannot be charged even if it seems reasonable. Running through the budget together, with both in the room, surfaces the interpretation gaps before they become misallocation findings.↵The reporting schedule section should produce a documented calendar: every report type, reporting period, due date, prep start date, who prepares, who reviews, and who submits. Not a verbal agreement — a table in the meeting record.↵The open items log matters because decisions made verbally in a kickoff meeting have a way of being remembered differently by different people six months later. Writing them down, assigning owners, and setting due dates converts a conversation into a compliance record.↵GrantPipe's free Grant Kickoff Meeting Template covers all seven agenda items with built-in worksheets and decision logs. grantpipe.com/free.

A $50,000 grant is not $50,000 for your mission. After compliance costs, it is closer to $40,000.↵The Nonprofit Finance Fund's "net grant" concept quantifies what grants managers already know: compliance labor eats a significant share of every award. The median nonprofit spends 6-8 hours per grant per year on reporting alone. Across a portfolio of 20 grants, that is 120-160 hours annually — before you count application prep, mid-term reports, and closeout documentation.↵That time is not free. An in-house grants manager costs $67,000-$87,000 annually. Outsourced compliance support runs $132-$159 per hour.↵The indirect cost gap makes it structural. GrantStation's 2024 survey of 2,306 organizations found 42% of non-government funders cap indirect reimbursement at 10% or below, while actual overhead runs 25-35%. Organizations absorb the 10-20 point gap from unrestricted revenue.↵Two things to audit inside your own portfolio: the hours your team spends on compliance per grant, and what you are actually recovering in indirect costs versus what you are spending.↵If reporting time averages more than 4 hours per grant per cycle, there is a process problem — not just a software problem. The first step is identifying which funders have unique format requirements versus which ones could share a common data pull. Standardizing what can be standardized before automating cuts more time than software alone.↵Software can then reduce that further. The structural indirect cost gap is a policy problem. The hours problem is solvable.

Federal grant draws are compliance events, not routine cash transfers. Each one must be supported by actual expenditures in the accounting system, reconciled monthly, and documented with enough detail that an auditor can trace every dollar from the draw request to the underlying expense.↵The two payment methods — advance and reimbursement — carry different timing requirements. Under 2 CFR 200.305(b)(3), advance cash must be disbursed within 30 calendar days. Cash held beyond 30 days is potentially subject to interest calculation and remittance. Interest earned on federal cash above $500 per year must be returned to the federal government.↵The reconciliation that prevents cash management single audit findings: monthly, cumulative draws to date should equal cumulative expenditures recorded in the general ledger for that award. If draws exceed expenditures, the organization is holding federal cash it has not yet spent — a compliance issue under 2 CFR 200.305 that requires the excess to be returned or offset against the next draw.↵Most organizations discover these gaps at audit time. Gaps accumulate monthly and become much harder to trace and correct in bulk than they would have been at each month-end close.↵Each draw should have a documented log entry: award number, payment system request number, date submitted, period covered, federal share claimed, the expenditure report that supported the draw, and the system confirmation. This log is the source data for the Federal Cash Transactions section of the SF-425.↵GrantPipe tracks draw history per award, surfaces reconciliation gaps at month-end close, and generates the draw log automatically. See it at grantpipe.com.

Massachusetts's $500,000 audit threshold is lower than the federal $1,000,000 Single Audit threshold — and most nonprofits do not realize that gap until they get a deficiency notice.↵↵A mid-sized nonprofit at $600,000 in gross support and revenue needs a CPA audit for Form PC purposes even though it is nowhere near the federal trigger.↵↵The Massachusetts Attorney General's Public Charities Division administers Form PC under M.G.L. Chapter 12 Sections 8E through 8M.↵↵Fees run from $35 (under $100,000) to $2,000 (above $100 million) — using the wrong tier triggers a deficiency notice with a 30-60 day cure window.↵↵Calendar-year filers typically file under the six-month extension, putting the practical deadline at November 15 — which is also when the audit engagement needs to be finished.↵↵Most rejections come down to four things: missing audit, wrong fee, missing Form 990 attachment, and late filing without documented extension.↵↵GrantPipe tracks Form PC deadlines alongside federal SF-425 cadence and restricted-fund workflow in one operating record — the compliance calendar does not require a separate system.

"Grant management software" means two completely different things depending on which side of the transaction you are on.↵↵Submittable is an application intake and review platform — it exists for organizations that receive applications, score them, and award funds.↵↵GrantPipe is a donor and grant compliance platform — it exists for organizations that apply for grants and need to operate the awards they win.↵↵Most $500K-$10M nonprofits are applicant-side. They do not need to run Submittable themselves.↵↵What they need is a tool that connects donor records, restricted fund balances, SF-425 deadlines, and the Single Audit threshold raised to $1,000,000 under the October 2024 Uniform Guidance revision.↵↵The two products do not meaningfully compete. They sit on opposite sides of the grant transaction.↵↵If you have been comparing them, the useful question is: are you primarily receiving applications or managing the grants you win?

A Single Audit finding is not a disaster. Responding to one without a Corrective Action Plan is.↵↵Under 2 CFR 200.511(c), every finding requires a written CAP that identifies five things: auditee position (agree or disagree), specific corrective action, responsible party, completion date, and the finding reference number.↵↵"We will strengthen our controls" does not satisfy any of those five requirements.↵↵The CAP goes to the Federal Audit Clearinghouse with the Single Audit package — due the earlier of 30 days after the auditor's report or nine months after fiscal year end, per 2 CFR 200.512(a)(1).↵↵A finding in two consecutive audits is a repeat finding. That triggers specific conditions under 2 CFR 200.208: prior approval for draws, enhanced monitoring, possible high-risk designation.↵↵Break the repeat pattern before the second audit, not after.↵↵Every questioned cost decision — repay, dispute, or request allowance — should be communicated to the awarding agency alongside the CAP, not months later.

Every nonprofit expense has two labels. Most finance teams only track one.↵↵The natural label says what you bought: salaries, rent, supplies, depreciation.↵↵The functional label says why you spent it: program services, management and general, or fundraising.↵↵FASB ASC 958-205 requires nonprofits to present expenses by both classifications. Acceptable methods under ASC 958-720 include time studies, FTE allocations, square footage, and direct charging.↵↵The most common error: treating the Executive Director as 100% program. Most EDs perform a mix of program oversight, management, and fundraising. Allocating the full salary to programs inflates the program ratio and is a routine audit finding.↵↵Stale percentages are the second most common error — applying the same 70/20/10 split for five years without a review. ASC 958-720 requires methods that reflect current resource consumption.↵↵Roughly 20% of Form 990 amendments filed by public charities relate to reclassification between functional expense categories, per Urban Institute analysis.↵↵The methodology must be documented, consistently applied, and defensible under audit.

Fluxx does not publish pricing. Fluxx is flexible — which means someone has to maintain the configuration. That ongoing cost does not appear in the sales quote.↵↵For the grantseeker tier at $20,000/year, the real first-year cost with implementation, migration, and a separate donor CRM (which Fluxx does not include) lands closer to $35,000 to $50,000.↵↵G2 reviewers describe implementations taking 3-6 months with dedicated internal IT support.↵↵The honest budget conversation starts with: what is the total annual cost of Fluxx plus a donor CRM plus the administrator time to maintain both?↵↵For a portfolio of 5-15 grants, that question rarely produces a number that the platform's capabilities can justify.

The evidence that survives a Single Audit is not created in the weeks before the auditor arrives. It is created throughout the year.↵↵Time records completed every pay period rather than reconstructed quarterly. Invoices attached to expenditure entries at payment rather than filed separately. Subrecipient monitoring completed on schedule rather than assembled retroactively.↵↵For a financial statement audit, the request list includes: general ledger, bank reconciliations for each month, board minutes, major contracts and grant agreements, fixed asset schedules, and functional expense allocation methodology.↵↵A Single Audit adds: the Schedule of Expenditures of Federal Awards (SEFA), all federal award agreements, personnel time records by grant, procurement records for federally funded purchases, and subrecipient monitoring documentation.↵↵The SEFA preparation should start 60-90 days before fiscal year end — not at year end. Missing federal programs (often passthrough awards from state agencies) result in audit adjustments.↵↵The formal evidence binder organized by auditor request categories reduces fieldwork duration and demonstrates that records were maintained contemporaneously.↵↵Organizations that close audits quickly are not doing more work at audit time. They are doing less — because the work was already done.

CRM licensing is only 5-15% of total cost. The rest shows up in implementation, training, data migration, ongoing administration, and integrations.↵↵A self-implemented mid-market CRM with a consulting partner for implementation runs $15,000-$50,000 over three years for a typical mid-sized nonprofit.↵↵Salesforce NPSP with a consulting partner for the same organization: $50,000-$150,000 or more — implementation is $55,000+ alone, plus a fractional admin retainer running $24,000/year.↵↵The retraining problem is the cost category most frequently omitted from vendor proposals. Staff turnover means CRM training has a shelf life. When the Development Director who was trained on the system leaves, that institutional knowledge leaves with them.↵↵Integration maintenance is the third surprise: every connection between a CRM and an accounting system, email platform, or payment processor is a maintenance liability. Pennsylvania's BCO-10 charitable registration has a deadline that most nonprofits get wrong: 315 days after fiscal year end, not the end of the calendar year.↵↵For a December 31 fiscal year end, that puts the renewal due date around November 11.↵↵Fees scale with gross annual contributions: $15 at the bottom tier (under $25,000), $250 at the top tier (above $1,000,000). Using the wrong tier is one of the five most common rejection reasons.↵↵The audit attachment threshold matches the top fee tier: audited financial statements are required above $1,000,000 in gross contributions. Reviewed statements apply at mid-tiers; compiled statements at lower tiers.↵↵A nonprofit that crosses $1,000,000 for the first time needs to engage a CPA early — an audit started the month before the 315-day deadline rarely finishes without rush billing.↵↵Pennsylvania accepts the Uniform Registration Statement (URS) in place of BCO-10, with a PA-specific supplement and fee. Organizations filing in multiple URS states use this to reduce duplicate data entry.↵↵The BCO-10 fee and audit thresholds can shift when the Department of State updates the schedule — verify against the current schedule before each filing, not the prior year.
